title: Game development with Unity for beginners
summary: A first course in making games for students who have never coded. They build three small games by following along, then design, build, playtest and share one of their own.
brief:
Game development with Unity for complete beginners: a 14-week asynchronous online course for undergraduates, 3 credits, about 9 hours of work a week. Students have never written code and never made a game. They work alone on their own Windows or Mac computer; there are no live sessions, and a student who follows the week's page with nobody to ask must be able to finish the week. Software, all free: Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6) installed through Unity Hub with a Unity Personal license, and Visual Studio Code with the Unity extension for writing C#. Projects start from the Universal 3D template, except the 2D game, which starts from the Universal 2D template. Version facts every page must respect: new projects use the Input System package only, so the old Input class (Input.GetAxis, Input.GetKey) throws an error and input is read with Keyboard.current or an InputAction; a Rigidbody's velocity is linearVelocity; on-screen text is TextMeshPro; an object is found with FindAnyObjectByType. My attached version notes list the exact menu names and code for this version: follow them. Students build three small games by following along, then one of their own. Game 1, Orb Collector (weeks 2 to 5): roll a ball around an arena, collect spinning pickups, show a score and a win message. Game 2, Dodge (weeks 6 to 9): move a player to avoid hazards that spawn faster and faster, with lives, game over and restart, sound, particles, and a start menu. Game 3, Hop (weeks 10 and 11): a 2D platformer with a tilemap level, jumping, sprite animation and collectibles. Weeks 12 to 14: each student designs, builds, playtests and shares a small game of their own. Week by week: 1, setting up Unity and a tour of the Editor, building a small scene from primitive shapes; 2, GameObjects and components, materials and light, physics with Rigidbody and colliders; 3, the first C# script: variables, Start and Update, the Console and how to read an error; 4, input and movement: vectors, forces, FixedUpdate, a camera that follows; 5, collisions, triggers and scoring: if statements, tags, counting, text on screen, winning; 6, prefabs and spawning: Instantiate, random positions, timers, destroying objects; 7, game state and UI: lives, game over, restart, methods, buttons; 8, sound, particles and game feel; 9, menus and scenes, building the game so a classmate can run it on Windows or Mac, then finishing and playtesting Dodge with a twist of your own; 10, 2D: sprites, tilemaps, 2D physics, running and jumping; 11, 2D animation, collectibles and a camera that follows, and the proposal for your own game; 12, scoping and prototyping your own game, and how to debug; 13, playtesting with classmates, iterating and polishing; 14, showcase, reflection, and what to learn next. Every week has the same shape: a guided build that leaves something working on screen, a challenge without steps, a self-check quiz, a forum post that shares a screenshot or short clip of the build (and replies after trying two classmates' ideas), and something to submit. Grading: weekly builds 40% (submitted as a short screen recording and a screenshot), forum participation 15%, the Dodge game with your own twist, due in week 9, 15%, and the final game project 30% (proposal in week 11, playable prototype in week 12, final build and showcase post in week 14), with rubrics for the two games.
Before planning, the teacher answered:
- Should Orb Collector and Dodge be built with 3D keyboard controls, or should Dodge move the player on a flat plane? Both 3D; Dodge uses a flat arena with top-down keyboard movement
- Where will students get the art and sound for Dodge and Hop in weeks 8 to 11? Folio points to free CC0 packs, such as Kenney
- How are the weekly build, forum post and challenge submitted and graded in the course platform? Upload to the LMS; graded complete or incomplete

blocks.text: Welcome. In this course you will make games in Unity, even if you have never written code or built a game. You start with a small scene made of simple shapes. Over the term you build three small games by following along, then design, build, test and share a game of your own. You work alone, at your own pace, on your own computer, and there are no live sessions. Each week has its own page that tells you everything you need, so if you follow it you can finish the week without asking anyone. If you get stuck, the forum is there, and the instructor reads it.

items: Read this page to the end, so you know how a week runs and what you will install.

Check that your computer can run Unity: open Unity’s system requirements page for Unity 6.6 (it is in the Unity Manual at docs.unity3d.com; search the web for Unity 6.6 system requirements) and compare it with your computer. Do this before you download anything.
Create a free Unity account, then install Unity Hub from the Unity website. The Week 1 page gives every step for this and for the next two items, so you can do them from there.
In Unity Hub, open Settings (the gear at the top right), choose Licenses, then Add license, and add a Unity Personal license. It is free.
In Unity Hub, install Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6) from the Installs section, then install Visual Studio Code and its Unity extension.
Open the course forum, find the introductions thread, and write a short hello. Then open this week’s page and start the first build.

items.meaning: The instructor posts an announcement and the week’s page goes live. Read the page through once, then start on the build. You will download any files from the page.

Work through the page step by step and build along with it. Give about 9 hours to the whole week, including building, reading, the forum and submitting. Spread it over several days rather than leaving it to the end.
Write your first forum post for the week. Say what you built, what went well, and where you got stuck or what surprised you.

Finish your build. Reply to two classmates’ posts with something useful, such as a tip, an answer to a question or a kind and specific comment. Do the week’s challenge and the self-check quiz; the quiz is practice with instant feedback and does not count toward your grade. If something breaks, the week’s Stuck? list is the first place to look, and the recap is what to reread before the next week.
Submit the week’s graded work online. In most weeks that is your weekly build: a short screen recording of your game running and a screenshot or two. All other work for the week is due by then too.

Your own Windows or Mac computer, with an internet connection for downloads and the forum. Before installing, check the system requirements pages for Unity 6.6 (in the Unity Manual at docs.unity3d.com) and for Visual Studio Code (at code.visualstudio.com/docs) to see what your computer must have, including free disk space. Cost: whatever you already own.
The free program that installs and opens Unity. Download it from the Unity website (unity.com) after creating a free Unity account. Cost: free.

Install it from the Installs section of Unity Hub. Use this version all term, so your screen matches the pages. After you open a new project, the window title shows Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1). Cost: free with a Unity Personal license.
Add it in Unity Hub under Settings (the gear at the top right) > Licenses > Add license. It comes with your Unity account. Cost: free.

items.term: Visual Studio Code with the Unity extension
items.meaning: The editor where you write C# code. Download Visual Studio Code from code.visualstudio.com, then add the Unity extension from inside it. Cost: free.

Any tool that can record your screen and save a short video, such as the one built into your operating system. You will use it each week to record your build running. In week 8 the recording should carry the game’s sound if your recorder can do that. Cost: free. Three more things come later in the course. From week 8 your games make sound, so you need speakers or headphones. In week 9 you share your game through a download link, for example the OneDrive or Google Drive of your school account, and you need one person to play it, a classmate or anyone at home. There are no books to buy: a few weeks suggest a chapter from a book your library may have, and these are optional.

You submit a weekly build in ten of the fourteen weeks (weeks 1 to 8, 10 and 13): a short screen recording and one or two screenshots, sometimes with a short note, uploaded online. In week 9 the Dodge game takes its place, and in weeks 11, 12 and 14 a part of your final project does. Each one is graded complete or incomplete, so the aim is to show your build working. Together the builds make up 40% of the course grade.

Each weekly module has a first forum post by Thursday and replies by Sunday night. Full marks need a first post by Thursday and two helpful replies by Sunday; late or one-line posts earn half. These posts and replies, across all the weekly modules, make up 15% of the course grade.

items.term: Dodge game with your own twist (15%)
items.meaning: One piece, due Sunday night of week 9 and scored with a rubric. You finish Dodge with a start menu and a build a classmate can run, watch someone play it, and add one change of your own to how it plays, such as a new hazard or a new rule. It makes up 15% of the course grade.

The game you design, build, playtest and share yourself, in three parts: a proposal in week 11, a playable prototype in week 12, and the final build with a showcase post in week 14. The full brief and rubric are in the module Showcase, reflection and next steps; read them when you start your proposal. It makes up 30% of the course grade.

blocks.text: Ask in the course Q&A forum. Search it first, because someone may already have your answer. A good question lets a reader fix your problem without asking you anything back. Include what you did, step by step; what you expected to happen; what actually happened; the exact error text, copied word for word from the Console; and a screenshot of the Editor showing the problem. Put the week in the title of your post. If you solve it yourself, post how, because it helps the next student.
What to expect from your instructor

items: Post an announcement when each week opens, saying what the week covers and what is due.
Answer questions in the forum within one working day.
Give feedback on submitted work within a week of the submission.
Read the weekly forum threads and join in where a student is stuck or a good idea deserves attention.
Your name, and how students can reach you.
Your office hours, or how students can ask for a one-to-one conversation.
A late work policy: how late work is treated and how to ask for more time.
A policy on what help and AI tools students may use, including for writing code.
An academic integrity policy, including how students should credit code or assets they take from tutorials or other sources.
An accessibility and accommodations statement, and how students ask for adjustments.

The link to the course Q&A forum and the name of the introductions thread. Open a forum thread for each week, and in week 9 a thread where students find a playtest partner on the same kind of computer. Record the short talk for each week, or tell students the transcript on the page replaces it. Create an assignment in the LMS for each weekly build, for Dodge game with your own twist (week 9) and for the three parts of the final project, and paste in each brief and rubric. Decide where students upload builds to share them, and tell students to run only builds from this course. Check whether your library has the optional chapters (Hocking, Swink); the Nystrom chapter is free online. Say how complete or incomplete and the rubric levels become points.

policies:
Weekly builds are submitted as a short screen recording and a screenshot.

Weekly builds are uploaded to the LMS and graded complete or incomplete. The Dodge game and the final project are scored with rubrics.

l_c1af38aae15b.title: Set up Unity and build a scene
l_c1af38aae15b.summary: Install Unity and Visual Studio Code, tour the Editor, and build a scene from primitive shapes; submit a screen recording and screenshot.
keyIdeas: The Editor is a set of windows, and each answers one question: what is in my scene (Hierarchy), what does it look like (Scene and Game views), what are its settings (Inspector), what files do I have (Project window) and what went wrong (Console).
Everything in a scene is a GameObject, and its Transform says where it is, how it is turned and how big it is. Typing exact Transform numbers lets you rebuild the same scene on any computer.
What the Game view shows depends on three things together: the camera’s position and rotation, its field of view, and the shape of the Game view itself.
Capturing your screen, as a picture and as a short recording, is a skill you will use all term, so you learn it on a small scene.

vocabulary.definition: The launcher that holds your Unity versions, your license and your list of projects.
The Unity program you build games in, made of windows such as the Hierarchy and Inspector.
The folder that holds everything for one game, including its scenes and files.
One saved level or screen of a game, holding the objects in it.
Anything that exists in a scene, such as a camera, a light or a cube.
A ready-made basic shape in Unity, such as a cube, sphere, capsule, cylinder or plane.
The part of every GameObject that holds its position, rotation and scale.
The window that lists every object in the open scene.
The window that shows the settings of whatever is selected.
The window where Unity shows messages, warnings and errors.
How wide an angle, in degrees, the camera can see.
The shape of the picture as width to height, such as 16:9.

study.overview: You can now get Unity 6.6 and Visual Studio Code running, open a Universal 3D project, name the six windows you will use every week, and build a scene by typing exact Transform numbers. You also know how to frame the Main Camera and capture your work as a screenshot and a short recording. Reread this page before next week, when you give these shapes components, materials and light.

points.heading: Name the Editor window that answers your question
points.explanation: The Editor is a set of windows, and each answers one question. The Hierarchy lists what is in your scene. The Scene and Game views show what it looks like: Scene is where you build, and Game is what the player sees through the Main Camera. The Inspector shows the settings of whatever you have selected. The Project window holds your files, and the Console shows what went wrong. Example: you want the settings of Tower. Click Tower in the Hierarchy, then read its Transform in the Inspector. If a window goes missing, choose Window > Layouts > Default.

points.heading: Place any GameObject with its Transform
points.explanation: Everything in a scene is a GameObject, and its Transform holds Position (where its center is), Rotation (how far it is turned, in degrees) and Scale (how big it is, as a multiplier). Position is the center, so a shape rests on the ground when its Position Y is half its height after scaling. Example: a Cylinder is 2 units tall at Scale 1, so at Scale Y 3 it is 6 units tall and Tower needs Position Y 3. A Cube at Scale Y 3 is 3 tall, so its center is at 1.5, as with Wall_Back. Typing the same numbers rebuilds the same scene on any computer. New objects appear where the Scene view is looking, so type their Position values first.

points.heading: Control what the Game view shows
points.explanation: The Game view depends on three things together: the camera’s position and rotation, its Field of View, and the shape of the Game view. Change any one and the picture changes. Example: with Game view set to 16:9 Aspect, Field of View 60, and the Main Camera at Position 0, 16, -16 with Rotation 45, 0, 0, the whole 20 by 20 courtyard fits in the picture. If the picture is cropped, check the aspect first, then each camera number in turn. Before you press Play, remember that Play runs the scene like a player, so click it again to stop before you edit. Changes made during Play are thrown away.

points.heading: Capture your work as a picture and a recording
points.explanation: You will show your work this way all term, so it is worth doing well now. Put Unity in the state you want to show: the Courtyard scene open, the Game tab selected, 16:9 Aspect and Play not pressed. Take a screenshot of the whole Editor. Then record about ten seconds of pressing Play, watching and pressing Play again. Open both files to check them. The picture should show the framed courtyard, and the recording should play. Both are what you submit for this week’s Weekly builds.

page.text: Every game you make this term lives inside the Unity Editor, so this week you get it running and learn your way around. This is where the course starts, so there is nothing to catch up on. You will install Unity 6.6 and Visual Studio Code, open a new project and learn the names of the windows you will use every day. Then you will build a small walled courtyard from simple shapes, placing each one by typing exact numbers. By Sunday night you will have a saved scene called Courtyard that shows everything in one view, and you will know how to capture it as a screenshot and a screen recording.

page.text: You will spend a term inside Unity, so start by seeing what this week builds, how the course runs and what you need at your desk.

page.alt: The instructor welcomes you, explains how each week works, and previews the Editor windows and the Courtyard scene.
page.shows: The instructor at a desk, speaking to camera. Cut in the finished Courtyard Game view when the courtyard is described, and an empty Unity Editor with its windows labeled Hierarchy, Scene, Game, Inspector, Project and Console when the windows are named.
page.transcript:
Hello, and welcome. Over this term you will make games in Unity, a free tool that real studios use for everything from phone games to big releases. You do not need to have written code or made a game before. If you can follow a page carefully, you can do this.

Here is how the course works. Every week is a page like this one. You work through it alone, whenever suits you. I do not lecture. I post an announcement at the start of the week, I answer questions in the forum, and I give feedback on your work. The page is written so you can finish the week without asking anyone. Each part ends with a checkpoint that tells you what you should see on screen, and what it looks like when something has gone wrong.

The rhythm is the same all term. Your first forum post is due on Thursday. Replies and everything else are due on Sunday night. Start early. Installing Unity means a big download, and that is the slowest part of this week.

What will you make? You will build small games by following along. First, a game where you roll a ball around an arena and collect spinning pickups. Then a game where you dodge hazards that fall faster and faster. Then a platformer in two dimensions. After that you design, build, test and share a small game of your own.

This week is about the ground you stand on. You will install Unity Hub, the launcher that manages your Unity versions, and then Unity 6.6 itself. You will install Visual Studio Code, where you will write code later in the course. Then you will create a project and learn the windows. The Hierarchy lists everything in your scene. The Scene view is where you look around and build. The Game view shows what a player will see. The Inspector shows the settings of whatever you have selected. The Project window holds your files, and the Console, beside it, shows messages.

Then you will build a small walled courtyard from simple shapes. Every object has a Transform, which is its position, its rotation and its scale. You will type exact numbers instead of dragging. Numbers are the same on your screen and mine, so when the page says the tower sits at 0, 3, 0, yours will too.

One habit before you start: save often. In Unity that is Control S on Windows, or Command S on a Mac. Now go on to the next part.

page.text: How the course is graded

items: Weekly builds: 40% of the course grade.
Forum participation: 15%.
Dodge game with your own twist: 15%.
Final game project: 30%.

page.text: How each week runs

Each week is one page like this. Your first forum post is due by Thursday. Replies and all other work are due by Sunday night. The instructor posts an announcement at the start of the week, answers questions in the forum and gives feedback on your work. Next week’s page opens on the same pattern.
What you need

items: A Windows or Mac computer of your own, with a keyboard and mouse. A trackpad works, but a mouse with a scroll wheel makes the Scene view easier.
A reliable internet connection for large downloads this week.
About 20 GB of free disk space for Unity, your projects and your recordings.
An email address you can check, for a free Unity ID.
No coding and no game experience. All the software is free: Unity Hub, Unity 6.6 with a Unity Personal license, and Visual Studio Code.

page.text: This page is written for Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6, shown as 6000.6.4f1 in the Editor’s title bar) and the Universal 3D template. A different 6000.6 patch number is fine. If your Editor is another version, such as 6.5 or 6.7, or your project uses another template, menus and fields will not match the page. Install 6.6 beside it from Unity Hub and use that one for the whole course. If Unity Hub ever offers to upgrade a project to another version, say no.
Make your course folder
A folder keeps every project in one place you can find. The steps differ by system, so follow the one for yours.
On Windows

items.text: Press the Windows key and E together to open **File Explorer**.
In the list on the left, click **Documents**.
Right-click an empty space in the main area and choose **New** > **Folder**.
Type UnityCourse and press Enter.

page.text: On a Mac

items.text: Click the Finder icon in the Dock.
In the sidebar, click **Documents**.
Choose **File** > **New Folder** from the menu bar, or press Shift, Command and N together.
Type UnityCourse and press Return.

page.text: You should see a folder named UnityCourse inside Documents. It is empty for now. If it is missing, you probably created it inside another folder, so open that folder and look there.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text: Windows only: if the path above the folder list contains OneDrive, Windows is syncing Documents to the cloud, and Unity projects stored there can be slow or fail to open. Fix: in File Explorer open **This PC**, then **Local Disk (C:)**, create a folder named UnityCourse there and use that folder wherever this week says UnityCourse.
Install Unity Hub, add your license and install Unity 6.6
Unity Hub is the launcher that holds your Unity versions, your license and your projects, so everything else this term starts here.

items.text: In your web browser, go to **unity.com/download**.
Click the download button for your system, Windows or Mac.
On Windows, double-click the downloaded file and follow the installer, accepting the defaults.
On a Mac, double-click the downloaded .dmg file and drag **Unity Hub** onto the **Applications** folder.
Open Unity Hub.
Click **Sign in**, then create a free Unity ID or sign in with the one you have, and follow the prompts.
Click the gear at the top right to open **Settings**.
Click **Licenses**.
Click **Add license**.

page.title: Why two steps
page.text: The Hub holds both things a project needs: a Unity version to open it with, and a license that lets you use that version. Both live on your computer, not in the project.

page.text: In **Installs** you should see an editor numbered 6000.6.4f1 (or another 6000.6 version) with no progress bar. In **Settings** > **Licenses** you should see a Unity Personal license. If **Installs** is empty, the download has not finished or was canceled. If **Licenses** is empty, repeat **Add license**.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. The progress bar stops moving, or the install shows as failed. Fix: check your connection and free disk space, then use the retry option on the entry, or choose **Install Editor** again. The install resumes.

2. Hub says there is no license, or a project later refuses to open. Fix: in **Settings** > **Licenses** choose **Add license** again, and make sure you are signed in with the same Unity ID as before.

3. Your computer is managed by a school or employer and will not let you install. Fix: ask the IT help desk to install Unity Hub and Unity 6.6, and say so in the forum so others can help.
Install Visual Studio Code and its Unity extension
You will write C# code in Visual Studio Code from later in the course, and installing it now means the tool is ready when you need it.

items.text: In your web browser, go to **code.visualstudio.com**.
Click the download button for your system.
On Windows, run the downloaded installer and accept the defaults, clicking **Next**, then **Install**, then **Finish**.
On a Mac, double-click the downloaded zip file in Finder. **Visual Studio Code** appears beside it. Drag it onto **Applications** in the Finder sidebar.
Open Visual Studio Code. On a Mac, click **Open** if it asks whether you are sure.
In the bar down the left edge, click the **Extensions** icon, or press Control, Shift and X (Windows) or Shift, Command and X (Mac).
Click the search box at the top and type Unity.
In the results, find the extension named **Unity** whose publisher is Microsoft, and click **Install**.
Wait until the button changes from **Install** to a button that says **Uninstall**. If a prompt asks you to sign in, you can dismiss it for now.

page.text: The Unity extension should appear in your installed extensions, and its page should show **Uninstall** rather than **Install**. Visual Studio Code may also have added a C# extension by itself, which is normal. If you still see **Install**, the install did not finish: click it again and wait.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. On a Mac, a message says the app cannot be opened because Apple cannot check it for malicious software. Fix: in **Applications**, right-click **Visual Studio Code**, choose **Open**, then click **Open** again.

2. The search shows many results named Unity. Fix: choose the one published by Microsoft. Extensions with similar names, such as snippet packs, are different.

3. On Windows, the installer asks for permission and fails on a managed computer. Fix: ask your IT help desk, or download the User Installer from the same page.
Create the Courtyard project and tour the Editor
A project holds everything about one game, and the Editor’s windows are where you will work all term, so you create a project now and learn the name of every window.
Create the project

items.text: In Unity Hub, click **Projects** in the sidebar.
Click **New project**.
At the top of the screen, check that the Editor version reads 6000.6.4f1, or another 6000.6 version.
Open the dropdown beside the search box. It may read **All** or **Learning**. Choose **Core**.

shot.alt: The New project screen in Unity Hub with Editor version 6000.6.4f1 at the top and the dropdown beside the search box open, listing All, Custom, New, Core, Sample and Learning, with Core outlined.
shot.caption: The dropdown beside the search box, open, with Core outlined.
shot.shows: Unity Hub on the New project screen with the template dropdown beside the search box open and Core visible. Outline Core. Capture on Windows or Mac, and say which.

items.text: Click **Universal 3D** in the list of templates.
In the panel on the right, open the dropdown on the **Project name** box and choose **Create new local project**.
Type Courtyard in the **Project name** box.
Click **Location**. In the folder picker, open Documents, open your UnityCourse folder and click **Select folder**.
Leave the other settings (**Unity organization**, **Use AI Assistant**, **Use Unity CLI**, **Source control provider**) as they are.
Click **Create project**.

shot.alt: The New project panel with Universal 3D selected, Project name Courtyard, the Location box (blurred here; yours shows your UnityCourse folder), Use AI Assistant and Use Unity CLI unticked, and the Create project button.
shot.caption: Check that Project name reads Courtyard, then find Create project at the bottom right.
shot.shows: Unity Hub on the New project screen with Universal 3D selected. The right panel shows Project name Courtyard, Location ending in UnityCourse, and the Create project button. Outline the Project name box and Create project.

items.text: Wait for the Editor to open. The first time can take several minutes.

page.title: Why a local project
page.text: A local project lives in a folder on your own computer. The other choice in that dropdown, the default, connects the project to Unity’s cloud services, which you do not need.
The six windows you will use every week

items: Hierarchy, on the left: what is in my scene? It lists every object in the open scene. A new project shows SampleScene with Main Camera, Directional Light and Global Volume beneath it.
Scene view, in the center: what does it look like, and where can I build? You look around freely here. A scene is one saved level or screen of a game.
Game view, the tab beside Scene: what will the player see? It shows the world through the Main Camera.
Inspector, on the right: what are this object’s settings? It always shows whatever you have selected.
Project window and Console, the tabs at the bottom: which files do I have, and what went wrong? The Project window holds your files. The Console shows messages from Unity and, later, from your code.

page.alt: The Unity Editor with Hierarchy at the left listing SampleScene, Main Camera, Directional Light and Global Volume, the Scene and Game tabs in the center, the Inspector at the right, and the Project and Console tabs along the bottom.
page.caption: The Editor on a Mac, in the Default layout. On Windows the menus sit inside the window; everything else is the same.
page.shows: The whole Unity Editor in the Default layout with a new Universal 3D project open and nothing selected. Outline and label the Hierarchy (left), the Scene and Game tabs (center), the Inspector (right) and the Project and Console tabs (bottom). The title bar must be visible. Capture on Windows or Mac, and say which.

page.text: Take the tour

items.text: Look at the title at the top of the Editor window. It names the scene, your project and the version, and reads like SampleScene - Courtyard - Windows, Mac, Linux - Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1). A short label in angle brackets may follow it, such as <Metal> on a Mac. Ignore that label, here and in later weeks.
In the **Hierarchy** window, find **SampleScene** with **Main Camera**, **Directional Light** and **Global Volume** beneath it.
In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Main Camera**.
In the **Inspector** window, find the name box, **Tag**, **Layer** and the **Transform** section with **Position**, **Rotation** and **Scale**.

shot.alt: The Inspector for Main Camera: the name box, Tag MainCamera, Layer Default, and the Transform section with Position 0, 1, -10, Rotation 0, 0, 0 and Scale 1, 1, 1.
shot.caption: Main Camera in the Inspector: find the name box, Tag, Layer and the three Transform rows.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Main Camera selected, Transform visible with its Position, Rotation and Scale fields. Outline the Transform heading.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Directional Light**. The **Inspector** now shows a **Transform** with **Position** 0, 3, 0 and **Rotation** 50, -30, 0, and a **Light** section.
In the **Project** window at the bottom, click the **Assets** folder. It holds InputSystem_Actions, Readme, Scenes, Settings and TutorialInfo.

shot.alt: The Project window showing the Assets folder with InputSystem_Actions, Readme, Scenes, Settings and TutorialInfo, and a Console tab next to the Project tab.

shot.shows: The Project window with the Assets folder selected, listing InputSystem_Actions, Readme, Scenes, Settings and TutorialInfo, and the Console tab beside it. Outline the Assets folder and the Console tab.

items.text: Click the **Console** tab beside the **Project** tab. Messages from Unity appear here, and it may be empty.
Click the **Game** tab above the center area, then click the **Scene** tab again.
In the **Scene** view, scroll the mouse wheel to zoom in and out. On a trackpad, slide two fingers up or down.

In the **Scene** view, hold the right mouse button and move the mouse to look around. Keep holding it and press W, A, S and D to fly. On a trackpad this is awkward and you can skip it: this course places objects by typing numbers, so zooming and the F key are enough.
In the **Scene** view, hold Alt (Windows) or Option (Mac) and drag with the left mouse button to circle around what you are looking at.
In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Main Camera**, move the pointer over the **Scene** view and press F to frame it.

page.alt: The Scene view of the finished Courtyard zooms in toward the tower and out again, then circles around the courtyard so the walls, crates, ball and capsule are seen from every side.
page.caption: Zooming in and out, then circling. It is shown in the finished Courtyard so there is something to look at; your scene is still empty.
page.shows: The Scene view only, in a new Universal 3D project, silent. Scroll to zoom in and out, hold the right mouse button to look around while pressing W, A, S and D, then hold Alt (Windows) or Option (Mac) and drag to circle the Main Camera. Under thirty seconds. Capture on Windows or Mac, and say which.

page.alt: The Editor with Directional Light highlighted in the Hierarchy under SampleScene, and the Inspector showing its Transform with Position 0, 3, 0 and Rotation 50, -30, 0 outlined, above a Light section with General and Emission open.
page.caption: Step 5: with Directional Light selected, check Position 0, 3, 0 and Rotation 50, -30, 0.
page.shows: The whole Editor with Directional Light selected in the Hierarchy. The Inspector shows its Transform with Position 0, 3, 0 and Rotation 50, -30, 0. Outline the selected name in the Hierarchy and the Position and Rotation values.

page.text: You should have a window named Hierarchy at the left, Scene and Game tabs in the center, an Inspector at the right, and Project and Console tabs at the bottom. Clicking an object in the Hierarchy should change what the Inspector shows. On first open the Inspector may show a readme for the URP Empty Template with a **Remove Readme Assets** button: leave it alone, because clicking any object replaces it. If a window is missing or in the wrong place, choose **Window** > **Layouts** > **Default**.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. The Editor looks frozen after **Create project**. Fix: the first open compiles and imports files and can take five minutes or more. Wait until the progress bar at the bottom of the window is gone.

2. The Console tab is not there. Fix: choose **Window** > **General** > **Console**.

3. The windows are in odd places after you dragged a tab. Fix: choose **Window** > **Layouts** > **Default**.

4. The title bar shows another Editor version, or you selected a template other than Universal 3D when creating the project. Fix: close the Editor, return to the version callout in the first part of this page and create the project again with Unity 6.6 and **Universal 3D**.
If the project would not create

If creating the project keeps failing, download this starter instead. It is the same empty Universal 3D project you would have made. After opening it, return to Take the tour above and follow those steps before continuing to build the courtyard.

page.label: Courtyard_start.zip
page.shows: A zipped Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1) project named Courtyard, made from the Universal 3D template and not yet changed: the Hierarchy holds SampleScene with Main Camera, Directional Light and Global Volume, and the Assets folder holds InputSystem_Actions, Readme, Scenes, Settings and TutorialInfo.

page.text: Open a downloaded project on Windows

items.text: Open **File Explorer** and go to the **Downloads** folder.
Right-click **Courtyard_start.zip** and choose **Extract All...**.
In the box that opens, click **Browse...**, choose your UnityCourse folder in Documents and click **Select Folder**.
Click **Extract**.
Open Unity Hub and click **Projects** in the sidebar.
Click the arrow beside **Add** and choose **Add project from disk**.
Choose the extracted Courtyard folder and click **Add Project**, then click the project in the list to open it.

page.text: Open a downloaded project on a Mac

items.text: Open **Finder** and click **Downloads** in the sidebar.
Double-click **Courtyard_start.zip**. A folder named Courtyard appears beside it.
Drag the Courtyard folder into your UnityCourse folder in Documents.
Open Unity Hub and click **Projects** in the sidebar.
Click the arrow beside **Add** and choose **Add project from disk**.
Choose the Courtyard folder in UnityCourse and click **Open**, then click the project in the list to open it.

page.text: Build the courtyard from primitive shapes
Every game scene is made of GameObjects, and the quickest way to learn them is to place a few by exact numbers, so you will build the courtyard one shape at a time.

A GameObject is anything that exists in a scene, such as a camera, a light or a cube. A primitive is a ready-made basic shape: cube, sphere, capsule, cylinder or plane. Every GameObject has a Transform, which holds three things. Position says where the object’s center is, in units along X (right), Y (up) and Z (forward). Rotation says how far it is turned, in degrees. Scale says how big it is, as a multiplier of its normal size.

Here is why numbers beat dragging. A Cylinder is 2 units tall at Scale 1. At Scale Y of 3 it is 6 units tall. Position is the center, so for it to stand on the ground at Y 0, its center must be half of 6, which is 3. Type 3 and it stands exactly on the ground, on your screen and on every other student’s.
Name the scene, then place the ground and the tower

items.text: Choose **File** > **Save As...**.

Type Courtyard as the name. Save it inside the Scenes folder: if the box shows Assets, open **Scenes** first (on a Mac, click the arrow beside **Where** to see the folders). Then click **Save**. The title bar now starts with Courtyard.
Choose **GameObject** > **3D Object** > **Plane**.
Type Ground and press Enter. The name is already in edit mode. A yellow note about the Plane’s Mesh Collider may show in the Inspector: it is harmless, so leave it.
In the **Inspector**, in the **Transform** section, set **Position** to 0, 0, 0. Click the **X** box, type 0, press Tab to jump to **Y**, type 0, press Tab, type 0.
Set **Rotation** to 0, 0, 0.
Set **Scale** to 2, 1, 2. The plane is now 20 by 20 units.

shot.alt: The Transform of Ground with Position 0, 0, 0, Rotation 0, 0, 0 and Scale 2, 1, 2.
shot.caption: Ground: Scale reads 2, 1, 2 and every other box reads 0.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Ground selected, showing the Transform with Position 0, 0, 0, Rotation 0, 0, 0 and Scale 2, 1, 2. Outline the three rows of values.

items.text: Choose **GameObject** > **3D Object** > **Cylinder**.
Type Tower and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to 0, 3, 0.
Set **Rotation** to 0, 0, 0.
Set **Scale** to 2, 3, 2.

shot.alt: The Transform of Tower with Position 0, 3, 0, Rotation 0, 0, 0 and Scale 2, 3, 2.
shot.caption: Tower: Position Y reads 3 and Scale reads 2, 3, 2.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Tower selected, showing the Transform with Position 0, 3, 0, Rotation 0, 0, 0 and Scale 2, 3, 2. Outline the three rows of values.

page.alt: The Editor with Courtyard in the title bar. The Hierarchy lists Main Camera, Directional Light, Global Volume, Ground and Tower, with Ground and Tower outlined. The Scene view shows a flat square ground with a tall cylinder standing at its center, and the Inspector shows Tower at Position 0, 3, 0 and Scale 2, 3, 2.
page.caption: The tower stands on the ground, neither floating nor sunk, and Ground and Tower are in the Hierarchy.
page.shows: The whole Editor after Tower is placed. The Scene view shows the flat Ground with the Tower standing in its middle, and the Hierarchy lists Ground and Tower under Courtyard. Outline the Hierarchy entries.

page.text: The Scene view should show a flat square with a tall cylinder standing in its middle. The Hierarchy should list Ground and Tower. If the tower floats or is half sunk into the ground, select Tower and check that **Position** Y is 3. If the ground looks tiny, check that **Scale** is 2, 1, 2.
Add the walls, crates, ball and guard
Six more objects, each made the same way. Here are their values.

items: Wall_Back: Cube, Position 0, 1.5, 10, Rotation 0, 0, 0, Scale 20, 3, 1
Wall_Left: Cube, Position -10, 1.5, 0, Rotation 0, 0, 0, Scale 1, 3, 20
Crate_A: Cube, Position 5, 0.5, -3, Rotation 0, 0, 0, Scale 1, 1, 1
Crate_B: Cube, Position 6.5, 0.75, -4.5, Rotation 0, 30, 0, Scale 1.5, 1.5, 1.5
Ball: Sphere, Position -5, 0.5, -4, Rotation 0, 0, 0, Scale 1, 1, 1
Guard: Capsule, Position -6, 1, -1, Rotation 0, 0, 0, Scale 1, 1, 1

items.text: Choose **GameObject** > **3D Object**, then the shape named in the list.
Type the object’s name and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to the values in the list.
Set **Rotation** to the values in the list.
Set **Scale** to the values in the list. Then go back to step 1 for the next object, until all six are in the Hierarchy.

page.title: Why those Y values
page.text: Each object’s Y position is half its height after scaling. A cube is 1 unit tall, so at Scale Y 3 it is 3 tall and its center is at 1.5. A sphere or capsule works the same way: the Ball is 1 unit tall and sits at 0.5, and the Guard is 2 units tall and sits at 1. That keeps every object resting on the ground instead of floating or sinking.

items.text: Press Control and S (Windows) or Command and S (Mac) to save the scene.

page.alt: The Hierarchy listing Main Camera, Directional Light, Global Volume, Ground, Tower, Wall_Back, Wall_Left, Crate_A, Crate_B, Ball and Guard, and a Scene view of the courtyard seen from beyond the corner where the two walls meet, so the crates appear on the left and the capsule on the right.
page.caption: All eleven entries are in the Hierarchy; this Scene view looks from behind the walls, so left and right are swapped.
page.shows: The whole Editor. The Hierarchy lists Main Camera, Directional Light, Global Volume, Ground, Tower, Wall_Back, Wall_Left, Crate_A, Crate_B, Ball and Guard. The Scene view is pulled back far enough to show every object. Outline the Hierarchy list.

page.text: The Hierarchy should list Ground, Tower, Wall_Back, Wall_Left, Crate_A, Crate_B, Ball and Guard under the camera, light and volume. In the Scene view, the two walls should meet at one corner of the ground, the crates should stand on one side of the tower and the ball and capsule on the other. Which side looks like the left depends on where your Scene view looks from: the picture above looks from beyond the corner where the walls meet, so its crates are on the left. The Game view in the next part shows the crates on the right. If an object is missing, check the Hierarchy for it. If one floats or sinks, select it and compare its Position Y with the list. A title ending in an asterisk means the scene is not saved yet.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. A new object appears at an odd position. Fix: that is normal, because new objects appear where the Scene view is looking. Type the Position values from the list.

2. You typed a value into the wrong box, so a wall is lying flat or stretched. Fix: select it and compare the **Rotation** and **Scale** rows with the list.

3. You cannot find an object in the Scene view. Fix: click it in the Hierarchy, move the pointer over the Scene view and press F.
Frame the camera, press Play and save
The Game view is what a player sees, so you point the Main Camera at the courtyard and check that nothing is cut off.

The goal is one view that shows the whole Ground, both walls and every object, in a Game view set to the 16:9 shape. Three things decide that together: where the camera is and which way it points, its field of view (how wide it sees, in degrees), and the shape of the Game view. Change any one and the picture changes. With a field of view of 60, a camera at 0, 16, -16 and tilted down 45 degrees fits the whole 20 by 20 courtyard, with the near edge of the ground a little above the bottom of the picture.

items.text: Click the **Game** tab.
In the bar along the top of the **Game** view, open the third dropdown, which reads **Free Aspect**, and choose **16:9 Aspect**.

shot.alt: The Game view toolbar with the third dropdown open, listing Free Aspect, 16:9 Aspect, 16:10 Aspect, Full HD, WXGA, QHD and 4K UHD, with 16:9 Aspect ticked and outlined.
shot.caption: The aspect dropdown in the Game view, with 16:9 Aspect chosen.
shot.shows: The top of the Game view with the aspect dropdown open and 16:9 Aspect chosen. Outline the dropdown. Capture on Windows or Mac, and say which.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Main Camera**.
In the **Inspector**, in the **Transform** section, set **Position** to 0, 16, -16.
Set **Rotation** to 45, 0, 0.
Set **Scale** to 1, 1, 1.
In the **Inspector**, scroll down to the **Camera** section and find **Field of View**.
Set **Field of View** to 60.

shot.alt: The Main Camera Inspector with Position 0, 16, -16, Rotation 45, 0, 0 and Scale 1, 1, 1 outlined in the Transform, and in the Camera section Field of View 60 outlined, with Physical Camera unticked.
shot.caption: Main Camera: Position 0, 16, -16, Rotation 45, 0, 0 and Field of View 60.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Main Camera selected: Transform with Position 0, 16, -16, Rotation 45, 0, 0, Scale 1, 1, 1, and the Camera section scrolled into view with Field of View 60. Outline all of those values.

items.text: Look at the **Game** view.

page.title: Why three settings
page.text: Field of view is how wide an angle the camera sees. A larger number sees more of the scene but makes everything smaller, and a smaller number zooms in. The Game view’s own shape matters too: a narrower view has less room on each side, which is why you chose 16:9 first.

page.alt: The Game view of the Courtyard in 16:9 with the whole ground, the tower, both walls, both crates, the ball and the capsule inside the picture and nothing cut off.
page.shows: The Game view only, aspect 16:9 Aspect, Play not pressed. The whole Ground is inside the picture: its near edge a little above the bottom of the view, its far edge behind Wall_Back, and its left and right edges inside the sides. Tower, Wall_Back, Wall_Left, Crate_A, Crate_B, Ball and Guard are all fully visible.

page.text: In the Game view you should see the whole ground with all four of its edges inside the picture, the tower in the middle, both walls, both crates, the ball and the capsule, with plain background around it. If anything is cut off, check these in order: the Game view says 16:9 Aspect; Position is exactly 0, 16, -16; Rotation is exactly 45, 0, 0; Field of View is exactly 60.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. The picture is cropped at the sides or bottom. Fix: the Game view is probably not set to 16:9 Aspect, so choose it again from the dropdown.

2. The view is far too zoomed in or out. Fix: Field of View is not 60. If the **Camera** section shows a focal length instead, a physical camera setting is on; untick **Physical Camera** and set **Field of View** to 60.

3. The Game view is a gray or blue empty picture. Fix: the camera points the wrong way. Check **Rotation** is 45, 0, 0 and that Position has a minus sign on the Z value.
Press Play and save

items.text: At the top center of the Editor, click the **Play** button.
Watch the **Game** view for ten seconds. It stays still, because nothing in the scene moves yet.
Click the **Play** button again to stop.
Press Control and S (Windows) or Command and S (Mac) to save the scene.

page.alt: The Game view of the Courtyard at 16:9 Aspect. Play is clicked and its button turns into a blue square, the courtyard stays still for about ten seconds, and a second click turns the button back to a triangle.
page.caption: Play is clicked, the button turns into a square while the game runs, and a second click stops it.
page.shows: The whole Editor, silent, with the Game tab selected at 16:9 Aspect. The pointer clicks Play at the top center, the Editor tints, ten seconds pass with the courtyard unchanged, then the pointer clicks Play again and the tint goes. Under thirty seconds.

page.title: Why stop before editing
page.text: Play runs your scene the way a player would see it. Changes you make while Play is on are thrown away when you stop, so always click Play again to stop before you edit anything.
After saving, the title bar should show Courtyard with no asterisk, and the Play button should not be pressed. If the Play button shows a square, you are still in Play mode: click it once more.

If your Courtyard does not match, or you want to check your work, download the finished project for this week. Close the Unity Editor. In File Explorer or Finder, open UnityCourse and create a folder named CourtyardReference. Follow the starter extraction and opening instructions, but use CourtyardReference as the destination instead of UnityCourse. In Unity Hub, add and open the extracted Courtyard folder inside CourtyardReference. Your own Courtyard project remains in its original folder. In the **Project** window, open **Assets** > **Scenes** and double-click **Courtyard** to open the finished scene. Then click the **Game** tab and set the aspect to **16:9 Aspect**, because that setting belongs to your Editor and is not stored in the project.

page.shows: A zipped Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1) Universal 3D project named Courtyard. Its scene Assets/Scenes/Courtyard holds Ground, Tower, Wall_Back, Wall_Left, Crate_A, Crate_B, Ball and Guard at the values on this page, and a Main Camera at Position 0, 16, -16, Rotation 45, 0, 0 with Field of View 60.

page.text: Take a screenshot and record your screen
Showing a game working means capturing a picture and a short recording of your screen, and you will do both all term, so you practice on the Courtyard now.

Before you start, put Unity in the state you want to capture: the Courtyard scene open, the Game tab selected, the aspect set to 16:9 Aspect and Play not pressed. Follow the steps for your system. The recording is a few seconds of you pressing Play, watching, and pressing Play again.
Screenshot on Windows

items.text: Click the Unity Editor window so it is in front, with the Game tab showing the framed courtyard.
Press the Windows key and PrintScreen together. On some laptops you also hold Fn. The screen dims for a moment.
Open **File Explorer** and click **Pictures** in the list on the left.
Open the **Screenshots** folder.
Double-click the newest file, named Screenshot with a number, and check that it shows the whole Editor.

page.text: Screenshot on a Mac

items.text: Click the Unity Editor window so it is in front, with the Game tab showing the framed courtyard.
Press Shift, Command and 3 together. A small preview appears in a corner of the screen.
On the Desktop, find the newest file named Screenshot followed by the date and time.
Double-click it and check that it shows the whole Editor.

page.text: Recording on Windows with Xbox Game Bar

items.text: Press the Windows key and I to open **Settings**, then click **Gaming**.
Open **Xbox Game Bar**, which is called **Game Bar** on Windows 11, and switch it on.
Click the Unity Editor window so it is the active window.
Press the Windows key and G together to open the Game Bar. If it asks whether this is a game, tick the box that says yes.
In the **Capture** widget, click the record button, the circle.
In Unity, click **Play**, wait ten seconds, then click **Play** again to stop.
Press the Windows key, Alt and R together to stop recording. A notification says the clip was recorded.
Open **File Explorer**, click **Videos**, open the **Captures** folder and double-click the newest .mp4 file to check it.

page.text: Recording on Windows 11 with Snipping Tool, if Game Bar will not record

items.text: Press the Windows key, type Snipping Tool and press Enter.
In the Snipping Tool toolbar, click the video camera icon to switch from pictures to recording.
Click **New**. The screen dims.
Drag a rectangle around the whole Unity Editor window.
Click **Start**. A short countdown runs, then recording begins.
In Unity, click **Play**, wait ten seconds, then click **Play** again to stop.
Click the stop button in the small recording bar.
In the preview that opens, click the **Save** icon, choose the **Videos** folder, type Courtyard-recording as the name and click **Save**.
Open **File Explorer**, click **Videos**, and double-click Courtyard-recording to check it plays.

page.text: Recording on a Mac

items.text: Press Shift, Command and 5 together. A toolbar appears at the bottom of the screen.
Click **Record Selected Portion**.
Drag the box that appears so it covers the whole Unity Editor window.
Click **Record**.
In Unity, click **Play**, wait ten seconds, then click **Play** again to stop.
Click the stop button in the menu bar at the top of the screen.
On the Desktop, double-click the newest file named Screen Recording followed by the date and time, and check that it plays.

page.alt: A screenshot of the full Unity Editor with Courtyard in the title bar, the Hierarchy listing Ground, Tower, Wall_Back, Wall_Left, Crate_A, Crate_B, Ball and Guard, and the Game view showing the whole courtyard.
page.caption: What your screenshot should show: the whole Editor, with the framed courtyard in the Game view.
page.shows: The finished screenshot opened in an image viewer. The whole Unity Editor is visible with the Courtyard scene, the Game tab selected and showing the framed courtyard, the Hierarchy listing the eight objects, and the title bar showing Courtyard. Capture on Windows or Mac, and say which.

page.text: You should now have two files on your computer: a picture of the whole Editor with the framed courtyard in the Game view, and a recording of about ten seconds in which Play is pressed and stopped. Both should open and play. If the picture shows another window, or the recording is blank or shows a different program, capture again with Unity in front.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. Game Bar does nothing when you press Windows and G. Fix: switch it on under **Settings** > **Gaming** as in the steps above, and click the Unity window before you press the keys. If it still will not record and you have Windows 11, use the Snipping Tool steps.

2. Game Bar says it cannot record, or the clip is black. Fix: click the Unity window first so it is active, then start again. On Windows 11 you can also use Snipping Tool instead.

3. On a Mac, you cannot find the recording. Fix: open the toolbar again with Shift, Command and 5, click **Options** and look under **Save to**.
Challenges: extend your Courtyard
These two challenges practice what you did with no steps, because building from numbers is easier once you work them out yourself. Save your scene first, and keep the Game view at 16:9 Aspect.
Challenge: close the courtyard and roof the tower

Add a Cube named Wall_Right along the right edge of the Ground, the same height and length as Wall_Left. Add a Sphere named Dome with Scale 2, 2, 2, as wide as the tower, that rests exactly on top of Tower, with its lowest point touching the top of the tower. Check in your Game view that both are fully visible.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Wall_Right is a mirror of Wall_Left, so only one number changes sign. For Dome, work out how tall Tower is after scaling and where its top is. A sphere at Scale 2 is 2 units across, so its center is one unit above its lowest point.
Optional challenge: a staircase against the back wall

Build three Cubes named Step_1, Step_2 and Step_3 on the right side of the courtyard, between Crate_A and Wall_Back. Each is 4 units wide and 2 units deep. Their tops are 1, 2 and 3 units above the ground, rising toward Wall_Back, and Step_3 touches the front face of Wall_Back. All three are centered 5 units to the right of the middle. Check that none overlaps a crate or the tower, and that all three show in your Game view.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Wall_Back is 1 unit thick and centered at Z 10, so its front face is at Z 9.5. A step 2 units deep that touches it has its center at Z 8.5. Each lower step sits one depth nearer the camera, so its center Z is 2 less than that of the step behind it. A step’s height is its Scale Y, and its center Y is half of that.

Your Game view should still show everything. With the first challenge you should see a wall on each side and a sphere sitting on top of the tower with no gap. With the optional challenge you should see three steps rising toward the back wall on the right, clear of the crates. If a step seems to float, compare its Position Y with half its Scale Y.
Wrap-up

You can now install Unity 6.6 and Visual Studio Code, open a Universal 3D project, name the Editor’s windows and build a scene by typing Transform values. Test yourself. Install: which two things does a project need that Unity Hub holds? Windows: which window lists every object, and which shows the settings of the one you select? Build: a Cube is 1 unit tall at Scale 1; at Scale Y 3, resting on the ground, what Position Y puts it there? Next week you give these shapes components, materials and light, then roll a ball around an arena using a Rigidbody.

l_770f41609628.title: Components, materials and physics
l_770f41609628.summary: Give a scene components, materials and light, then roll a ball in an arena using a Rigidbody; submit a recording and screenshot.
keyIdeas: Every GameObject is a container, and its components decide what it looks like, what is solid and how it moves. The Inspector lists them, and you can switch each one off, change it or add another.

A material is a file that says how a surface looks, and its color is the color box beside Base Map. A light is a component too, with a color of its own, so what you see is the surface and the light together.

A Rigidbody hands an object to the physics engine, so gravity and collisions move it. A collider gives it a solid shape. Without a Rigidbody an object does not move, and without colliders it passes through everything.
Changes you make while Play is on are thrown away when you stop. Make your fixes while the game is stopped.

vocabulary.definition: A part you add to a GameObject that gives it one job, such as drawing it, making it solid or letting physics move it.
The component that holds an object’s shape.
The component that draws an object’s shape on screen with its material.
The component that gives an object a solid shape for other objects to bump into.
The component that hands an object to the physics engine so gravity and collisions can move it.
A file that says how a surface looks, including its color, which you can put on many objects.
The small program that decides how light falls on a surface and so how a material looks.
How heavy a Rigidbody is to the physics engine.
A file you put on a collider to set how bouncy or slippery its surface is.

study.overview: This week you learned that a game object is a container, and that its parts decide how it looks, what is solid and how it moves. You can now open the Inspector, read the components on an object, and change them. You built the Arena from a floor and four walls, colored it with materials and a light, and made a red-orange ball fall, roll down a ramp and bump a wall. This is the start of Orb Collector. Reread this page before next week, when you write your first script.

points.heading: Every object is a stack of components
points.explanation: A GameObject does nothing by itself. Its components do the work, and the Inspector lists them from the top. A Cube has a Transform for where it is, a Mesh Filter for its shape, a Mesh Renderer that draws it and a Box Collider that makes it solid. You can switch each one off with its checkbox, change its values, or add another with Add Component. Example: when you unticked the Mesh Renderer on Floor, the floor vanished from the Scene and Game views, but it was still there. Looks and solidity are separate jobs. When something goes wrong, select the object and read its components first.

points.heading: Materials and lights both set the color you see
points.explanation: A material is a file that says how a surface looks. Its color is the color box beside Base Map, under Surface Inputs. There is no field called Albedo or Color. You made M_Floor with hexadecimal 3B4A5A and dragged it onto Floor in the Hierarchy. A light is a component with a color of its own. On the Directional Light, set Light Appearance to Color, then use the color box under Emission. When you typed FF8A1F, every surface turned orange. Typing FFF4E0 gave a gentle warm white. What you see is the surface and the light together, so one light can change the mood of a whole scene.

points.heading: A Rigidbody moves it, a collider makes it solid
points.explanation: A Rigidbody hands an object to the physics engine, so gravity and collisions move it. A collider gives the object a solid shape. You need both. Example: before you added a Rigidbody, the Ball hung in the air when you pressed Play. After you added one, it fell onto the Ramp and rolled to Wall_North. When you unticked the Sphere Collider, the ball still fell, but it passed through the ramp and the floor. Without a Rigidbody an object does not move. Without colliders it passes through everything. The Floor has a collider but no Rigidbody, because it should never move.

points.heading: Fix things while Play is off
points.explanation: Changes you make while Play is on are thrown away when you stop. When you changed the Ball’s Mass to 50 during Play, it read 1 again after you stopped. Use Play to watch what happens, then press Play again to stop before you fix anything. Switching one thing off at a time, such as Use Gravity or a collider, is a quick way to find which component does which job. You can use the same trick to find bugs later.

page.text: Last week you built the Courtyard from plain shapes and learned the name of every Editor window. This week those shapes start to behave. You will see that every object is a stack of components, give surfaces color with materials, tint a light, and add a Rigidbody to a ball so that gravity and collisions move it. This is the start of Orb Collector, the first game you build. By Sunday you will have an Arena scene where a red-orange ball drops onto a ramp, rolls across a floor and bumps a wall. You will also know which component does which job.
