page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Keys do nothing in a test. Click once inside the Game view first.

The Ball leaps past the walls or gets stuck. Check that Force reads 20 and Linear Damping reads 1.

A red line appears in the Console. Double-click it, read the file, line and column, fix the first error and save.
Challenges

These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change the code is how scripting sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks. Click inside the Game view before each test.
Challenge: sprint with Left Shift

Change BallController so that holding Left Shift makes every push twice as strong. The multiplier shows in the Inspector as Sprint Multiplier, set to 2. With Force at 20, a Ball you push with W gets a push of 20 normally and 40 while Shift is held, and it goes back to 20 when you let go. Diagonals stay no stronger than straight pushes. Setting Sprint Multiplier to 1 turns the sprint off.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Add a new public float, as you did for force. The Left Shift key is `Keyboard.current.leftShiftKey.isPressed`. Read it in Update, next to the other keys, and use it in FixedUpdate when you multiply: the strength is force, or force times the multiplier.
Optional challenge: steer with an InputAction

Change BallController so it steers with the project’s own Move action instead of the four key lines, and the Ball still moves as before with W, A, S and D. The action gives a pair of numbers, and its first number should become x and its second should become z. Holding W gives a push forward, holding D gives a push to the right, and with no key held the push is nothing. Keep the line that makes the arrow length 1. The Sprint keys from the other challenge can stay.

page.title: Hint
page.text: The project’s InputSystem_Actions asset has a Player map with Move, Look, Attack, Interact, Crouch, Jump, Previous, Next and Sprint. Find the action with `InputSystem.actions.FindAction("Move")`, once, in Start, and keep it in a private variable of type `InputAction`. In Update, `ReadValue<Vector2>()` gives its x and y. You need `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;`, which the file already has.
Wrap-up

You can now read the keyboard with Keyboard.current, push a Rigidbody with AddForce from FixedUpdate, and write a script that keeps the camera behind the Ball. Test yourself. First, which two Keyboard.current properties tell you that a key is held and that a key just went down? Second, why do you read keys in Update but call AddForce in FixedUpdate? Third, what does CameraFollow add to the Ball’s position, and why does it run in LateUpdate? Next week you add spinning pickups that the Ball collects by touching them, using triggers and tags, and you show a score and a win message with TextMeshPro.

l_9e49f2c4974f.title: Collisions, triggers and scoring
l_9e49f2c4974f.summary: Collect spinning pickups using triggers and tags, show a score and win message in TextMeshPro; submit Orb Collector as a recording and screenshot.
keyIdeas: A collider with Is Trigger ticked does not block anything. Things pass through it, and Unity runs OnTriggerEnter on your scripts when something enters.
A tag is a text label on a GameObject. CompareTag asks whether the object you touched wears the label you name, so only pickups count and floors and walls do not.
An if statement runs the lines inside its braces only when its condition is true. A counter is an int that you add 1 to each time something happens.
A TMP_Text variable points at a text object on the screen. Setting its text property changes what the player sees, so you set it every time the score changes.

vocabulary.definition: A collider with Is Trigger ticked, which lets things pass through while Unity still tells your scripts that something went in.
A text label on a GameObject that a script can check to tell kinds of objects apart.
A method Unity runs once on your script when something enters a trigger collider, and it gives you the other collider as other.
A method that answers true when an object wears the tag you name, for example other.CompareTag(“Pickup”).
A method that removes a GameObject from the scene, for example Destroy(other.gameObject).
A question followed by braces, where the lines inside run only when the answer is true.
An int variable that you add 1 to each time something happens, such as score = score + 1.
Unity’s text tool for the screen, whose type in code is TMP_Text and whose text property holds what is shown.
The flat layer that holds on-screen text and buttons, which Unity adds the first time you make a UI object.

study.overview: This week you made the Ball react to what it touches. You can now build a pickup the Ball drives through, spot it with a tag, count it, and show the player the score and a win message on screen. Reread this page before next week. The same idea, ask what two things are and decide what happens, drives most of Dodge too.

points.heading: Triggers and tags tell the game what was touched
points.explanation: A collider with Is Trigger ticked does not block anything. The Ball passes through it, and Unity runs OnTriggerEnter on the Ball’s script. A tag is a text label, and CompareTag asks whether the touched object wears the label you name. Example: the Pickup cube has Is Trigger ticked and the tag Pickup. In BallController, `void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)` runs when the Ball enters it, and `if (other.CompareTag("Pickup"))` is true, so `Destroy(other.gameObject)` removes the cube. The Floor and walls are not triggers and do not wear the tag, so nothing is removed for them. Spell the tag exactly: Pickup and pickup are different tags. If the Ball bumps the cube, Is Trigger is not ticked. If nothing happens and the Console is empty, check the tag spelling and that the method is named exactly OnTriggerEnter.

points.heading: A counter and an if keep the score
points.explanation: A counter is an int that you add 1 to each time something happens. An if statement runs the lines inside its braces only when its condition is true. Example: `public int score = 0;` starts the count. After each pickup, `score = score + 1;` takes the number in score, adds 1 and stores it back, so 3 becomes 4. Then `if (score >= totalPickups)` asks whether score has reached 8. It is true only when the eighth pickup is taken, so the win code runs once. If You win! comes too early or never, Total Pickups on the Ball does not match the number of Pickups you made in the scene.

points.heading: A TMP_Text variable puts the score on screen
points.explanation: A counter only remembers. The player sees nothing until you set the text. A `TMP_Text` variable points at a text object, and setting its `text` property changes what the player sees. You need `using TMPro;` at the top of the file. Example: `scoreText.text = "Score: " + score + " / " + totalPickups;` reads Score: 3 / 8 when score is 3. Set it in Start and again after every change, so the screen always matches the counter. In Start, `winText.text = "";` hides the win message until `winText.text = "You win!";` fills it in. Drag ScoreText and WinText from the Hierarchy onto the Ball’s Score Text and Win Text boxes. If they still read None, you get a NullReferenceException when you press Play.

points.heading: Reading a problem: what to check first
points.explanation: When something fails, work from what you see. A red line in the Console names the problem and the line to look at. CS0246 about TMP_Text means `using TMPro;` is missing. CS0103 means a name is spelled differently in two places. The Ball does not move: click once inside the Game view first. Also try the trap challenge on paper before you code it. With 3 pickups collected the text reads Score: 3 / 8, and after the Trap it reads Score: 2 / 8. If you hit the Trap first, it still reads Score: 0 / 8, because the score never drops below 0. Tracking collected pickups in a separate variable keeps the Trap from blocking a win. Submit your Weekly builds work by Sunday night.

page.text: Last time the Ball learned to move. This week it gets something to do. You build spinning pickups, teach the Ball to notice when it touches one, and count what it collects. By Sunday your Orb Collector removes each pickup you touch, shows a score in the top-left corner, and shows a win message when you have collected them all. You also meet an idea behind nearly every game: when two things meet, the game asks what they are and decides what happens.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text: 1. The Ball does not move: keys go to the window you clicked last. Click once inside the Game view, then try again. 2. A red InvalidOperationException when you press a key: the script is reading keys with the old Input class. The project will not open or looks very different from the checkpoint: unzip the starter project above and open that instead.
Make a Pickup you can drive through

You need something to collect, and the Ball must be able to reach it. In this part you build one pickup and make it a trigger. A collider is the invisible shape Unity uses to detect touching. Normally two colliders block each other. When you tick Is Trigger on a collider, it stops blocking: things pass through it, but Unity can still tell your scripts that something went in. A pressure plate in a game works this way. You step on it without bumping into it, and something happens.

page.title: Why spell it exactly
page.text: A tag is plain text and must match exactly. The tag is Pickup with a capital P. Your script will compare against that same spelling, and Pickup and pickup are different tags.

Make the Pickup spin

A spinning pickup catches the eye and tells the player it is something to grab. You wrote a script like this in week 3: Spinner turned a cube around one axis. Rotator is a shorter version that turns around all three axes at once, and it brings back Time.deltaTime, which you need again for timers in Dodge.

The method Update runs once per frame, and a frame can be quicker or slower depending on the computer. If you turned the Pickup by a fixed 2 degrees every frame, it would spin faster on a fast computer. So you give a speed in degrees per second and multiply by Time.deltaTime, the seconds the last frame took. For example, a speed of 90 and a frame of 0.02 seconds gives 1.8 degrees that frame. Fifty such frames add up to 90 degrees, one quarter turn per second on every computer. Last time you did not multiply the force by Time.deltaTime because AddForce, with its default ForceMode.Force, already accounts for the physics timestep. Here, transform.Rotate takes an angle, so you multiply degrees per second by Time.deltaTime to get the angle for this frame.

It sits in `Update`, so it runs every frame. The file name and the class name, `Rotator`, must match exactly.

Detect a touch with a trigger and a tag

page.alt: A slide showing a Ball entering a Pickup trigger, then the OnTriggerEnter method with CompareTag and Destroy highlighted.
page.caption: Watch first: how Unity tells your script that the Ball touched something.
page.shows: A simple drawn slide: a circle labeled Ball with a Rigidbody, and a square labeled Pickup with Is Trigger ticked and Tag Pickup. An arrow shows the circle entering the square. Then the code of OnTriggerEnter appears, with the lines CompareTag and Destroy highlighted one at a time as they are spoken.
page.transcript: Last time you moved the Ball by pushing it. This week the Ball has to notice something, and that is a different job. Unity does most of it for you. Every physics step, Unity checks whether colliders overlap. Most colliders are solid: the Ball hits a wall and stops. A trigger collider is different. You tick Is Trigger and the collider stops blocking. The Ball passes straight through it. But Unity still notices, and when the Ball goes in, Unity looks for a method called OnTriggerEnter on the scripts attached to the Ball, and runs it once. Think of a doorbell. You do not watch the door all day. You write what should happen when the bell rings, and OnTriggerEnter is the bell. It hands you one thing: the other collider, which we call other. Now, the Ball will ring this bell for anything that is a trigger, and later your game may have many kinds. So you ask: what did I just touch? That is the job of a tag. A tag is a text label on an object. CompareTag asks whether other wears the label you name. If other dot CompareTag, Pickup, is true, we run the lines inside the curly braces. That is an if statement: a question, then lines that run only when the answer is yes. For this to work, three things must be true. One of the two objects needs a Rigidbody, and your Ball has one. The collider on the pickup needs Is Trigger ticked. And the tag must be spelled exactly the same in the Inspector and in your script, capital P included. Inside the braces we write Destroy, other dot gameObject. That removes the touched object from the scene. We write gameObject because other is only the collider; gameObject is the whole thing the collider belongs to. In the next part you type this yourself. Keep one picture in mind: a bell, a question, an action.

page.text: Now you write the bell. The method goes in BallController, because the Ball is the object that touches the pickups. An if statement is a question followed by braces: the lines inside the braces run only when the answer is yes.

items.text: In the **Project** window, open **Assets > Scripts** and double-click **BallController**. Visual Studio Code opens with the file.

Scroll to the end of the file. Click at the end of the line with the closing } of `FixedUpdate`. It is usually the second-to-last } in the file. If you added code in last week’s challenges, your AddForce line may look different: that is fine.

Press Enter twice, then type or paste the new method from the code block below. Lines marked already in your file only show where the new code goes: do not type them again. Keep the final } of the file below it.
Save the file (Ctrl+S on Windows, Command+S on a Mac), then click back into Unity and wait for the spinning icon at the bottom right to stop.

page.caption: End of BallController.cs

page.text: Line by line: the first two lines are the end of the `FixedUpdate` you wrote last time, so do not type them again if they are already there. `void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)` is the bell: Unity runs it when the Ball goes into a trigger, and `other` is the collider it touched. `if (other.CompareTag("Pickup"))` asks whether that collider wears the tag Pickup. The lines inside the braces run only when the answer is yes. `Debug.Log("Touched a pickup");` writes a line in the Console so you can prove the bell rang. `Destroy(other.gameObject);` removes the touched object from the scene. The name has to be `OnTriggerEnter` with those exact capitals, or Unity never calls it. The new method goes inside the final }, which closes the class.

items.text: Check that **Play** is off, then click **Play**.
Click once inside the **Game** view.
Roll the Ball into the Pickup.

shot.alt: Game view with the Ball where the Pickup was and no yellow cube left.
shot.caption: Just after the touch: the Pickup is gone.
shot.shows: The Game view only, in Play, just after the Ball has touched the Pickup: the Ball is on the Floor and the yellow cube is gone.

items.text: Click the **Console** tab and look for the line Touched a pickup.

shot.alt: Console with one message: Touched a pickup.
shot.caption: The line your new method wrote.
shot.shows: The Console window only, with one line reading Touched a pickup. Outline that line.

items.text: Click **Play** again to stop.

page.text: When the Ball touches the Pickup, the Pickup disappears and the Console shows Touched a pickup once. It has gone wrong if the Ball bumps the cube, or the cube stays and the Console stays empty.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text: 1. The Ball bumps the cube: Is Trigger is not ticked on the Pickup’s Box Collider. 2. Nothing happens and the Console is empty: the tag is spelled differently in the Inspector and in the script, the method name is not exactly OnTriggerEnter, or the Ball lost its Rigidbody. 3. A red line says error CS1022: Type or namespace definition, or end-of-file expected: the method sits outside the final } of the class, or a } is missing. Move it inside, save, and wait for Unity to compile.
Count the score with a counter and an if

One pickup that vanishes is a start. A game needs to remember how many you have taken. A counter is a variable of type int, a whole number, that you add 1 to each time something happens. Then a second if can ask whether the counter has reached the total. You also make seven more pickups, so there are eight to collect.

items.text: In the **Project** window, open **Assets > Scripts** and double-click **BallController**.

Find the line `private Vector3 moveInput;`. Click at the end of it, press Enter, and add only `public int score = 0;` and `public int totalPickups = 8;`, each on its own line. In the first code example below, the moveInput line and the Start declaration show where these variables belong; do not copy those two lines.
Select the whole `OnTriggerEnter` method, from `void OnTriggerEnter` down to its closing }, and replace it with the second code block below.
Save the file (Ctrl+S on Windows, Command+S on a Mac), then click back into Unity and wait for the spinning icon at the bottom right to stop.

page.caption: New variables in BallController.cs
The new OnTriggerEnter

page.text: Line by line: `public int score = 0;` is the counter. It starts at 0 and shows in the Inspector, so you can watch it. `public int totalPickups = 8;` is how many pickups the game holds. `score = score + 1;` reads: take the number in score, add 1, store the answer back in score. If score is 3, it becomes 4. `Debug.Log("Score: " + score);` joins the words and the number into one line for the Console. `if (score >= totalPickups)` asks whether score is greater than or equal to 8. It is true only when the eighth pickup is taken, so the win line runs once.
These are the positions of the seven copies of the Pickup, as Position X, Y, Z. The first Pickup already sits at -4, 1, -4.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, click **Pickup**.
Choose **Edit > Duplicate** (Ctrl+D on Windows, Command+D on a Mac). The copy is named Pickup (1) and is selected.
In the **Inspector**, type the first position from the list into **Position** X, Y and Z.
Choose **Edit > Duplicate** again, then type the next position from the list into **Position**.
Repeat the last step until you have used all seven positions. If a copy sits inside a wall or the Ramp, change its X and Z a little.

shot.alt: Hierarchy with Pickup and Pickup (1) through Pickup (7).
shot.caption: Pickup and its seven copies in the Hierarchy.
shot.shows: The Hierarchy window only, listing Pickup and Pickup (1) to Pickup (7) with the other objects of the scene. Outline the eight Pickup entries.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, click **Ball**. In the **Inspector**, find **Ball Controller (Script)** and check that **Score** is 0 and **Total Pickups** is 8.

shot.alt: Ball Controller (Script) with Score 0 and Total Pickups 8.
shot.caption: Score 0 and Total Pickups 8 on the Ball. Three components above are folded here to save room.
shot.shows: The Inspector only for Ball, scrolled to Ball Controller (Script), with Score 0 and Total Pickups 8 visible.

items.text: Click **Play**, click once inside the **Game** view, and roll the Ball through the pickups.
Click the **Console** tab and read the lines. Click **Play** again to stop.

shot.alt: Console lines Score: 1 to Score: 8 followed by You win!.
shot.caption: The last lines after all eight: the score counts up, then You win!
shot.shows: The Console window only, after all eight pickups were taken, with lines Score: 1 through Score: 8 and then You win!. Outline the last two lines.

page.title: Why the Console for now
page.text: A counter only remembers. Setting score to score + 1 does not change anything on the screen by itself. Right now the Console is the only place you can see it. You fix that next.

You have eight Pickups in the Hierarchy. Each one vanishes when touched, and the Console shows Score: 1 up to Score: 8, then You win! once. It has gone wrong if You win! appears early or never: Total Pickups does not match the number of Pickups you made.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text: 1. A copy does not vanish or count: its tag is not Pickup. Click it and check the Tag dropdown. 2. The score goes up by more than 1 for one pickup: the Ball is touching two copies at the same place. Check the positions list and move one. 3. error CS0103: The name ‘totalPickups’ does not exist in the current context: the new variables were not saved. Check the spelling and that the lines sit inside the class, above `Start`.
Show the score and a win message on screen

A player never opens the Console, so the score has to be on screen. Unity draws text with TextMeshPro, and a Canvas is the flat layer that holds on-screen text and buttons. In this part you make two text objects, one for the score and one for the win message, and let the script change them.

items.text: In the top menu bar, choose **GameObject > UI (Canvas) > Text - TextMeshPro**.

If a window titled **TMP Importer** opens, click **Import TMP Essentials**, then click **Import Anyway** in the box titled Unofficial Unity source that follows (the package comes with Unity itself). Wait for it to finish and close the TMP Importer window. This happens once per project. If the Console shows a red line or two about layout straight after, click **Clear**: they do not come back.

shot.alt: Box titled Unofficial Unity source. It lists TMP Essential Resources by UnityTechnologies and has two buttons, Cancel and Import Anyway; Import Anyway is outlined.
shot.caption: After you click Import TMP Essentials, Unity asks about the package: click Import Anyway.
shot.shows: The TMP Importer window only, with the Import TMP Essentials button. Outline the button.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, find **Text (TMP)** under **Canvas** and click it.
Choose **Edit > Rename** (F2 on Windows, Enter on a Mac), type ScoreText and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, find **TextMeshPro - Text (UI)** and type Score: 0 / 8 into the **Text Input** box.
Set **Font Size** to 36.
In **Rect Transform**, click the square anchor presets button at the top left of the component. In the grid that opens, click the preset in the row marked top and the column marked left.
Type 220 into **Pos X**, -40 into **Pos Y**, 400 into **Width** and 60 into **Height**.

shot.alt: ScoreText Inspector with Pos X 220, Pos Y -40, Width 400, Height 60 and text Score: 0 / 8.
shot.caption: ScoreText: anchored top left, Pos X 220, Pos Y -40, Width 400, Height 60, and the text Score: 0 / 8.
shot.shows: The Inspector only for ScoreText, with Rect Transform showing Pos X 220, Pos Y -40, Width 400, Height 60, and the Text Input reading Score: 0 / 8.

items.text: Choose **GameObject > UI (Canvas) > Text - TextMeshPro** again.
In the **Hierarchy**, click the new **Text (TMP)** under **Canvas**. Choose **Edit > Rename**, type WinText and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, type You win! into the **Text Input** box.
Set **Font Size** to 80.
Under **Alignment**, click the horizontal center button, the second one in the first group of icons.
In **Rect Transform**, type 0 into **Pos X** and 0 into **Pos Y**, then 800 into **Width** and 150 into **Height**.

shot.alt: Game view with Score: 0 / 8 at the top left and You win! in the center.
shot.caption: Both texts in the Game view before Play: the score at the top left, the win message in the middle.
shot.shows: The Game view only, at 16:9 Aspect, with Score: 0 / 8 at the top left and You win! in the middle.

page.text: Now the script. A `TMP_Text` variable works like the Rigidbody variable you already know, but it points at a text object on the screen. Setting its `text` property changes what the player sees. You add one line at the top, two variables, two lines in `Start`, and a new `OnTriggerEnter`.

items.text: Open **BallController** in Visual Studio Code.
At the top, add `using TMPro;` under the existing using lines, as in the first code block below.

Find the line `public int totalPickups = 8;` and add only `public TMP_Text scoreText;` and `public TMP_Text winText;` under it, each on its own line. In the second code example, the totalPickups line and the Start declaration show the surrounding code; do not copy those two lines.
In `Start`, add the two lines under the line that fills `rb`, as in the third code block.
Replace the whole `OnTriggerEnter` method with the fourth code block.
Save the file (Ctrl+S on Windows, Command+S on a Mac), then click back into Unity and wait for the spinning icon at the bottom right to stop.

page.caption: Top of BallController.cs
Text variables
Inside Start
The OnTriggerEnter with text

page.text: What changed: `using TMPro;` lets the script use `TMP_Text`. `winText.text = "";` in `Start` empties the win message, so it is hidden until the player has earned it. `scoreText.text = "Score: " + score + " / " + totalPickups;` joins words and numbers: with score 3 and totalPickups 8 it reads Score: 3 / 8. It runs at the start and after every pickup, so the screen always matches the counter. When the counter reaches the total, the win message is filled in. The variables stay empty until you drag the text objects into them, which you do now.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, click **Ball**.
In the **Inspector**, find **Ball Controller (Script)**. It now shows **Score Text** and **Win Text**, both reading None.
Drag **ScoreText** from the **Hierarchy** onto **Score Text**.
Drag **WinText** from the **Hierarchy** onto **Win Text**.

shot.alt: Ball Controller (Script) with Score Text ScoreText and Win Text WinText.
shot.caption: Score Text and Win Text filled in on the Ball.
shot.shows: The Inspector only for Ball, scrolled to Ball Controller (Script), with Score Text set to ScoreText and Win Text set to WinText.

items.text: Click **Play**, click once inside the **Game** view, and collect all eight pickups.
Click **Play** again to stop.

page.alt: Score: 0 / 8 at the top left rises to Score: 8 / 8 as the pickups vanish, then You win! appears in the center.
page.caption: All eight pickups in one run.
page.shows: The Game view only, at 16:9 Aspect, in Play. Roll the Ball over all eight pickups. Keep the top-left score text and the center of the screen both in frame. End two seconds after You win! appears. Under one minute.

page.text: In Play, the screen shows Score: 0 / 8 at the top left and no win message. Each pickup raises the score by 1. After the eighth, You win! appears in the middle. It has gone wrong if the Console shows red text when you press Play.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text: 1. NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object, as soon as you press Play: Score Text or Win Text still says None on the Ball. Drag the text objects in again. 2. error CS0246: The type or namespace name ‘TMP_Text’ could not be found: the line `using TMPro;` is missing or misspelled at the top of the file. 3. You win! is visible before you collect anything: the script is not saved, or Unity has not finished compiling. Save, wait for the spinning icon to stop, and press Play again. 4. The score text is cut off or not visible: check the Rect Transform values and that the Game view is on 16:9 Aspect.
Playtest your build and save a checkpoint

You play your game on purpose, trying to break it, so you find problems before anyone else does. You also practice the recording and the screenshot you will need to show your game at the end of the week.

items.text: Click **Play** and click once inside the **Game** view.
Collect all eight pickups, then watch the screen for You win!.
Click **Play** to stop, then start it again and click inside the **Game** view.
Drive the Ball along a wall and onto the Ramp, and check that no pickup is missed or counted twice.

Click **Play** to stop, then click the **Console** tab and look for red or yellow lines. If any appear, fix their causes before continuing. Once those checks pass, click **Clear** in the Console toolbar to remove the messages from your earlier tests.
Choose **File > Save**. The asterisk after Arena in the **Hierarchy** disappears.

shot.alt: Hierarchy with Arena saved, no asterisk.
shot.caption: Saved: no asterisk after Arena at the top of the Hierarchy.
shot.shows: The Hierarchy window only, with Arena at the top and no asterisk after its name, and the Console tab empty beside it.

page.text: Practice a screenshot and a screen recording now, so they are easy later. Screenshot, Windows: press the Windows key + Shift + S, drag a box around the Game view, then click the notification that appears and choose Save. Screenshot, Mac: press Command + Shift + 4, drag a box around the Game view, and the picture lands on your Desktop. Recording, Windows 11: open Snipping Tool, click the video camera button, click New, drag a box around the Game view, click Start, play your game, then click Stop; the clip is saved for you. On Windows 10, press the Windows key + G to open Xbox Game Bar and use its Capture panel. Recording, Mac: press Command + Shift + 5, click Record Selected Portion, drag a box around the Game view, click Record, play your game, then click the stop button in the menu bar; the file lands on your Desktop. Keep both practice files small: a 20-second clip is plenty.

page.label: OrbCollector_Collisions_Checkpoint.zip
page.shows: A zipped Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1) project named OrbCollector, as it should stand at the end of this week: Assets/Scripts holding BallController (with score, totalPickups, scoreText, winText and OnTriggerEnter), CameraFollow and Rotator; eight yellow Pickup objects tagged Pickup with Is Trigger ticked and Rotator attached; the PickupYellow material; a Canvas with ScoreText and WinText; an EventSystem; the Ball with its two text objects assigned; the scene saved.

page.text: Use the checkpoint project to compare with your own, or to carry on if your project is broken beyond repair. Do not unzip it into the folder that holds your own OrbCollector. Unzip it onto your Desktop. Windows: right-click the ZIP in File Explorer, choose Extract All..., choose the Desktop, then click Extract. Mac: double-click the ZIP in Finder and drag the folder it makes onto the Desktop. To open it: in Unity Hub, click Projects, open the Add dropdown, choose Add project from disk, select the unzipped folder (the one that contains an Assets folder), then click the project in the list.

page.alt: Game view showing Score: 8 / 8 at the top left and You win! in the center.
page.caption: Score: 8 / 8 and You win!
page.shows: The Game view only, at 16:9 Aspect, in Play, just after the last pickup: Score: 8 / 8 at the top left and You win! in the middle.

page.text: All eight pickups vanish, the score reaches Score: 8 / 8, You win! appears, the Console is clear and the scene is saved. You also have a practice screenshot and a practice recording of the Game view. It has gone wrong if the Console has red lines, or the asterisk still shows after Arena.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text: 1. The recording is black or empty: on a Mac, allow screen recording for your recorder in System Settings > Privacy & Security, then try again. 2. The Game view is too small in the picture: make the box larger, or open the Play Focused dropdown in the Game view toolbar and choose Play Maximized before you record. 3. A missed pickup: it may sit inside a wall or the Ramp. Move its X and Z in the Inspector and save again.
Challenges

These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change the code is how scripting sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks. Click inside the Game view before each test.
Challenge: a trap (this is the build you submit)

Add a Trap to the Arena. It is a cube at any open spot on the Floor, with a material named TrapRed whose Hexadecimal is E02020, and the tag Trap. When the Ball touches it, the Trap vanishes and the score drops by 1, but never below 0, and the score text on screen shows the new number.

Try it on paper: if you have collected 3 pickups, the text reads Score: 3 / 8 and then Score: 2 / 8 after the Trap. If you hit the Trap first, the text still reads Score: 0 / 8.

Track collected pickups separately so the Trap cannot prevent a win. The Trap changes score only. You win after collecting all eight pickups, even if the penalty leaves the score at 7 / 8.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Add the tag Trap the same way you added Pickup. A copy of a Pickup keeps the Pickup tag and Rotator, so change its tag. In `OnTriggerEnter`, put `else if (other.CompareTag("Trap"))` after the closing brace of the Pickup `if`. Inside, `Destroy` the Trap, then use `if (score > 0)` before you subtract 1, and set `scoreText.text` the same way as for a pickup. To keep the win within reach, add `private int pickupsCollected = 0;` beside the score variable in BallController. Inside the Pickup branch, add `pickupsCollected = pickupsCollected + 1;` immediately after the score increases. Change the win condition to `if (pickupsCollected >= totalPickups)`.
Optional challenge: a timer

Add a third text object named TimerText at the top right. It reads Time: 0.0 when you press Play and counts up in seconds, with one digit after the point. If you wait 5 seconds without touching a pickup, it reads about Time: 5.0. When the eighth pickup is collected it stops, so the number you see with You win! stays on screen.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Add a public float named timeUsed and a public TMP_Text named timerText. In `Update`, add `Time.deltaTime` to timeUsed only while `pickupsCollected < totalPickups`. The text shows `"Time: " + timeUsed.ToString("0.0")`. Do not forget to drag TimerText onto Timer Text on the Ball.

Your Trap vanishes and lowers the score, never below 0, and the score text matches. If you did the timer, it counts up and stops at the win. It has gone wrong if the Trap raises the score: it still has the tag Pickup.
Wrap-up

You can now make a trigger, tag an object, and write OnTriggerEnter with CompareTag so the Ball reacts to pickups. You can count with an int and an if, and show the score and a win message with TMP_Text. Test yourself. First, what must be ticked on the pickup’s collider so the Ball passes through it, and what does CompareTag check? Second, what does score = score + 1 do, and what does the if after it ask? Third, why must you drag the text objects onto the Ball? Next week has an optional reading, the Object Pool chapter of Nystrom (2014), Game programming patterns; next week’s page gives the link and questions to guide you. Next time you start Dodge: you spawn a hazard at random positions on a faster and faster timer, and destroy it.

facilitation.announcement: This week the Ball learns to collect. You build a spinning Pickup, detect the touch with a trigger and a tag, count a score, and show a score and a win message on screen. The one thing to get right: the tag is spelled exactly the same in the Inspector and in your script, capital P included. Post your first forum post by Thursday. Replies, the weekly build and all other work are due Sunday night. If something breaks, post the exact red text from the Console in the forum.
watchFor: Tag typos, such as pickup against Pickup, or a tag never saved in the Tags list. Ask for the Inspector’s Tag box and the CompareTag line side by side; they must match letter for letter.
Is Trigger left unticked, so the Ball bumps the pickup and nothing happens. Ask what the Console shows when they touch it, then point them to Box Collider.
NullReferenceException on Play, because Score Text or Win Text on the Ball still says None. Tell them to drag ScoreText and WinText from the Hierarchy onto the Ball’s fields.
Total Pickups not matching the real number of pickups, so the win comes early or never. Ask them to count the Pickup entries in the Hierarchy.

Old-style code from older tutorials, such as Input.GetKey or rb.velocity, pasted into BallController. Point them to Keyboard.current from week 4, and tell them rb.velocity is now called linearVelocity.
Submitted recordings that cut off before the win message, or a Game view too small to read. Ask for a new recording that shows the score and You win!.
feedback: Your pickups vanish and the score counts up correctly. Your recording shows Score: 8 / 8 and You win!, which is exactly the loop this week asked for.
The Console is clear and the scene is saved, so your project is in good shape. Keep checking that habit before you submit anything.
Your tag matches in the Inspector and in the script. Tags are plain text, so this is the detail that most often goes wrong, and you got it right.
Your score text reads well in the corner. Try a bigger Font Size or a different position, and see how it changes how the game feels.
Your recording shows the Game view only, which is clear. Next time try to show a few seconds of play before the first pickup, so a viewer sees what you are aiming for.
If you tried the Trap or the timer, tell the forum what you changed in OnTriggerEnter or Update. Explaining it in your own words is how it sticks.

Offer the checkpoint project from the page and ask them to post the exact error text so the group can help. Pay particular attention to students who wrote that they are behind on setup from earlier in the course.

l_f92b7bf6c031.title: Prefabs and spawning
l_f92b7bf6c031.summary: Start Dodge: spawn a hazard prefab at random positions on a faster-and-faster timer, and destroy it; submit a recording and screenshot.
suggestedReadings: Nystrom, R. (2014). Game programming patterns. Genever Benning. (Object Pool chapter)
keyIdeas: A prefab is a saved template of a GameObject, kept as a file in your Project window. Every copy made from it is an instance. Change the template and the instances follow, except for values you changed on one copy.

`Instantiate` makes a new instance of a prefab while the game runs. You tell it which prefab, where to put it and which way to face. `Random.Range` picks a number between two values, so each copy lands somewhere different.

A timer is a float that you add `Time.deltaTime` to every frame. When it passes the interval, you act and reset it to 0. Multiplying the interval by a number below 1 after each spawn makes the game faster, and `Mathf.Max` with a floor value stops it reaching 0.

Whatever the game creates, it must also remove. `Destroy(gameObject, seconds)` removes an object after a delay, so hazards do not pile up and slow the game. Nystrom (2014) describes an object pool, which reuses objects instead.

vocabulary.definition: A saved template of a GameObject, kept as a file in the Project window, that you can copy again and again.
One copy made from a prefab, which follows the prefab unless you change a value on that copy.
The method that makes a new instance of a prefab while the game runs, at a position and rotation you give.
A method that returns a number between two values you give it, so each call can give a different result.
The value that means no rotation, used when a new copy should not be turned at all.
The number of seconds the spawner waits before making the next hazard.
A method that returns the larger of two numbers, used here to stop the interval falling below a floor.
An object in the scene whose script creates new objects while the game runs.
A set of objects made once and reused, instead of being destroyed and created again, to save the game from creating thousands of objects.

study.overview: This week you started Dodge and built the loop that makes it run. You can now save one hazard as a prefab, spawn copies of it at random spots on a timer that gets shorter, and remove each copy when it has done its job. You also met the object pool, which Nystrom (2014) offers as another way to handle objects a game makes and frees often. Come back to this page before next week, when you add lives, a game over and a restart on top of the same project.

points.heading: A prefab is a template, and copies are instances
points.explanation: A prefab is a saved template of a GameObject, kept as a file in your Project window. Every copy made from it is an instance. When you change the template, the instances follow, except for values you changed on one copy. For example, you dragged two Hazard copies into the scene and typed a different Position on each. Then you set the prefab’s Scale to 1, 1, 1. Both copies took the new Scale, but each kept its own Position. You can now turn any object into a prefab by dragging it from the Hierarchy into a folder such as Prefabs, then delete the original so the spawner is the only thing making hazards.

points.heading: Instantiate and a timer spawn hazards at random spots
points.explanation: `Instantiate(hazardPrefab, position, Quaternion.identity);` makes one new instance while the game runs. You give it three things: which prefab, where to put it and which way to face. `Quaternion.identity` means no turn. `Random.Range(-areaHalfWidth, areaHalfWidth)` picks a number between -6 and 6, so each copy lands somewhere different. Run it once for x and once for z. The timer is a float: `timer += Time.deltaTime;` adds the seconds each frame took. When `timer >= interval`, you reset it to 0 and call `Spawn()`. To speed the game up, write `interval = Mathf.Max(interval * speedUp, minInterval);`. With speedUp at 0.95, each wait is 5 percent shorter, and `Mathf.Max` stops it going below 0.4. In your build the wait began at 2 seconds and fell toward 0.4. If nothing spawns and the Console says the prefab is not assigned, drag the Hazard prefab into the Hazard Prefab field on Spawner.

points.heading: Whatever the game creates, it must also remove
points.explanation: If hazards are only ever created, they pile up on the Floor and slow the game. `Destroy(gameObject, lifetime);` in `Start` gives every copy its own countdown. With a lifetime of 6, a hazard made at second 10 disappears at second 16. That is why the Hierarchy list stayed short while you played: it held about three Hazard(Clone) entries early on and about fifteen once the interval reached 0.4. Put the script on the prefab, not on a copy, so every new hazard carries it. Nystrom (2014) describes an object pool, which keeps objects and reuses them instead of destroying them. You used `Instantiate` and `Destroy` because they are easy to follow with a few hazards. You can now explain this choice, and say that a pool is worth considering if removing and creating objects causes performance problems you have measured.

page.text: Last time you finished the main loop of Orb Collector: touch a pickup, change the score, tell the player. This week you start a second game, Dodge, and turn the idea around. Instead of things you collect, things come for you. You make one hazard, save it as a prefab, and let a script create copies at random spots, faster and faster. Each copy is removed when it is no longer needed. By Sunday you will have a Dodge project where you move a player while hazards fall and vanish, and you will be able to explain how each piece works.

page.text: Update reads the keys and stores them in moveInput. Each line with `isPressed` adds 1 or takes away 1, so pressing A and D together cancels out. Part 3: Learn the idea: read about reusing objects and watch how spawning works
Before you build the spawner, you need the ideas behind it: a prefab, Instantiate, a timer and Destroy. Reading about a different way to handle them also lets you explain why you choose this one.

Optional reading: the Object Pool chapter of Nystrom, R. (2014). Game programming patterns. Genever Benning. It is free to read at gameprogrammingpatterns.com/object-pool.html. Its code samples are in C++, a different language from yours: skip the code and read the prose. You do not need the chapter to finish the week, because the video below gives the idea you use. The pattern is an alternative to creating and destroying objects over and over. If you read it, look for three things and write a sentence for each in your own words:

items: What goes wrong when a game keeps creating and freeing many small objects, and why a game with a few hazards is much less at risk than a game with thousands of particles.
What a pool holds, and what it does when the game asks for a new object and when the game is finished with one.
What you must take care of when you reuse an object, such as its leftover state and the size of the pool.

page.text: Dodge starts with one hazard every 2 seconds and speeds up to one every 0.4 seconds. You use `Instantiate` and `Destroy` because they make the object lifecycle easy to follow. If creating and removing objects later causes measured performance problems, consider an object pool. Now watch the video.

page.alt: Four slides: a prefab and its copies, the Instantiate line with its three parts, a timer and shrinking interval, and Destroy with a delay.
page.caption: Watch for the four words: prefab, Instantiate, interval and Destroy.
page.shows: A slide deck. Slide 1: one Hazard prefab file with three copies named Hazard(Clone) beside it. Slide 2: the line Instantiate(hazardPrefab, position, Quaternion.identity) with the three parts labeled. Slide 3: a timer bar filling up, with Interval 2 shrinking to 1.9 and 1.8. Slide 4: a hazard with Destroy(gameObject, 6f) and a countdown.
page.transcript:
Hi. This week you make hazards fall in Dodge. Four ideas do the work: a prefab, Instantiate, a timer and Destroy.

First, the prefab. Last time you made eight pickups by hand, one at a time. A hazard that appears while the game is running cannot be made by hand, because you are not there to drag it in. So you save one hazard as a prefab. A prefab is a saved template of a GameObject, kept as a file in your Project window. It remembers the shape, the material, the Rigidbody and every script on it. Each copy made from it is called an instance. Change the template, and the instances follow, except for any value you changed on one copy.

Second, Instantiate. This is the line that makes a copy while the game runs. It takes three things: which prefab, where to put it, and which way to face. For the position you want a different spot each time, so you use Random.Range. Random.Range of minus six and six gives a number somewhere between those two values. Do it once for x and once for z, and each hazard gets an independently chosen spawn position. Positions can repeat. For facing, you write Quaternion dot identity, which means no turn at all. A sphere does not care which way it faces.

Third, the timer. A timer is a float that you add Time.deltaTime to in every frame. Time.deltaTime is the seconds the last frame took, so the number counts real seconds on any computer. When the timer passes the interval, you spawn a hazard and set the timer back to zero. To speed the game up, you multiply the interval by point nine five after each spawn. Two seconds becomes one point nine, then one point eight, and so on. Without a limit it would shrink toward zero and flood the game, so you use Mathf.Max to keep the interval from dropping below a floor of point four.

Fourth, Destroy. Everything you create has to be removed, or the hazards pile up and slow the game down. Destroy takes an object and, if you like, a delay in seconds. Destroy of gameObject, comma, six, removes the hazard six seconds after it was made. Lower case gameObject means this very object.

Now connect this to the optional reading. Nystrom describes an object pool, which keeps finished objects and reuses them instead of destroying them. A pool can help when frequent object creation and removal causes performance problems. Dodge makes a few hazards per second, so you start with `Instantiate` and `Destroy` and check how the game runs. Knowing why you are choosing it is the point.

Next you build each piece in order: the prefab, then the spawner, then the cleanup. Go and build it.

page.text: You can say in your own words what a prefab, Instantiate, an interval and Destroy each do. If you read the optional chapter, you have also written one sentence for each of the three questions. If one is unclear, watch the matching part of the video again before you build.

Part 5: Spawn hazards with Instantiate and a timer
Now the game makes its own hazards. In this part you write the spawner: a timer that counts seconds, makes a hazard at a random spot when the interval passes, then waits a little less each time.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the **Scripts** folder under **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type HazardSpawner and press Enter.
Double-click **HazardSpawner**. Select everything in the file (Ctrl+A on Windows, Command+A on a Mac), delete it, then type or paste the code from the block below.

page.caption: HazardSpawner.cs

items: `[SerializeField] private GameObject hazardPrefab;` is a slot in the Inspector. You drag the prefab into it, so the script knows what to copy.

`public float interval = 2f;` is the wait in seconds. It shows in the Inspector, so you can watch it change while the game runs. It is public, like the variables in Orb Collector; the other settings use `[SerializeField] private`, which shows them in the Inspector too.
`timer += Time.deltaTime;` adds the seconds the last frame took, so timer counts real seconds on any computer.
`if (timer >= interval)` asks whether enough time has passed. If yes, the lines inside run: timer goes back to 0 and `Spawn()` runs.
`interval = Mathf.Max(interval * speedUp, minInterval);` makes the next wait 5 percent shorter. `Mathf.Max` returns the larger of two numbers, so the result is never below 0.4.
`Random.Range(-areaHalfWidth, areaHalfWidth)` gives a number between -6 and 6. It runs once for x and once for z.
`Instantiate(hazardPrefab, position, Quaternion.identity);` makes the copy. The three parts are which prefab, where, and which way to face. `Quaternion.identity` means no turn.

items.text: Save the file (Ctrl+S on Windows, Command+S on a Mac), then click back into Unity and wait for the spinning icon at the bottom right to stop.

Part 6: Destroy hazards you no longer need
A game that only creates objects slowly chokes on them. In this part you give every hazard a lifetime, so it removes itself, and you check that the cleanup works.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the **Scripts** folder under **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type HazardLifetime and press Enter.
Double-click **HazardLifetime**. Select everything in the file, delete it, then type or paste the code from the block below.

page.caption: HazardLifetime.cs

page.text: `Start` runs once, when a copy is made. `gameObject` means the object this script is on, and `Destroy(gameObject, lifetime)` removes it after `lifetime` seconds. Every copy carries its own countdown, so a hazard made at second 10 disappears at second 16.

items.text: Save the file (Ctrl+S on Windows, Command+S on a Mac), then click back into Unity and wait for the spinning icon at the bottom right to stop.
In the **Project** window, click the **Prefabs** folder, then click the **Hazard** prefab.
In the **Inspector**, click **Add Component**, type HazardLifetime and press Enter.
Check that **Hazard Lifetime (Script)** is listed with **Lifetime** 6.
Choose **File > Save**.
Click **Play**, then click once inside the **Game** view.
Look at the **Hierarchy**. Each **Hazard(Clone)** appears when it is made and vanishes about 6 seconds later.
Keep watching for 20 seconds. Older entries disappear while new ones appear. The number alive rises as spawning speeds up: expect about three entries early on and about five at 20 seconds.
Click **Spawner** in the **Hierarchy** and watch **Interval** in the **Inspector** go down.
Click **Play** to stop.
Check that **Play** is no longer highlighted and that the **Hierarchy** lists no **Hazard(Clone)** entries. Leave Play off: the next part begins by pressing it.

Part 8: Challenges

These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change the code is how scripting sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks. Click inside the Game view before each test.

Challenge 1: double up. Change HazardSpawner so that once Interval is below 1, each timer tick makes two hazards instead of one, at two different random spots. Try it on paper: with Interval at 1.5 one hazard appears per tick, with Interval at 0.9 two appear, and with Interval at 0.4 it is still two, not more.

page.title: Hint for challenge 1
page.text: `Spawn()` picks random coordinates every time it runs. Calling it twice gives two independently chosen positions, which can coincide. For this challenge, two independent selections satisfy the requirement for two random spots. After the call to Spawn() inside the timer if, add a second if that asks whether interval is below 1f and, if so, calls Spawn() again.

Challenge 2 (optional): random sizes. Give each hazard a random size. Every hazard is a sphere between 0.5 and 1.5 across, the same on x, y and z, and a new size is picked for each one. Try it on paper: if Random.Range gives 1.2, the Scale is 1.2, 1.2, 1.2. No hazard is ever smaller than 0.5 or larger than 1.5. It should work with challenge 1, so both hazards of a pair get their own size.

page.title: Hint for challenge 2
page.text: Instantiate gives back the new object. Catch it in a variable: `GameObject hazard = Instantiate(hazardPrefab, position, Quaternion.identity);` Then set its size on the next line with `hazard.transform.localScale = Vector3.one * size;` after you pick `float size = Random.Range(0.5f, 1.5f);`. Change it in Spawn() only, so both hazards in challenge 1 are covered.
Your challenge version still runs with the Console clear. If a change breaks the game, undo it in the script until it runs again, then retry in smaller steps. Choose File > Save when it works.
Wrap-up

You can now save a GameObject as a prefab, spawn copies at random positions with Instantiate and a timer that speeds up, and remove hazards with Destroy once they have done their job. Test yourself. First, what does a prefab hold, and what is a copy of it called? Second, what are the three things you give Instantiate, and what does Random.Range add? Third, why must every hazard be destroyed, and what does an object pool do differently? Next time you add lives, a game over and a restart, using methods and buttons, so Dodge can be lost and played again.

l_facbf674ef99.title: Game state and UI
l_facbf674ef99.summary: Add lives, game over and restart with methods and buttons, so Dodge can be lost and replayed; submit a recording and screenshot.
keyIdeas: Game state is the set of values that describe the game right now, such as how many lives are left and whether the game is over. Scripts change it and the screen shows it.
A method is a named block of code that does one job. Writing `LoseLife()` once lets any script run it by name, and `public` is what lets another script call it.
UI text and buttons live under a Canvas. A Button’s On Click list can call any public method on an object in your scene, with no code on the button itself.
`SceneManager.LoadScene` reloads the saved scene, so lives, hazards and the spawner interval all start fresh. `Time.timeScale` set to 0 freezes the game and stays 0 until you set it back.

vocabulary.definition: The values that describe the game right now, such as lives left and whether the game is over.
A named block of code that does one job and runs when you call its name.
A script that keeps one part of the game state, so other scripts ask it instead of keeping their own copy.
A public method can be called from other scripts, and a private one only from its own script.
A keyword that leaves a method early, before the rest of it runs.
A number that sets how fast game time runs: 1 is normal and 0 freezes it until you set it back.
A method that loads a saved scene, so loading the running scene again restarts the game.
A list on a Button that names the public methods to run when the button is clicked.
A UI rectangle that holds other UI objects, so you can show or hide them together.

study.overview: This week Dodge became a game you can lose and play again. You can now keep the game’s state in one script, write your own methods that other scripts and buttons can call, show lives and a Game over screen with TextMeshPro and a Button, and reload the scene so every game starts fresh. Reread this page before next week, when you add sound and particles on top of this working loop.

points.heading: Game state lives in one manager script
points.explanation: Game state is the set of values that describe the game right now. In Dodge that is `int lives` (for example 3) and `bool isGameOver` (true or false). Keep both in `GameManager` and let other scripts ask the manager instead of keeping their own count. Scripts change the state, and the screen shows it: `UpdateLivesText()` copies the number onto the screen with `livesText.text = "Lives: " + lives;`, so 3 reads Lives: 3. Add a guard at the top of `LoseLife()`, `if (isGameOver) { return; }`, so a late hazard cannot take a life after the game has ended and push the text below zero. You can now decide what values your game needs, store them in one place and refresh the text whenever they change.

points.heading: Write methods that other scripts can call
points.explanation: A method is a named block of code that does one job. Write `LoseLife()` once and any script can run it by name. `public` is what lets another script call it, while `private` keeps a method for its own script. `void` means it does its job and gives nothing back. Example: `PlayerHit` finds the manager with `FindAnyObjectByType<GameManager>()`. When `OnCollisionEnter` sees an object where `CompareTag("Hazard")` is true, it calls `gameManager.LoseLife();` and then `Destroy(collision.gameObject);`, so one hazard costs one life. The Player only says it was hit. The manager decides what that means, and when lives reach 0 it runs `GameOver()`. The tag goes on the Hazard prefab, so every copy the spawner makes carries it. You can now split a job into small methods and call them from other scripts.

points.heading: Build UI under a Canvas and wire a button without code
points.explanation: All UI text and buttons live under a Canvas, and the EventSystem lets a Button notice a click. Your Game over screen is a GameOverPanel holding a Text - TextMeshPro that reads Game over and a Button - TextMeshPro named RestartButton. The button needs no script. In its On Click () list you add an entry, drag the GameManager object from the Hierarchy into the box, and choose GameManager > Restart (). That works only because `Restart()` is `public`. You can now build a screen, hide it at the start with `gameOverPanel.SetActive(false);` and show it with `SetActive(true)` when the game ends.

points.heading: Reload the scene and set time running again
points.explanation: `SceneManager.LoadScene(SceneManager.GetActiveScene().name);` loads the running scene again from its saved file, so lives, hazards and the spawner’s Interval all start fresh. Save with File > Save before you test, or Restart brings back an older version. At game over `Time.timeScale = 0f;` freezes the hazards, and it stays 0 until you set it back. That is why `Start` begins with `Time.timeScale = 1f;`. Without that line the second game starts frozen. You can now restart a game cleanly and explain why the frozen state has to be reset. If a game opens frozen or with the panel showing, check `Start` first.

page.text: Last week Dodge learned to fill the arena with hazards that spawn more and more frequently. This week it becomes a game you can lose and play again. Each hit costs a life, and at zero lives a Game over screen appears with a Restart button. You write your own methods to hold that logic, build the screen with TextMeshPro and a Button, and reload the scene with `SceneManager.LoadScene`. By Sunday you will have a Dodge that you can lose, restart and replay, ready to be made more exciting next time.

page.text: Last week you built the game’s moving parts: a Player, a spawner and hazards that clean up after themselves. This week the game learns to end. Before you add anything, you check that your project is exactly where last week left it, so the new code has solid ground to stand on.

page.caption: Watch this first. It explains the ideas behind the week’s code, and the written explanation follows in Part 3.

page.transcript:
Hi. This week Dodge learns to be lost. Here is the idea before you touch Unity.

A game remembers things. How many lives you have. Whether the game is over. We call those values the game state. In code, state lives in variables. Lives is a whole number, an int. Is the game over is a bool, which is either true or false.

Something has to change that state. That something is a method. A method is a named block of code that does one job. You already use methods: Start, Update, and Spawn from last week. This week you write your own. One called LoseLife takes a life away and checks whether you have hit zero. One called GameOver ends the game. One called Restart loads it again.

Why give them names? Because the player script does not need to know how losing a life works. When a hazard touches the player, it just says: game manager, lose a life. The details stay in one place. If you change the rules later, you change one method.

The word public means other scripts can call the method. Private means only this script can. LoseLife is public because the player calls it. UpdateLivesText is private, because only the manager uses it.

On screen, you build a Canvas with a text object for the lives, and a panel with a Game over message and a Button. Clicking the button calls Restart, and Restart calls SceneManager dot LoadScene, which reloads your saved scene. Everything starts fresh: lives, hazards, the spawner’s interval.

One trap. When the game ends we freeze time by setting Time dot timeScale to zero. That stays zero after a reload unless you set it back, so the manager sets it back in Start.

Let’s build it.

page.title: Why a Canvas and an EventSystem?
page.text: The Canvas holds every piece of UI and keeps it on screen. The EventSystem is what lets a Button notice a mouse click. Unity added both when you made the first UI object.

No text in the Game view. You may be looking at the Scene view: click the **Game** tab. Then check that **Pos X** is 130 and **Pos Y** is -40 and that you chose the top-left anchor preset.

Part 3: Write the GameManager methods

This part writes the code that remembers and changes the lives. You wrote your own `Spawn()` method last time. This week you write methods that another script and a button can call, so the reasons come first and then the code.

A method is a named block of code that does one job. `Start` and `Update` are methods Unity calls for you. `Spawn()` in HazardSpawner is a method that you call yourself, by writing its name with brackets. This week you write several. A method that nobody should call from outside is `private`. One that other scripts need to call is `public`. The word `void` means the method does its job but gives nothing back.

The lives themselves are game state. A variable `int lives` holds a whole number. A variable `bool isGameOver` holds true or false. Methods change them, and one method, `UpdateLivesText`, copies the number onto the screen. Keeping the state in one script, called a manager, means every other script asks the manager instead of keeping its own count.

page.text: Line by line. `using TMPro;` lets the script use `TMP_Text`, the type of TextMeshPro text. `[SerializeField] private int startingLives = 3;` makes a box in the Inspector for the starting number. `[SerializeField] private TMP_Text livesText;` makes a box that you filled by dragging LivesText into it. `private int lives;` and `private bool isGameOver;` are the game state. They are private because only this script changes them.

`Start` runs once when Play begins. It sets `lives` to the starting number, says the game is not over, and calls `UpdateLivesText();`, which runs the method at the bottom. `public void LoseLife()` is the method other scripts will call. Its first job is a guard: `if (isGameOver) { return; }`. The word `return` leaves the method early, so once the game is over a late hazard cannot take another life. Then `lives = lives - 1;` takes a life, the text is refreshed, and `if (lives <= 0)` calls `GameOver();`. In `UpdateLivesText`, `"Lives: " + lives` joins the words and the number, so 3 becomes Lives: 3. For now `GameOver` sets the flag and `Debug.Log` writes Game over to the Console. Part 5 gives it a screen.
The Game Manager (Script) has Starting Lives 3 and LivesText in its Lives Text box. In Play the Game view shows Lives: 3 and the Console shows no red lines. Nothing takes a life yet. That comes next.

Part 4: Make a hit cost a life

The manager can now lose a life, but nothing asks it to. Here a small script on the Player notices a hazard touching it and calls `LoseLife()`. The Player does not need to know how a life is lost. It only needs to say that it was hit.

The script has to tell hazards from anything else the Player touches, such as the Floor. A tag is a label you put on an object. You give the Hazard prefab the tag Hazard, and the script checks for it with `CompareTag`. Because you tag the prefab, every copy the spawner makes carries the tag too.

page.text: `private GameManager gameManager;` is a box that will hold a reference to your manager. In `Start`, `FindAnyObjectByType<GameManager>()` searches the scene and returns a GameManager, and you keep it. `OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)` is a method Unity calls on its own the moment this object touches another solid object. `collision.gameObject` is the thing that touched you. `CompareTag("Hazard")` is true only for objects with the Hazard tag. Then `gameManager.LoseLife();` is a call to the public method you wrote in Part 3, and `Destroy(collision.gameObject);` removes that hazard, so one sphere costs one life, not three.

page.text: What the new lines do. `SetActive(false)` hides a GameObject and `SetActive(true)` shows it, so the panel is hidden when Play begins and appears at game over. `Time.timeScale = 0f;` freezes everything that depends on time, so hazards stop falling. page.text: Part 7: Challenges

These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change the code is how scripting sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks. Click inside the Game view before each test.

Challenge 1: a survival timer. Add a second TextMeshPro text at the top right of the Game view that reads Time: 0.0 and counts up in seconds while you play. It stops counting when the game is over and starts again from 0.0 after Restart. Try it on paper: after 12 seconds alive it reads Time: 12.0. If your third hit comes at 12.3 seconds it stays at Time: 12.3 behind the Game over panel. After Restart it reads Time: 0.0.

page.title: Hint for challenge 1
page.text: Keep a float in GameManager and add `Time.deltaTime` to it in `Update`, only while `isGameOver` is false. Write it on screen with `timerText.text = "Time: " + survivedTime.ToString("F1");`. Make `timerText` a `[SerializeField] private TMP_Text`, like `livesText`, and drag the new text into it. A scene reload sets the float back to 0 for you.

Challenge 2 (optional): press R to restart. When the Game over panel is showing, pressing R does the same as clicking Restart. While you are still playing, R does nothing. Try it on paper: at Lives: 2 pressing R changes nothing. At Game over pressing R brings back Lives: 3 and falling hazards.

page.title: Hint for challenge 2
page.text: Add `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` at the top of GameManager. In `Update`, check `isGameOver` first, then read `Keyboard.current.rKey.wasPressedThisFrame`, and call `Restart();` when it is true. Do not use the old `Input.GetKey`: in this version it throws an error. `Update` still runs while `Time.timeScale` is 0.
Challenge 1 shows a timer in the top-right corner that stops at game over and starts from 0.0 after Restart. If you tried challenge 2, R restarts only at game over. The Console is clear.

The timer keeps counting after game over. Check that the line adding `Time.deltaTime` sits inside an `if (!isGameOver)`.

Console: InvalidOperationException about the Input class. An old `Input.GetKey` line is still there. Replace it with `Keyboard.current.rKey.wasPressedThisFrame`.
Wrap-up

You can now write your own methods, build a text and button UI, and reload a scene. Test yourself. First, what makes `LoseLife` public, and what does `return` do inside it? Second, what does the EventSystem do for a Button, and what does On Click call? Third, why does `Start` set `Time.timeScale` back to 1? Next time you add free CC0 sound effects and particle bursts to Dodge and tune how it feels. Next week has an optional reading: chapter 1, Defining game feel, of Swink, S. (2008). Game feel: A game designer’s guide to virtual sensation. Morgan Kaufmann. The book is not free and you do not need it; next week’s page says what to look for if your library has it.

l_9c6e64ac7518.title: Sound, particles and game feel
l_9c6e64ac7518.summary: Add free CC0 sound effects and particle bursts to Dodge and tune how it feels; submit a recording and screenshot.
suggestedReadings: Swink, S. (2008). Game feel: A game designer's guide to virtual sensation. Morgan Kaufmann
keyIdeas: Game feel is how an action feels to do, apart from the rules. A hit that makes a sound and a burst of sparks feels like a hit. The same hit in silence feels like a bug.

An Audio Source plays sound. Your script tells it which AudioClip to play, how loud, and at what pitch. Each Audio Source has one pitch, so a sound that must always play at normal pitch gets its own Audio Source.
A Particle System makes many small shapes at once. In a script, `Emit(20)` makes exactly 20 at that moment, which suits a burst on a hit.
Tuning means changing one value, playing, and judging that one change. If you change two things at once, you cannot tell which one helped.

vocabulary.definition: How an action feels to do and to see, apart from the rules of the game.
Small touches such as sound and particles that do not change the rules but change how the game feels.
A component that plays sound, like a speaker on an object.
A sound file that an Audio Source can play.
A method that plays a clip once at a given volume, without cutting off a sound already playing.
How high or low a sound is: 1 is the recording as made, lower is deeper, higher is higher.
A license that lets anyone use a work for any purpose, with no credit needed.
A component that makes and moves many small shapes at once, for effects like sparks.
A method that makes an exact number of particles at that moment.
A Particle System setting that decides whether particles move with the object or stay where they were made.
Changing a value, playing, and judging the change, to make an action feel better.

study.overview: You can now make Dodge react to what the player does. A hazard hit plays a thud from a script and bursts orange sparks. The end of the game plays its own falling tone. You also tuned five values by feel, one change per run. This page is what to reread before next week, and it helps with the Weekly builds submission due Sunday night.

points.heading: Game feel is how an action feels to do
points.explanation: Game feel is separate from the rules. In Dodge the rule never changed: a hazard touches you and Lives drops by one. At the start of the week that hit was silent and nothing on screen moved. Once it made a thud and a burst of sparks, it read as a hit. Swink (2008), in Game feel: A game designer’s guide to virtual sensation, raises two ideas: what makes a control feel responsive, and what the author means by polish. Use them as questions when you judge your own game: does the action answer at once, and does it feel finished?

points.heading: Play sound from a script with the right Audio Source
points.explanation: An Audio Source is the speaker and an AudioClip is the recording. Your script chooses the clip, the volume and the pitch. `hitSource.PlayOneShot(hitClip, hitVolume)` plays the clip once, and a second hit can overlap the first. `hitSource.pitch = Random.Range(pitchMin, pitchMax)` gives each hit a slightly different pitch between 0.9 and 1.1. Each Audio Source has only one pitch, and it stays at the last value picked. That is why the game over tone plays from a second Audio Source on GameManager, so its pitch is never changed by a hit. Check for this when you build a sound: if it must always play at normal pitch, give it its own Audio Source.

points.heading: Make a burst with Emit
points.explanation: A Particle System makes many small shapes at once. For a hit you want a burst and not a constant stream. On Sparks you turned off Looping and Play On Awake and set Rate over Time to 0, so it stays quiet. Then `sparks.Emit(sparkCount)` makes exactly that many sparks at that moment. With `sparkCount` at 20, each hit sends 20 orange sparks outward. Simulation Space set to World leaves them where the burst happened while the Player moves on. If sparks appear on their own, check Play On Awake and Rate over Time first.

points.heading: Tune one change at a time
points.explanation: Tuning means changing one value, playing, and judging that one change. If you change two things in one run, you cannot tell which one helped. In your five runs you changed Hit Volume, then Pitch Min, then Pitch Max, then Spark Count, then Sparks Start Speed. After each run you kept the new number or went back to the old one. Edit values with Play off, because changes to objects in the scene are undone when Play stops. Write down every value you keep. You can then rebuild your settings and explain your choices in your forum post and in your weekly build.

page.text: Last week Dodge learned to end: lives, a Game over panel and a working Restart. It works, but a hit is silent and nothing on screen reacts. This week you fix that. You add free CC0 sound effects played from a script, a burst of sparks when a hazard hits you, and a falling tone when the game ends. Then you tune the numbers by feel, one change at a time. By Sunday your Dodge sounds and looks like a game that notices what you do.
