page.transcript:
Here is a small test. Play Dodge as you built it last week. A hazard hits you, the text changes from Lives: 3 to Lives: 2, and nothing else happens. The rules worked. The game still feels flat.

Now imagine the same hit with a short thud and a burst of sparks. The rules have not changed by one line. But now the hit feels like something. That difference is called game feel.

Steve Swink wrote the book on it, and its first chapter is this week’s optional reading. He describes three building blocks: real-time control, simulated space and polish. Polish is the part we work on this week. Polish is sound, particles and small touches that do not change the rules but change how the game feels.

Three ideas will help you. First, feedback should be fast. If the sound comes a second after the hit, it feels wrong. So we play it in the same moment the hit is noticed. Second, variety matters. A sound that plays exactly the same every time gets dull. So we change the pitch a little on each hit. Third, tune one thing at a time. Change the volume, play, judge it. Then change the particle count, play, judge it. If you change two things together, you will not know which one made it better.

Here is the plan. You add a hit sound from a script. You vary its pitch. You add a game over sound. You add a burst of sparks. Then you tune the numbers by feel. Let’s go.

page.title: Version and template
page.text: This page is written for Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6.4f1) and the Universal 3D template, the same as your Dodge project. Your Editor window title should read Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1), or another 6000.6 version. If it reads anything else, open Unity Hub, click Installs, install Unity 6.6, and open Dodge with that Editor. The menus and code on this page are checked for Unity 6.6 only.

page.label: Dodge-week7-end.zip
page.shows: Dodge as last week ended: lives, the Game over panel and Restart working, with no sound or particles yet.

page.text: Use the starter only if your own Dodge is broken and you cannot fix it. Unzip it into your Documents folder, never inside your own Dodge project folder, so it does not replace your project. On Windows, open File Explorer, right-click Dodge-week7-end.zip in Downloads, choose Extract All..., click Browse, pick Documents, then click Extract. On a Mac, double-click Dodge-week7-end.zip in Finder, then drag the new folder into Documents. To open it, start Unity Hub, click Projects, open the dropdown beside Add, choose Add project from disk, pick the Dodge-week7-end folder (the one that holds Assets, Packages and ProjectSettings), then click the project in the list.

page.label: dodge-sounds.zip
page.shows: Two CC0 sound effects: hit.wav, a short thud, and gameover.wav, a falling tone, plus a licence.txt. CC0 means free to use for any purpose with no credit needed.

page.text: Unzip dodge-sounds.zip into your Documents folder the same way: on Windows with Extract All..., on a Mac by double-clicking it in Finder. Later in the course you can look for more CC0 sounds, for example the audio packs on kenney.nl.

items.text: In Unity Hub, click **Projects**, then click your Dodge project to open it.
In the **Hierarchy**, check that **Player**, **Spawner**, **GameManager**, **Canvas** and **EventSystem** are all there.
In the **Project** window, click the **Scripts** folder under **Assets** and check that **GameManager** and **PlayerHit** are in it.
Click **Play**, then click once inside the **Game** view. Move into hazards with W, A, S and D until the Game over panel appears, then click **Restart**. Lives: 3 comes back.
Click **Play** again to stop the game.
In the **Project** window, click **Assets**, then choose **Assets > Create > Folder**. Type Audio and press Enter.
Unzip dodge-sounds.zip as described above.

Drag hit.wav and gameover.wav from the unzipped folder into the **Audio** folder in the **Project** window. If dragging does not work, right-click the **Audio** folder, choose **Show in Explorer** on Windows or **Reveal in Finder** on a Mac, and copy the two files into the folder that opens.

shot.alt: Project window, Assets > Audio holding two audio clips named hit and gameover.
shot.caption: Compare: your Audio folder holds hit and gameover.
shot.shows: The Project window only, with Assets > Audio selected, showing two clips named hit and gameover. Outline the Audio folder name.

items.text: Click **hit** in the **Audio** folder. At the bottom of the **Inspector**, press the play button in the preview to hear it.

shot.alt: Inspector for the hit audio clip with the preview play button at the bottom.
shot.caption: The clip in the Inspector. Its preview, with a play button, is at the very bottom.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with hit selected. Show the audio preview strip at the bottom with its play button. Outline the play button.

page.text: Dodge runs and restarts as before. The Audio folder holds hit and gameover, and the hit preview plays a short thud. The Console shows no red lines. It went wrong if Restart does not give Lives: 3, or if the Audio folder is empty. Fix last week’s game first, or open the starter, because everything this week builds on it.

page.title: If something went wrong
page.text:
Two likely causes.

The preview plays nothing: turn up your computer volume, then press the preview play button again.

Dragging the files does nothing: use the **Show in Explorer** or **Reveal in Finder** route in the steps above.
Play a hit sound from a script

You do this so a hit is heard in the same moment it happens. Sound in Unity needs two things. An Audio Source is the speaker, and an AudioClip is the recording it plays. Last week the Player told the GameManager it was hit. Now it also tells a new script that plays the sound.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, click **Player**.
In the **Inspector**, click **Add Component**, type Audio Source and press Enter.
In the new **Audio Source** component, untick **Play On Awake**, so the sound only plays when your script asks.
In the **Project** window, click the **Scripts** folder under **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type HitFeedback and press Enter.
Double-click **HitFeedback**. In Visual Studio Code, select everything in the file and delete it. Then type or paste the code from the next block.

page.caption: HitFeedback.cs

page.text: Line by line. `[SerializeField]` puts a private variable in the Inspector so you can fill it by dragging. `AudioSource hitSource` is a slot for the speaker, and `AudioClip hitClip` is a slot for the recording. `float hitVolume = 1f` is a decimal number that starts at 1. `public void Play()` is a method like last week’s `LoseLife()`: `public` lets PlayerHit call it. `PlayOneShot` plays the clip once at the volume you give it, and a second hit can play on top of a first without cutting it off.

items.text: Save the file with Ctrl+S on Windows or Command+S on a Mac. Return to Unity.
In the **Project** window, double-click **PlayerHit**. Select everything in the file, delete it, then type or paste the code from the next block.

page.caption: PlayerHit.cs

page.text: This file replaces last week’s. It still ignores anything not tagged Hazard, calls `LoseLife()` and removes the hazard, as last week’s did. The new line is `feedback.Play()`. Every hit now passes through this one method, in one fixed order: feedback, then the life. `GetComponent<HitFeedback>()` finds the HitFeedback script on the same object. `OnCollisionEnter` and `OnTriggerEnter` both call `Hit`, so it works whether your hazards are solid or triggers.

items.text: Save the file and return to Unity. Wait until the Console shows no red lines.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Player**.
In the **Inspector**, click **Add Component**, type HitFeedback and press Enter.

Drag **Player** from the **Hierarchy** onto the **Hit Source** field. This puts the Player’s Audio Source in the slot. If dragging is hard, click the small circle at the right of the field and double-click **Player** in the list; this works for every slot this week.
Drag **hit** from the **Audio** folder in the **Project** window onto the **Hit Clip** field.

shot.alt: Inspector for Player: Audio Source with Play On Awake unticked, and below it Hit Feedback (Script) with Hit Source Player (Audio Source), Hit Clip hit and Hit Volume 1.
shot.caption: Audio Source with Play On Awake unticked, and Hit Feedback (Script) with its two slots filled. Other components are folded here to save room.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Hit Feedback (Script) on Player showing Hit Source as Player (Audio Source), Hit Clip as hit, Hit Volume 1.

items.text: Choose **File > Save**.
Click **Play**, click once inside the **Game** view, and move into a falling hazard with W, A, S and D. Then click **Play** again to stop.

page.text: You hear a short thud when a hazard touches the Player, and Lives drops by one as before. The Console has no red lines. It went wrong if the lives drop in silence, or if a red error appears when you are hit.

page.title: If something went wrong
page.text:
Likely causes, with the exact error text.

error CS0122: ‘HitFeedback.Play()’ is inaccessible due to its protection level. The method exists but is not public. Make sure the line reads `public void Play()`. The same error naming ‘GameManager.LoseLife()’ means last week’s `LoseLife` is missing `public`.

error CS1061: ‘HitFeedback’ does not contain a definition for ‘Play’. The name is spelled differently in the two files. Check that it is `Play` with a capital P in both.

NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object, with HitFeedback.Play in the message. A slot is empty. Redo the two drags in the steps above.

No error but no sound: in the **Game** view toolbar, check that **Mute Audio** is not switched on, and check your computer volume.
Vary the pitch of the hit

A sound that plays exactly the same every time gets dull fast. Pitch is how high or low a sound is, and changing it a little each hit keeps the sound lively. You do this so the third hit in a game does not sound like a copy of the first.

items.text: In the **Project** window, double-click **HitFeedback**.
Select everything in the file, delete it, then type or paste the code from the next block.
Save the file and return to Unity. Wait until the Console shows no red lines.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Player**. In the **Inspector**, find **Hit Feedback (Script)**: it now has **Pitch Min** 0.9 and **Pitch Max** 1.1.

shot.alt: Hit Feedback (Script): Hit Volume 1, Pitch Min 0.9, Pitch Max 1.1.
shot.caption: Compare: Pitch Min 0.9 and Pitch Max 1.1 are new fields.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Hit Feedback (Script) on Player showing Hit Source, Hit Clip, Hit Volume 1, Pitch Min 0.9 and Pitch Max 1.1. Outline Pitch Min and Pitch Max.

items.text: Click **Play**, click once inside the **Game** view, and take two hits. Listen for the second thud to sound a little different from the first. Then click **Play** again to stop.

page.caption: HitFeedback.cs

page.text: `Random.Range(pitchMin, pitchMax)` picks a decimal number anywhere from 0.9 to 1.1. A pitch of 1 is the recording as it was made. Below 1 it sounds deeper and a little slower, and above 1 it sounds higher. The pitch belongs to the Audio Source, so it stays at the last value picked until the next hit. That is why the game over sound, which comes next, gets an Audio Source of its own.

Each hit uses a randomly selected pitch between Pitch Min and Pitch Max, and the Console is clear. Two hits can sound similar. Restart and listen across several runs before deciding that pitch variation is missing. If the sound stays unchanged across those runs, check the values and saved script below. If you cannot hear the sound, check by eye: during Play, click **Player** and watch **Pitch** on its **Audio Source** change after each hit.

page.title: If something went wrong
page.text:
Two likely causes.

Every hit sounds the same: Pitch Min and Pitch Max in the Inspector are equal, or the file was not saved. Set 0.9 and 1.1 and save the script.

error CS0103: The name ‘Random’ does not exist in the current context. The first line of the file must read `using UnityEngine;`.
Add a game over sound

The end of a game deserves its own sound. You play it from GameManager, using a second Audio Source that never has its pitch changed. This does not clash with the hit sound: the hit uses the Player’s Audio Source, and the game over tone uses the GameManager’s.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, click **GameManager**.
In the **Inspector**, click **Add Component**, type Audio Source and press Enter.
In the new **Audio Source** component, untick **Play On Awake**.
In the **Project** window, double-click **GameManager** in the **Scripts** folder.
Directly under the opening `{` of the class, add the two lines shown in the next block.

page.caption: GameManager.cs: new fields (the first and last lines are already in your file)

items.text: Find your `GameOver` method. Directly under its opening `{`, add the line shown in the next block.

page.caption: GameManager.cs: the new line in GameOver (the first, second and last lines are already in your file)

page.text: `gameOverSource.PlayOneShot(gameOverClip)` plays the falling tone once. It still plays when the game freezes with `Time.timeScale` at 0, because sound does not depend on it. Because `gameOverSource` is a different Audio Source from the one HitFeedback uses, the last hit cannot change its pitch.

items.text: Save the file and return to Unity. Wait until the Console shows no red lines.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **GameManager**. In the **Inspector**, find **Game Manager (Script)** with **Game Over Source** and **Game Over Clip** both reading None.
Drag **GameManager** from the **Hierarchy** onto the **Game Over Source** field.
Drag **gameover** from the **Audio** folder in the **Project** window onto the **Game Over Clip** field.

shot.alt: Game Manager (Script): Game Over Source GameManager (Audio Source), Game Over Clip gameover.
shot.caption: Compare: both slots filled.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Game Manager (Script) showing Game Over Source as GameManager (Audio Source) and Game Over Clip as gameover.

items.text: Choose **File > Save**.
Click **Play**, click once inside the **Game** view, and take all three hits. Then click **Play** again to stop.

page.text: Each of the first two hits plays the thud. The third hit plays the thud and, as the Game over panel appears, the falling tone at its normal pitch. It went wrong if the tone never plays, or if a red error appears when the game ends.

page.title: If something went wrong
page.text:
Likely causes, with the exact error text.

NullReferenceException with GameManager.GameOver in the message: a slot on Game Manager (Script) is empty. Redo the two drags.

error CS0103: The name ‘gameOverSource’ does not exist in the current context. The two new fields must sit inside the class, directly under its opening `{`, not inside a method.

The tone sounds odd: check that the Audio Source on GameManager is the one in the **Game Over Source** slot, not the Player’s.
Add a particle burst when you are hit

Sound tells the ears you were hit. Sparks tell the eyes. A Particle System makes many small shapes at once and moves them for you. You make one that stays quiet until a hit, then bursts. You do this because a hit with sparks and a thud is easier to read than a changing number.

items.text: Choose **GameObject > Visual Effects > Particle System**. Type Sparks and press Enter.
In the **Hierarchy**, drag **Sparks** onto **Player**, so it sits inside it.
In the **Inspector**, set **Transform > Position** to 0, 0, 0.
In the main section of the **Particle System** component, untick **Looping** and untick **Play On Awake**.
In the same section, set **Start Lifetime** to 0.5, **Start Speed** to 4 and **Start Size** to 0.15, and set **Simulation Space** to World.

shot.alt: Particle System main section: Looping off, Start Lifetime 0.5, Start Speed 4, Start Size 0.15, Play On Awake off, Simulation Space World.
shot.caption: Compare: your main section values.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with the main section of the Particle System component open. Show Looping and Play On Awake unticked, Start Lifetime 0.5, Start Speed 4, Start Size 0.15, Simulation Space World.

items.text: Click the color box beside **Start Color**. In the window titled **Color**, type FF8800 into the box labeled **Hexadecimal**, press Enter and close the window.
Open **Emission** and set **Rate over Time** to 0, so the system makes nothing by itself.
Open **Shape**. Set **Shape** to Sphere and **Radius** to 0.3.

page.text: Simulation Space set to World means the sparks stay where the burst happened while the Player moves on. Rate over Time 0 and Looping off mean the system does nothing until your script asks. Next you ask it. Replace the whole HitFeedback file with the next block.

items.text: In the **Project** window, double-click **HitFeedback**. Select everything, delete it, then type or paste the code from the next block.

page.caption: HitFeedback.cs

page.text: `ParticleSystem sparks` is a slot for the Particle System. `int sparkCount = 20` is a whole number: how many sparks one hit makes. `sparks.Emit(sparkCount)` makes exactly that many at that moment. It works even though Looping and Play On Awake are off.

items.text: Save the file and return to Unity. Wait until the Console shows no red lines.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Player**. In the **Inspector**, find **Hit Feedback (Script)**, which now has **Sparks** (None) and **Spark Count** 20.
Drag **Sparks** from the **Hierarchy** onto the **Sparks** field of **Hit Feedback (Script)**.

shot.alt: Hit Feedback (Script): Sparks Sparks (Particle System), Spark Count 20.
shot.caption: Compare: the Sparks slot is filled.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Hit Feedback (Script) on Player. Show Sparks as Sparks (Particle System) and Spark Count 20. Outline the Sparks field.

items.text: Choose **File > Save**.
Click **Play**, click once inside the **Game** view, and take a hit. Then click **Play** again to stop.

page.alt: Dodge in Play: a hit makes about 20 orange sparks fly outward from the Player and fade out.
page.caption: A hit: the burst of orange sparks, then one life fewer.
page.shows: Only the Game view in Play, about 10 seconds: a hazard touches the Player, about 20 orange sparks fly outward and fade in half a second, and Lives drops by one. Silent recording.

page.text: Every hit makes a quick orange burst around the Player, with the thud. The sparks stay quiet between hits. On the third hit they freeze in the air behind the Game over panel along with the hazards, because the game is frozen. It went wrong if sparks appear on their own, or if nothing appears at a hit.

page.title: If something went wrong
page.text:
Likely causes, with the exact error text.

NullReferenceException with HitFeedback.Play in the message: the **Sparks** slot is empty. Drag **Sparks** onto it.

No sparks, no error: check that Rate over Time is 0 only (not Spark Count), that Start Size is 0.15 and that Start Lifetime is 0.5. A Start Size of 0 hides them.

Sparks appear at the start without a hit: **Play On Awake** is still ticked on Sparks, or **Rate over Time** is not 0.
Tune the feel one change at a time

Tuning means changing a value and judging how the game feels. You change one value per run, so you know which change did what. Dodge ends after three hits, so each run is three hits, then you stop. Edit values with Play off: changes to objects in the scene are undone when Play stops. Judge particles only by playing Dodge in the Game view, not from the small Particles panel that appears in the Scene view when Sparks is selected, because the Game view is what a player sees. Write down each value you keep.

items.text: With Play off, write down the starting values: Hit Volume 1, Pitch Min 0.9, Pitch Max 1.1, Spark Count 20, and Sparks Start Speed 4.

Run 1, volume. Click **Player**. In **Hit Feedback (Script)**, set **Hit Volume** to 0.5. Click **Play**, click inside the **Game** view, take three hits, then stop Play. Decide which feels better, 1 or 0.5, and type that value in.

shot.alt: Hit Feedback (Script): Hit Volume 0.5, Pitch Min 0.9, Pitch Max 1.1, Spark Count 20.
shot.caption: Compare: only Hit Volume has changed.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Player selected, Hit Feedback (Script) showing Hit Volume 0.5 and the other values unchanged. Outline Hit Volume.

items.text: Run 2, lowest pitch. Set **Pitch Min** to 0.7 and leave **Pitch Max** alone. Play, take three hits, stop. Keep 0.7 or go back to 0.9, whichever sounds better.
Run 3, highest pitch. Set **Pitch Max** to 1.3 and leave **Pitch Min** at the value you kept. Play, take three hits, stop. Keep 1.3 or go back to 1.1.
Run 4, spark count. Set **Spark Count** to 50. Play, take three hits, stop. Keep 50 or go back to 20.

shot.alt: Hit Feedback (Script): Spark Count 50.
shot.caption: Compare: Spark Count set to 50 for this run.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Player selected, Hit Feedback (Script) showing Spark Count 50. Outline Spark Count.

items.text: Run 5, spark speed. Click **Sparks**, set **Start Speed** to 8 in the main section of **Particle System**. Play, take three hits, stop. Keep 8 or go back to 4.
Choose **File > Save**, then play one full game from start to Game over, and write down your final five values.

page.text: You have five values you chose by playing, each judged on its own, and a saved scene. A full game plays from start to Game over with thud, sparks and the falling tone. It went wrong if you changed two values in one run and cannot say which helped: go back and redo that run with one value.

page.title: If something went wrong
page.text:
Two likely causes.

A value you typed is back to its old number after Play: you edited it during Play. Stop Play and type it again.

Hits sound the same after changing the pitch: the number you changed belongs to the Hit Feedback on **Player**, not to another object. Click **Player**.

page.label: Dodge-week8-end.zip
page.shows: Dodge as it should stand at the end of this part: hit sound with random pitch, game over sound on its own Audio Source, a Sparks particle burst on every hit, and the Console clear.

page.text: Use the checkpoint only if one of your own parts will not work. Unzip it into your Documents folder, never inside your own Dodge project folder. On Windows, right-click Dodge-week8-end.zip in Downloads, choose Extract All..., click Browse, pick Documents, then click Extract. On a Mac, double-click it in Finder, then drag the new folder into Documents. To open it, start Unity Hub, click Projects, open the dropdown beside Add, choose Add project from disk, pick the Dodge-week8-end folder (the one that holds Assets, Packages and ProjectSettings), then click the project in the list.
Challenges

These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change the code is how scripting sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks. When your Dodge sounds and looks the way you want, it is ready for the weekly build in your checklist.

Challenge: a hit sound that gets deeper. Each hit should use a lower pitch range than the one before. The ranges overlap, so an individual hit can still sound higher than the previous hit. Try it on paper with Pitch Min 0.9 and Pitch Max 1.1 as the starting range, a drop of 0.1 for each hit already taken. The first hit picks between 0.9 and 1.1. The second picks between 0.8 and 1.0. The third picks between 0.7 and 0.9. After Restart the first hit is back at 0.9 to 1.1.

page.title: Hint for the challenge
page.text: Keep an `int hitCount` in HitFeedback. Add 1 to it with `hitCount++;` in `Play`, after you use it. Subtract `0.1f * hitCount` from the number you give `Random.Range`, where `hitCount` is how many hits came before this one. Restart reloads the scene, which makes a new HitFeedback with `hitCount` at 0, so you do not need to reset it.

Optional challenge: a screen shake. On every hit the Main Camera jumps up to 0.2 units in a random direction for 0.15 seconds, then returns to exactly where it started. Try it on paper: a hit at 10.00 seconds shakes the camera until 10.15, and at 10.16 the camera is at its starting position. On the last hit, the camera must still return, even though the game freezes.

page.title: Hint for the optional challenge
page.text: Add a new script to the Main Camera. In `Start`, save `transform.position` in a variable. Write a `public void Shake()` that sets a float timer to 0.15f. In `Update`, while the timer is above 0, subtract `Time.unscaledDeltaTime` and set `transform.position` to the saved position plus `Random.insideUnitSphere * 0.2f`. When the timer is 0 or below, set the position back to the saved one. `Time.unscaledDeltaTime` keeps counting when `Time.timeScale` is 0. Call `Shake()` from PlayerHit, found with `FindAnyObjectByType<CameraShake>()`.
Wrap-up

You can now play a sound from a script, make particles burst when a hit lands, and tune values one at a time. Test yourself. First, why does the game over sound use its own Audio Source? Second, what does `Emit(20)` do, and why are Looping and Play On Awake off on Sparks? Third, why do you edit values with Play off, and why change only one per run? Next week you add a start menu, build a version a classmate can run, and add your own twist to Dodge. You submit the finished game, and it is scored with a rubric.

facilitation.announcement: This week Dodge gets sound and sparks. You add free CC0 sound effects played from a script, a particle burst when a hazard hits you, and a game over tone, then tune the numbers by feel. The one thing to get right: change only one value at a time when you tune, and edit with Play off. Your first forum post is due Thursday. Replies, the weekly build and all other work are due Sunday night. Post in the forum if you are stuck, and say what you see in the Console.
watchFor: Silent hits: the Hit Source or Hit Clip slot is empty, Mute Audio is on in the Game view, or the computer volume is low. Ask for a screenshot of the Hit Feedback (Script) and point them to the Stuck? list.
CS0122 inaccessible due to its protection level: a method is missing `public`. Tell them the method exists and only needs the word `public`; do not suggest renaming it.
NullReferenceException at HitFeedback.Play or GameManager.GameOver: a slot is empty, usually Sparks or Game Over Source. Ask them to click the object and check the slot.
The game over tone sounding odd: the student put the game over clip through the Player’s Audio Source. Point them back to the second Audio Source on GameManager.
Students who change several values in one run and then cannot say what helped. Ask which single value they changed in the run they are describing, and have them redo it.
Sparks that never appear or appear at the start: Start Size 0, Rate over Time not 0, or Play On Awake still ticked on Sparks.
feedback: Your hit sound now has a clear job: it tells me the moment a hazard lands. Say in your next post how you chose the final volume.
You changed one value per run and you can say what each change did. That is exactly how tuning works; keep doing it for your own game.
Your pitch range is wide enough to hear. If it ever sounds like a different sound, narrow the range.
Your sparks are easy to see and fade quickly. Try to describe in one sentence what a player should feel when they land.
Your game over tone plays at normal pitch because it has its own Audio Source. Nice use of that idea.
If your recording is silent, say so, and check that Mute Audio is off in the Game view before you record again.
Your forum reply gave a specific suggestion and a reason. Next, say which of your own values you would test first.
facilitation.atRisk: By Wednesday, contact any student who has not opened the page or posted in the forum, and any student whose Dodge from last week still cannot restart. Offer the starter project and a direct message with the first step to fix.

Assets/Audio holding hit and gameover
Player with an Audio Source (Play On Awake off) and Hit Feedback (Script) with Hit Source, Hit Clip, Hit Volume, Pitch Min, Pitch Max, Sparks and Spark Count filled
Assets/Scripts/HitFeedback.cs and an updated PlayerHit.cs that calls feedback.Play() before LoseLife()
GameManager with its own Audio Source and Game Manager (Script) with Game Over Source and Game Over Clip filled, and GameOver playing the tone
Sparks Particle System inside Player: Looping and Play On Awake off, Rate over Time 0, Shape Sphere
Five tuned values the student chose one at a time
Challenge hit sound that gets deeper, and the screen shake challenge only if tried
A screen recording and a screenshot uploaded for the weekly build

l_cb785d60b296.title: Menus, builds and the finished Dodge
l_cb785d60b296.summary: Add a start menu, build a version a classmate can run, and add your own twist; submit the finished Dodge, graded by rubric.

homework.toward: Dodge game with your own twist

keyIdeas: A menu is its own scene. The Play button loads the Dodge scene by name with `SceneManager.LoadScene`, and a scene can only be loaded if it is in the build’s scene list.

A build is a copy of your game that runs without Unity. It holds only the scenes in the scene list and works on one system: a Windows build does not run on a Mac, and a Mac build does not run on Windows.
A playtest means watching someone else play without helping. What they do tells you more than what they say, because you cannot see your own game with fresh eyes.
A twist is one change to how Dodge plays. Keep it small enough to finish and easy to test, and choose it because something you saw in a playtest gave you a reason.

vocabulary.definition: A copy of your game that runs on its own, without Unity.
The list of scenes in File > Build Profiles that a build contains, in the order they are numbered.
The part of Unity your script uses to load a scene by name with `SceneManager.LoadScene`.
The list on a Button where you choose which public method runs when the button is clicked.
The speed of time in the game: 1 is normal, 0.5 is half speed and 0 is stopped.
Watching someone else play your game without helping, so you learn what they do and where they struggle.
One change to how a game plays, chosen for a reason you can state.

study.overview: This week Dodge became a game someone else can start and play. You built a MainMenu scene with Play and Quit buttons, made a build that runs without Unity, watched a real player, and used what you saw to add one twist. After this page you can explain how each piece works and check it yourself. You can also say why your twist answers a real problem. Reread it before next week and before you submit Dodge game with your own twist, which is scored with its rubric: Exemplary, Proficient, Developing or Beginning.

points.heading: A menu is its own scene, and a scene must be in the scene list
points.explanation: You can now build a start menu and make its buttons load the game. MainMenu is a separate scene with a Canvas, a title and two buttons. A small script, MenuController, holds two public methods. `PlayGame` calls `SceneManager.LoadScene(gameSceneName)` and `QuitGame` calls `Application.Quit()`. The methods must be public, or they will not appear in a button’s On Click list. Unity can only load a scene that is in the build’s scene list, so open each scene and click Add Open Scenes in File > Build Profiles. Put MainMenu first, as number 0, so the build opens on the menu. Example: if Play gives the error that SampleScene has not been added to the build settings, open SampleScene, click Add Open Scenes, and build again. In the Editor, `Application.Quit()` does nothing, so the line `Debug.Log("Quit pressed")` shows in the Console that the button ran your code.

points.heading: A build is a copy that runs without Unity, on one system only
points.explanation: You can now make a build with File > Build Profiles and send it to someone else. A build holds only the scenes in the scene list. It works only on the system it was made for. A Windows build does not run on a Mac, and a Mac build does not run on Windows. So choose Windows or macOS before you click Build. Zip the whole DodgeBuild folder, share a download link, and find a playtester who uses the same kind of computer as you. Example: after you change the game, run Build again and make a fresh zip. If the new build still shows the old game, your classmate is playing an old file, so replace your shared link. Test the build yourself too: Play should start Dodge, and Quit should close the application.

points.heading: A playtest means watching without helping
points.explanation: You can now run a playtest and turn it into a decision. You made every rule of Dodge, so you cannot see it with fresh eyes. Give a player the game, say nothing, and watch their hands. Write down what they do, such as pauses before clicking, missed movement and restarts. What they do tells you more than what they say. Then ask what they would change and record the answer. Example of a useful note: a player stopped for several seconds on the menu because they did not know which keys moved the Player. A note such as “it is fun” gives you nothing to act on. Pick the one problem that cost the player the most and fix it first, by changing one value and playing again. A twist on top of a broken moment will not help anyone.

points.heading: A twist is one small change, chosen for a reason
points.explanation: You can now add a twist you can defend. A twist is one change to how Dodge plays. Keep it small enough to finish and easy to test. Complete this sentence in your notes: My twist is ___ because I saw ___. If you cannot finish it from something you saw, choose a different twist. The guided example was slow focus. The script sets `Time.timeScale` to 0.5 while Left Shift is held through `Keyboard.current.leftShiftKey.isPressed`, and back to 1 otherwise. Everything that uses `Time.deltaTime` slows with it, including the hazards. The line `if (Time.timeScale == 0f) return;` stops it restarting a game that has ended. Your own twist could be hazards that come faster, a bigger or smaller Player, or a second hazard kind made from a copy of your hazard prefab. Change one value at a time, play for a minute, and keep the value that feels right.

page.text: Last week Dodge learned to make sound and sparks. This week it becomes a game that someone else can start and play. You build a start menu with Play and Quit buttons, make a build a classmate can run without Unity, and watch someone play it. Then you use what you saw to add one twist of your own. By Sunday night you have a finished Dodge: a menu, a build, and a twist you chose because a real player gave you a reason.

page.text: You start by making sure Dodge is where you left it last week, so the new work has solid ground under it. The menu, the build and the twist all sit on top of the game you already have.

Everything you make this week prepares you for Dodge game with your own twist, due Sunday night through the LMS. This component counts for 15% of your course grade. Open its separate brief and rubric before you begin. The finished game is scored with that rubric, using Exemplary, Proficient, Developing and Beginning. The twist itself comes late in the week, after you have watched someone play. Before you build anything, read the Stuck? list that goes with this week. It is in your checklist, and it is the quickest way out of the usual problems.

page.title: Version and template
page.text: This page is written for Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6.4f1) and the Universal 3D template, the same as your Dodge project. Your Editor window title reads: SampleScene - your project name - Windows, Mac, Linux - Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1). If yours shows a different version, open Unity Hub, click Installs, and check which editor your project uses. If it is not a 6000.6 version, install Unity 6.6 from Installs and open Dodge with that Editor: the menus and code on this page are checked for Unity 6.6 only.

items.text: Open Unity Hub and click **Projects** in the sidebar.
Click your Dodge project in the list and wait for the Editor to open.
In the **Hierarchy**, check that **SampleScene** holds **Player** (with **Sparks** inside it) and **GameManager**, plus the objects you made in earlier weeks.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
A red line in the Console after you open the project: click it and read the first line. A missing semicolon or a spelling mistake in a script is the usual cause. Fix it, save, and wait for the Console to settle.

A box titled Script Updating Consent asks whether to update files: click No, then fix the line by hand. It appears only when a script uses old code such as `rb.velocity`. Use `rb.linearVelocity`.

Dodge is broken and you cannot see why: download Dodge-week8-end.zip above. It is Dodge as it should stand at the end of last week, with sounds, sparks and tuned values included. Use it only if your own Dodge will not open or is missing something. Unzip it into your Documents folder, next to your own Dodge folder and never over it. To open it, start Unity Hub, click Projects, open the Add dropdown, choose Add project from disk, and pick the Dodge-week8-end folder that holds Assets, Packages and ProjectSettings. Then click it in the list and carry on from that project.
Make the MainMenu scene
A start menu is a second scene: its own screen with a title and two buttons. You make it first and wire it up in the next part, so that Play can carry the player from the menu into Dodge.

Choose **Assets > Create > Scene > Scene**. Type MainMenu and press Enter.

Choose **GameObject > UI (Canvas) > Panel**. Unity adds a **Canvas**, a **Panel** inside it and an **EventSystem**.

Click **Canvas**. In the **Canvas Scaler** component, set **UI Scale Mode** to **Scale With Screen Size** and type 1920 and 1080 into **Reference Resolution**. This keeps the menu the same shape at any window size.
Click **Panel**. In the **Inspector**, find the **Image** component and click the color box beside **Color**.
In the window titled **Color**, type 1B1F3B into the box labeled **Hexadecimal**, press Enter, and set **A** to 255. Close the window.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Canvas**. Choose **GameObject > UI (Canvas) > Text - TextMeshPro**. Type TitleText and press Enter.

In the **TextMeshPro - Text (UI)** component, type DODGE in the **Text Input** box, set **Font Size** to 120, and click the Center and Middle alignment buttons.

page.text: Line by line. `using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;` gives you SceneManager, the part of Unity that loads scenes. `[SerializeField] string gameSceneName = "SampleScene";` makes a text field in the Inspector, so you can change which scene Play loads without editing code. The word `public` on `PlayGame` and `QuitGame` matters: only public methods appear in the On Click dropdown. `Time.timeScale = 1f;` sets the speed of time to normal, because a game that ended with time stopped would otherwise start frozen. `SceneManager.LoadScene(gameSceneName);` closes the menu and opens the scene with that name. `Debug.Log("Quit pressed");` prints a line in the Console. `Application.Quit();` closes a built game. In the Editor it does nothing, which is why the Debug.Log line is there: it proves your button ran the code.

Add your scenes to the build and make it
A build is a copy of your game that runs on its own, with no Unity needed. You make one so a classmate can play it. A build contains only the scenes in its scene list, so you add both scenes first.

When it finishes, open DodgeBuild. On Windows, double-click the application that has your project’s name and the Unity icon (its full name ends in .exe, which Windows may hide). Do not open UnityCrashHandler64. On a Mac, double-click the `.app` file. A build can also leave a second folder whose name ends in DoNotShip or BackUpThisFolder_ButDontShipItWithYourGame. page.text: A build in DodgeBuild opens on the menu, Play starts Dodge, and sound and sparks work. It went wrong if the build opens straight into Dodge, which means MainMenu is not first in the scene list, or if Play fails to start Dodge. Check that SampleScene is included and that MenuController’s Game Scene Name is SampleScene.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
The Console shows Scene ‘SampleScene’ couldn’t be loaded because it has not been added to the build settings: open File > Build Profiles, open SampleScene, click Add Open Scenes, and build again.

Your platform is missing from the list or cannot build: open Unity Hub, click Installs, click the gear beside your editor, choose Add modules, and tick the build support for your system. Windows users building for Windows and Mac users building for macOS normally need nothing extra.

A classmate’s build shows a blue box titled Windows protected your PC, or a Mac says it could not verify the app: follow the playtest part below, which says when it is safe and which buttons to click. Your own build, made on your own computer, opens without this warning.
Share your build and playtest

You cannot see your own game with fresh eyes. You made every rule, so nothing surprises you. A playtest is watching someone else play and learning from what they do. You do it now so your twist answers a real problem, not a guess.

page.alt: The instructor explaining three rules for watching a playtest: say nothing, watch the hands, write it down.
page.caption: Compare with how you run your own playtest: you watch, you stay quiet, you write.
page.shows: The instructor at a desk, head and shoulders, with a laptop beside them showing Dodge. Three short lines appear on screen one at a time: Say nothing, Watch the hands, Write it down.
page.transcript:
A playtest is simple. You give someone your game and you watch them play it. The hard part is doing nothing. When your player gets stuck, you will want to say, press Shift, or, the hazards are meant to be fast. Don’t. If you help, you hide the problem you came to find.

Here are three rules.

Rule one: say nothing. Give them the game and one sentence, such as, play it as you like. If they ask a question, say, what would you try? Their confusion is the result.

Rule two: watch the hands and the face, not just the screen. Do they find the Play button at once? Do they flinch at the first hit? Do they smile when the sparks fly? Do they lean in after the first game over, or put the controller down? Wanting another go is the best sign a game can get.

Rule three: write it down while it happens. Three lists work well. What went wrong. What went well. What they said. Keep the lists separate, and write what you saw, not what you think it means. Saw: three hits in four seconds, then quit. That is data. Too hard is a guess.

When it ends, ask one question: what would you change? Then thank them and stop. You choose the fix, not them. Their idea is a clue about the problem underneath it.

items.text: Ask in the forum for a classmate who uses the same kind of computer as you, Windows or Mac, because a build only runs on the system it was made for. Post by Tuesday in the week’s forum thread, and say Windows or Mac. If nobody has answered by Wednesday, ask a friend or family member: someone in the same room can play on your computer, so their own computer does not matter.

Make your zip. On Windows, open File Explorer, go to Documents, right-click the **DodgeBuild** folder and choose **Compress to**, then **ZIP File** (on Windows 10, choose **Send to**, then **Compressed (zipped) folder**), and type Dodge_YourName. On a Mac, open Finder, go to Documents, right-click the **DodgeBuild** folder, choose **Compress “DodgeBuild”**, and rename the new file Dodge_YourName.zip.

Upload the zip to a file-sharing service, such as the OneDrive or Google Drive that comes with your school account, and set the link so that anyone with the link can download. Send the link to your classmate or friend. You can switch the link off once the course has graded your game.

Download your classmate’s zip. Only run builds that classmates posted in this course’s forum. On Windows, right-click the zip, choose **Extract All**, and click **Extract**. On a Mac, double-click it. Open the new folder and start the game as you did in the build part. Because the game came from the internet and is not signed, your computer warns you the first time. On Windows, in the blue box titled Windows protected your PC, click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. On a Mac, click **Done** in the warning, open **System Settings > Privacy & Security**, scroll down to the line that names the game, click **Open Anyway** and confirm. On an older Mac, right-click the app, choose **Open**, then click **Open**. If a school or work computer will not let you, do not force it: skip playing their build and say so in your notes.
Open a new plain text file named PlaytestNotes (Notepad on Windows, TextEdit on a Mac). Write three headings: What went wrong, What went well, What they said.

Play your classmate’s Dodge for ten minutes without reading anything about it first. If your playtester is not a classmate, play any build a classmate posted in the forum for your system; if there is none, skip this step and say so in your notes. Under each heading, write what you saw and felt. Write at least one thing that confused you.

Now watch someone play yours. If they are beside you, give them the computer and stay silent. If they are far away, ask them to record their screen while they play and send you the video. On Windows, press Win+Alt+R to record with the Game Bar. On a Mac, press Shift+Command+5, then click **Record Entire Screen**.

Add to PlaytestNotes what you could observe: pauses before clicking, movement attempts, hits and restarts. If the player is beside you, you can also note visible reactions. Afterward, ask what they would change and have them send or write their answer. Put that answer under What they said.
Read the notes and type [FIX] at the start of the one problem that cost them the most. That is your fix for the next part.

page.text: You have a PlaytestNotes file with something under every heading from both playtests, and one problem marked [FIX]. It went wrong if your notes say only things like it is fun or it is too hard, with no moment you saw.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
The game will not open and you see a message about the wrong system: a Windows build does not run on a Mac, and a Mac build does not run on Windows. Ask the forum for a playtester on your kind of computer.

The zip is too large to send: delete nothing from the build, but upload it through a file-sharing link instead of an email attachment.

Nobody can sit at your computer this week: send your zip to a friend with the same kind of computer, and ask them to share their screen on a video call while they play, so you can watch and stay silent. If you have nobody at all, write to your instructor before Friday so they can pair you or play it themselves.
Fix the problem, then add your twist

Now the playtest pays off. You fix the biggest problem first, because a twist on top of a broken moment will not help anyone. Then you add a twist: one change to how Dodge plays. You try a guided one first, so you see how a twist is built, then you make your own.

items.text: Open **SampleScene** from the **Scenes** folder and open your PlaytestNotes.

Under your [FIX] problem, write one line: what the player saw, and the smallest change that could help. For example, hazards that come too thick at the start could mean a larger **Interval** on your **Spawner**, and a lives text that nobody noticed could mean a bigger **Font Size**.
In the **Hierarchy**, click the object that holds the value you want, and in the **Inspector** change that one value.
Click **Play**, click inside the **Game** view, and play for a minute. Stop **Play**, then judge: is the problem smaller?
If not, change the same value again. If it is, write the value that worked next to your notes.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.text: The guided twist is slow focus: hold Left Shift and time runs at half speed, so the player gets a moment to dodge. It is a small script that changes `Time.timeScale`, the speed of time in the game. A value of 1 is normal and 0.5 is half speed. Everything that uses `Time.deltaTime` slows with it, including the hazards and the Player.

items.text: With **SampleScene** open, choose **GameObject > Create Empty**. Type SlowFocus and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, set **Transform > Position** to 0, 0, 0.
In the **Project** window, click the **Scripts** folder under **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type SlowFocus and press Enter.
Double-click **SlowFocus**. In Visual Studio Code, select everything in the file and delete it. Then type or paste the code from the next block.
Save the file and return to Unity. Wait until the Console shows no red lines.
Drag **SlowFocus** from the **Project** window onto the **SlowFocus** object in the **Hierarchy**.

shot.alt: SlowFocus object with Slow Focus (Script) and Slow Scale 0.5
shot.caption: Compare the component: Slow Scale reads 0.5.
shot.shows: The Inspector for the SlowFocus object showing Transform at 0, 0, 0 and the Slow Focus (Script) component with Slow Scale 0.5. Hierarchy visible with SlowFocus. Outline the Slow Focus (Script) component.

items.text: Click **Play**, click inside the **Game** view, and hold Left Shift while hazards fall. Release it. Take hits until game over, then stop **Play**.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.caption: SlowFocus.cs

page.text:
Line by line. `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` gives you `Keyboard.current`, the way this version of Unity reads keys. `slowScale` is a number you can change in the Inspector. `if (Time.timeScale == 0f) return;` leaves the method early when time is stopped, so your script never restarts a game that has ended. `Keyboard.current.leftShiftKey.isPressed` is true for as long as the key is down. `held ? slowScale : 1f` means: if held is true, use slowScale, otherwise use 1. `OnDestroy` runs when the object is removed, such as when a scene reloads, and it makes sure time never stays slow.

Now tell the player about the new key. Open **MainMenu** from the **Scenes** folder and choose **GameObject > UI (Canvas) > Text - TextMeshPro**. Type ControlsText and press Enter. Set **Pos X** to 0, **Pos Y** to -280, **Width** to 1000, **Height** to 120 and **Font Size** to 36, and click the Center and Middle alignment buttons. In **Text Input** type: Move with W, A, S and D. Hold Left Shift for slow focus. Later, add any key your own twist uses. Choose **File > Save**, then open **SampleScene** again.

items.text: Slow focus was practice and does not count as your twist. Your twist may grow out of the fix you made above, but it must change how Dodge plays, not only one number that was wrong. In PlaytestNotes, write one sentence: My twist is ___ because I saw ___. If you cannot finish the sentence from something you saw, pick a different twist.

Choose a twist you can finish in about an hour. Some that fit Dodge: make hazards come faster by lowering **Min Interval** or **Speed Up** on the Spawner, make the Player bigger or smaller, give a second kind of hazard a different color and speed by making a copy of your hazard prefab, or change what a hit costs.
Make the smallest version first. Change one value, or add one object, with Play off.
Click **Play**, click inside the **Game** view, and play for a minute. Stop **Play** and judge: does the game feel different in the way you meant?
Adjust one value at a time until it feels right. Write the value you keep in PlaytestNotes.
Choose **File > Save**.

Choose **File > Build Profiles**, click your profile under **Build Profiles**, click **Build**, choose your DodgeBuild folder, and click **Replace** if asked. Run the new build once to check the menu still works and your twist is in it. Then zip the DodgeBuild folder again, as you did when you shared it, and replace the file behind your shared link: this new zip is the one you hand in. Record the built game, not the Editor: start it from DodgeBuild and record the menu, a click on Play, your twist in action, a game over, Restart and Quit. Take two screenshots: the Scene List in **File > Build Profiles** with MainMenu at 0 and SampleScene at 1, and your PlaytestNotes showing the moment you saw and your twist sentence. Then open the brief for Dodge game with your own twist and hand in the link, the recording and the two screenshots.

page.text: Dodge has a fix for the problem you saw and a twist you can explain in one sentence, and a new build runs from DodgeBuild. It went wrong if Left Shift does nothing, if time stays slow after you let go, or if the new build still shows the old game. If your own project is stuck, use Dodge-week9-end.zip above: it is Dodge as it should stand at the end of this week, with MainMenu, SampleScene, MenuController, the scene list set, and slow focus added. Unzip it into your Documents folder, next to your own Dodge folder and never over it. To open it, start Unity Hub, click Projects, open the Add dropdown, choose Add project from disk, and pick the Dodge-week9-end folder that holds Assets, Packages and ProjectSettings.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Left Shift does nothing: click inside the Game view first, so it has focus, and hold the key again. Check too that the SlowFocus script sits on the SlowFocus object in SampleScene.

Time stays slow after game over: your game over code may set `Time.timeScale` itself. Leave the `if (Time.timeScale == 0f) return;` line in place, and check that Restart sets it back to 1.

The Console shows The type or namespace name ‘Keyboard’ could not be found: the line `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` is missing or misspelled at the top of the file.
Challenges
These challenges have no steps, because working out how to change the code is how scripting sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks.

Optional challenge: Escape returns to the menu. While Dodge is running, pressing Escape should load MainMenu. Then Play should start a fresh Dodge with all lives back. Try it on paper first. You press Escape with one life left. The menu loads. You click Play, and `PlayGame` loads SampleScene again, so Dodge starts as new with three lives.

page.title: Hint for the Escape challenge
page.text: Make a small script with an `Update` method and put it on an object in SampleScene. Use `Keyboard.current.escapeKey.wasPressedThisFrame` as you read keys in week 4, and `SceneManager.LoadScene("MainMenu")` to load the menu. You need `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` and `using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;`. MainMenu must be in the scene list, which you did this week.

Optional challenge: a focus that runs out. Change SlowFocus so slow time works only while a meter has some left. The meter starts at 3 and drains by 1 for every real second you hold Left Shift. It refills by 0.5 for every real second you do not hold it, and never goes above 3. Try it on paper: hold for 3 real seconds and the meter is 0, so time returns to normal. Release for 2 seconds and the meter is 1, so you can hold again for 1 second.

page.title: Hint for the focus challenge
page.text: Keep a `float focus = 3f;` in the script. While time is slowed, `Time.deltaTime` is only half as big, so use `Time.unscaledDeltaTime` to count real seconds. `Mathf.Clamp(focus, 0f, 3f)` keeps the number between 0 and 3. Only slow time when Shift is held and `focus > 0f`.

Escape takes you from Dodge to the menu, and Play starts a fresh game. Save your changes, stop Play, and rebuild through File > Build Profiles into DodgeBuild. Test Escape and Play in that executable. Then create a fresh zip of the entire DodgeBuild folder and replace your shared download with it. For the focus challenge, a 3-second hold drains the meter and time speeds back up. It went wrong if Escape does nothing in Play or the menu does not load.
Wrap-up

You can now build a start menu that loads Dodge, make a build a classmate can run, and use a playtest to choose a twist. Test yourself. First, why must both scenes be in the scene list, and which one comes first? Second, why does a Windows build not run on a Mac, and what do you do when your classmate uses the other system? Third, what did you see in a playtest that gave you a reason for your twist? Next week you start Hop, a 2D game, from the Universal 2D template. You paint a tilemap level and make a character run and jump, and you submit a recording and a screenshot.

Build files only run on the system they were made for, so ask in the forum for a playtester on your kind of computer. Your first forum post is due Thursday. Your replies, the self-check quiz and Dodge game with your own twist are due Sunday night. There is no separate weekly build this week: the Dodge game takes its place. l_7066b70b87f9.title: 2D: sprites, tilemaps and jumping
l_7066b70b87f9.summary: Start Hop from the Universal 2D template: paint a tilemap level and make a character run and jump; submit a recording and screenshot.
keyIdeas: A sprite is a flat picture. A tilemap lets you paint a level from small repeated tiles on a grid, so you build a floor with one drag instead of placing dozens of objects.
Pixels Per Unit decides how big a sprite is in the world. At 32 pixels per unit, a 32-pixel tile is exactly one unit square.
Hero needs a Rigidbody 2D to move with physics and a 2D collider to touch things. The level needs colliders too, merged into outlines with a Composite Collider 2D.

Running sets the horizontal part of linearVelocity every physics step. A jump is an upward impulse, allowed only when a thin box at Hero’s feet overlaps the Ground layer, so a wall at Hero’s side never counts as ground.

vocabulary.definition: A flat picture that a 2D game draws on screen, such as Hero.
The setting that says how many pixels of a picture fit in one unit of the game world, so it decides the picture’s size.
A sprite prepared so a tilemap can paint it into one cell of its grid.
A tray of tiles that you pick from when you paint a tilemap.
A grid of cells, each holding at most one tile, used to paint a level.
The object that holds a tilemap and sets the size of its cells.
The component that lets 2D physics move an object with gravity and forces.
A component that gives a 2D object a shape so it can touch other objects.
A component that merges touching colliders on a tilemap into one outline.
A named group of objects, such as Ground, that code and physics can pick out.
A test, here a thin box at Hero’s feet, that tells the script whether Hero is standing on ground.

study.overview: This week you built Hop, a 2D platformer, from the Universal 2D template. You can now import pixel-art sprites at the right size, paint a level from tiles, give a character 2D physics, and script running and jumping with the Input System. Reread this page before next week, when you animate Hop and add collectibles. Next week’s reading is Schell, The art of game design, Chapter 7.

points.heading: Sprites, Pixels Per Unit and the tilemap
points.explanation: A sprite is a flat picture. Pixels Per Unit says how many picture pixels fit in one world unit. Your tiles are 32 pixels wide and you set 32, so each tile is exactly one unit square and Hero is one unit tall. The default of 100 would make a tile about a third of a unit wide. A tilemap lets you paint the level on a grid from small repeated tiles. One Box Fill drag laid the whole dirt row, where placing each block as its own object would take dozens of steps. You can now check any sprite by asking: pixels wide divided by Pixels Per Unit is its width in units.

points.heading: Rigidbody 2D and colliders
points.explanation: Hero needs two components. A Rigidbody 2D lets physics move it, and a Box Collider 2D gives it a shape that can touch things. You set the collider to 0.8 by 1, a little narrower than the picture, so Hero does not catch on edges. The level needs colliders too. Tilemap Collider 2D boxes every tile, and Composite Collider 2D with Merge joins touching boxes into outlines. The floor is one connected shape, so it becomes one outline. Each platform floats apart, so each keeps its own outline: four in all. Level’s Rigidbody 2D is Static, so it never moves when Hero lands on it. Level is also on the Ground layer, which Hero’s script uses to find the floor.

points.heading: Running with linearVelocity
points.explanation: Running sets only the horizontal part of the speed, every physics step in FixedUpdate. `rb.linearVelocity = new Vector2(x * moveSpeed, rb.linearVelocity.y);` For example, x is -1 when you hold A, so with a Move Speed of 6 Hero’s sideways speed is -6. The y part is copied from the current speed, so gravity still works. You read x from the Move action with `InputSystem.actions.FindAction("Move")`, because the old Input class throws an error in this project.

points.heading: Jumping only from the ground
points.explanation: A jump is one upward impulse: `rb.AddForce(Vector2.up * jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);`. It is allowed only when `Physics2D.OverlapBox` finds the Ground layer inside a thin box at Hero’s feet. The box is 0.7 wide, narrower than Hero’s 0.8. A wall at Hero’s side is 0.4 from Hero’s middle, but the box reaches only 0.35, so a wall never counts as ground. Tapping Space against the side of Platform 1 does nothing. You can also check the numbers on paper. Gravity Scale 3 gives a pull of 3 × 9.81 = 29.43. A jump at speed 12 rises 12 × 12 ÷ (2 × 29.43), about 2.45 units. Each platform is 2 units higher than the one before, so Hero clears it.

page.text: Last week you finished Dodge. This week you start Hop, a 2D platformer, in a brand-new project made from the Universal 2D template. You import pixel-art sprites, paint a level from tiles, give a character a Rigidbody 2D and colliders, and script running and jumping with the Input System. The 2D tools differ from the 3D ones you know, but the ideas carry over: objects, components, physics and scripts. By Sunday you will have a level with a floor and three platforms, and a hero who runs along it and jumps up each platform, plus a practice recording and screenshot.
