page.text: Start Hop and import your sprites

page.alt: Hop’s Game view: a floor of grass and dirt tiles with three floating platforms rising from left to right. Hero runs along the floor and jumps up onto each platform in turn.
page.caption: This is Hop as you will have it by Sunday: compare it with your own Game view as you go.
page.shows: The Game view of the finished Hop in Play mode at 16:9 Aspect, on either system. Hero starts on the floor at the left, runs right, jumps onto the first platform, then the second, then the third. Frame only the Game view so the whole level is visible. About 20 seconds, no sound.

page.text: Hop is a new game, so it gets a new project. You start from the Universal 2D template, which sets up a camera and a light made for flat pictures. Your Dodge project stays exactly as you left it. Nothing you do this week touches it.

This page is written for Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6.4f1), made through Unity Hub with a Unity Personal license, using the Universal 2D template, with Visual Studio Code for C#. When Hop is open, the Editor window title ends with Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1). If your Editor does not show 6000.6.4f1, or you do not have the Universal 2D template, open Unity Hub, click Installs, and install Editor 6000.6.4f1. Then create Hop from Universal 2D with that Editor selected. If you made Hop from Universal 3D by mistake, make a new project from Universal 2D instead: the 3D project has no Tilemap entries in its menus.

items.text: Open **Unity Hub** and click **Projects** in the left sidebar.
Click **New project**.
At the top of the screen, check that the Editor version reads 6000.6.4f1, or another 6000.6 version.
Open the dropdown beside the search box and choose **Core**.
Click **Universal 2D**.
In the panel on the right, open the **Project name** dropdown and choose **Create new local project**.
Type Hop into the **Project name** box.
Click **Create project**.
Wait for the Editor to open. If a window titled **2D URP Project** opens over it, close that window.

shot.alt: Editor with Hierarchy listing SampleScene, Main Camera and Global Light 2D, Scene and Game tabs in the center, Inspector on the right.
shot.caption: Your new project should look like this, with the Hierarchy on the left.
shot.shows: The Unity Editor just after the project opens, Default layout, 2D URP Project window closed. The Hierarchy shows SampleScene; the Project window shows Assets. Whole Editor window, on your system.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, check that **SampleScene** holds **Main Camera** and **Global Light 2D**.
Click the **Game** tab.
In the Game view toolbar, open the third control, which reads **Free Aspect**, and choose **16:9 Aspect**.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Main Camera**.
In the **Inspector**, find the **Camera** component and check that **Projection** reads Orthographic and **Size** reads 5.

shot.alt: Inspector for Main Camera: Camera component, Projection Orthographic, Size 5.
shot.caption: Projection is Orthographic and Size is 5.
shot.shows: The Inspector with Main Camera selected, the Camera component expanded. Projection reads Orthographic and Size reads 5. Outline both fields.

page.title: Why the camera matters
page.text: An orthographic camera draws everything flat, with no perspective: far things are not smaller. Size 5 means the view reaches 5 units up and 5 units down from the middle, so the view is 10 units tall. At 16:9 it is about 17.8 units wide. Keep these numbers in mind: they are why the level you paint later fits the screen.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Sprites and press Enter.
Click **Assets** again, choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Tiles and press Enter.
Click **Assets** again, choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Scripts and press Enter.

page.label: HopSprites.zip holds three pixel-art pictures, each 32 by 32 pixels: Hero.png (a small character facing right), Grass.png (a dirt block with a grass top) and Dirt.png (a plain dirt block). Download it from this page and unzip it into your Documents folder, in a new folder named HopSprites. Do not unzip it inside your Hop project folder.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the **Sprites** folder under **Assets**.
Open your Documents > HopSprites folder in File Explorer (Windows) or Finder (Mac).

Select the three files Hero.png, Grass.png and Dirt.png and drag them into the **Project** window, onto the **Sprites** folder’s contents. If you prefer a menu, choose **Assets > Import New Asset...**, select the three files and click **Import**.
In the **Project** window, click **Hero**, then Ctrl+click (Command+click on a Mac) **Grass** and **Dirt**, so all three are selected.
In the **Inspector**, check that **Texture Type** reads Sprite (2D and UI), and set **Sprite Mode** to **Single**.
Type 32 into **Pixels Per Unit**.
Set **Filter Mode** to **Point (no filter)**.
Set **Compression** to **None**.
Click **Apply** at the bottom of the Inspector.

shot.alt: Inspector for three sprites: Texture Type Sprite (2D and UI), Pixels Per Unit 32, Filter Mode Point (no filter), Compression None.
shot.caption: The import settings for Hero: Sprite Mode Single, Pixels Per Unit 32, Filter Mode Point (no filter), Compression None.
shot.shows: The Inspector with Hero, Grass and Dirt selected in the Project window. Texture Type Sprite (2D and UI), Pixels Per Unit 32, Filter Mode Point (no filter), Compression None, and the Apply button. Outline those four fields and Apply.

page.title: Why these settings
page.text: Unity measures the world in units, not pixels. Pixels Per Unit says how many picture pixels fit in one unit. The default is 100, which would make your 32-pixel tiles about a third of a unit wide. At 32, each tile is exactly one unit, so Hero is one unit tall. Point (no filter) keeps the pixels crisp instead of smearing them. Compression None keeps the colors true.

page.alt: Project window, Assets > Sprites: Hero, Grass and Dirt sprite thumbnails.
page.caption: Compare your Sprites folder: three sprites, each shown as a small picture.
page.shows: The Project window with the Sprites folder open, showing the Hero, Grass and Dirt sprites as thumbnails. Whole Project window.

page.text: You should now have a project named Hop opened in the Universal 2D template, the Game view set to 16:9 Aspect, folders named Sprites, Tiles and Scripts, and three sprites in Sprites with Pixels Per Unit 32. It went wrong if the sprites look blurry, if the Hierarchy lacks Global Light 2D, or if the Project window has no Sprites folder.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

The sprites look blurry: Filter Mode is not Point (no filter), or you did not click Apply. Select the three sprites again and repeat the settings.

The Editor says 3D, or the Hierarchy has a Directional Light and no Global Light 2D: you made the project from Universal 3D. Make a new project from Universal 2D named Hop.

The three files will not drag in: use **Assets > Import New Asset...** instead, and make sure you unzipped the folder first.
Make tiles and paint your level
A level in a 2D game is a painting more than a pile of objects. You do this now so that the floor and platforms are quick to build, and quick to change when you playtest later.

page.caption: Watch this first: it names every piece you use in this part.
page.shows: The instructor on camera beside a simple diagram: a 32-pixel square picture labeled sprite, a grid of cells labeled tilemap, and a tray of two tiles labeled tile palette. Later, the diagram shows one outline around a floor and one outline around each separate platform.
page.transcript:
Hi. This week your level is a painting, not a pile of objects. Here is how the pieces fit.

Start with a sprite. A sprite is a flat picture that a 2D game draws on screen. Your Hero is one sprite. Your ground is made of two more: Grass and Dirt. Each is a tiny picture, 32 pixels wide and 32 pixels tall.

Now size. Unity measures the world in units, not pixels. The setting Pixels Per Unit says how many pixels of the picture fit in one unit. We set it to 32, so a 32-pixel picture is exactly one unit square. That makes the arithmetic easy: one tile is one unit, and Hero is about one unit tall.

A tile is a sprite wrapped so a tilemap can use it. A tile palette is a tray of tiles, like a painter’s palette. A tilemap is a grid of cells, and each cell holds at most one tile. You pick a tile in the palette and paint cells in the Scene view. A Grid object holds the tilemap and decides the cell size, which is one unit.

Why paint? Because levels are made of the same few pieces repeated. A floor of forty cells takes one drag. Forty separate objects take forty steps.

One more idea. Tiles are only pictures. Hero cannot stand on a picture. The tilemap needs colliders, shapes the physics system can feel. A Tilemap Collider 2D makes one box for each tile. A Composite Collider 2D merges boxes that touch into one outline. The floor becomes one shape. A platform that floats apart from everything else stays its own shape. That is right: a floor and three floating platforms give four outlines.

Keep that chain in mind: sprite, tile, palette, tilemap, collider. Then follow the steps.

items.text: Choose **GameObject > 2D Object > Tilemap > Rectangular**. A **Grid** appears in the Hierarchy with a child named **Tilemap**.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Grid**.
In the **Inspector**, set **Transform > Position** to 0, 0, 0.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Tilemap**.
Choose **Edit > Rename** (F2 on Windows, Enter on a Mac), type Level and press Enter.

shot.alt: Hierarchy: SampleScene with Main Camera, Global Light 2D, Grid and its child Level.
shot.caption: Level is the child of Grid.
shot.shows: The Hierarchy with SampleScene expanded: Main Camera, Global Light 2D and Grid, with Grid expanded to show its child Level. Show the Hierarchy only.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the **Tiles** folder under **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > 2D > Tile Palette > Rectangular**. Type HopPalette and press Enter.
Choose **Window > 2D > Tile Palette**.
At the top of the **Tile Palette** window, open the palette dropdown and choose **HopPalette**.
In the **Project** window, click the **Sprites** folder, click **Grass**, then Ctrl+click (Command+click on a Mac) **Dirt**.
Drag the two selected sprites into the empty grid area of the **Tile Palette** window.
When a window asks where to save the new tiles, choose the **Tiles** folder and confirm.

shot.alt: Tile Palette window, palette HopPalette, containing the Grass tile and the Dirt tile.
shot.caption: Your palette holds two tiles: Grass and Dirt.
shot.shows: The Tile Palette window with HopPalette chosen in its palette dropdown, holding two tiles side by side: Grass and Dirt. Show the whole window with its toolbar visible.

page.title: Find the middle first
page.text: Select **Main Camera** in the Hierarchy and set **Transform > Position** to 0, 0, -10. Click the **Scene** tab and enable **2D** in its toolbar. Paint using the world grid, rather than the middle of the window. The origin is where the world x- and y-axes meet. Cell (0, 0) is immediately above and to the right of that intersection. Positive cell numbers go right and up; negative numbers go left and down. Zoom until you can distinguish individual cells and see the camera outline. Paint Dirt in cells x = -12 through 11 at y = -5, and Grass in the same columns at y = -4. Paint Platform 1 in cells x = -4 through -2 at y = -2, Platform 2 in cells x = 0 through 2 at y = 0, and Platform 3 in cells x = 4 through 6 at y = 2. Use these coordinates for the layout described below.

items: Dirt: one row of tiles, the fifth row below the middle line. This is the bottom row of the Game view.
Grass: one row of tiles directly on top of the dirt, the fourth row below the middle line. Make both rows reach at least three tiles past the left and right edges of the Game view.
Platform 1: three Grass tiles in the second row below the middle line. Its right end is one tile left of the middle line.
Platform 2: three Grass tiles in the first row above the middle line. Its left end is exactly on the middle line.
Platform 3: three Grass tiles in the third row above the middle line. Its left end is four tiles right of the middle line.

Each platform sits one empty row higher than the one before it, so its top is two tiles above the top before it. The floor’s grass top is two tiles below Platform 1's top. Hero’s jump later is built for that gap.

items.text: In the **Tile Palette** window, set **Active Tilemap** to **Level**.
Click the **Dirt** tile in the palette.
Click the **Box Fill** tool in the Tile Palette toolbar (shortcut U).
In the **Scene** view, drag a rectangle one tile tall along the dirt row.
Click the **Grass** tile in the palette.
In the **Scene** view, drag a Box Fill rectangle one tile tall along the grass row, directly above the dirt.

shot.alt: Scene view with a two-row floor: dirt at the bottom, grass on top; Grass tile selected in the Tile Palette.
shot.caption: The grass row sits directly on top of the dirt row.
shot.shows: The Scene view in 2D mode after the floor is painted: a row of dirt tiles with a row of grass tiles on top, running across the whole view. Show the Scene view and the Tile Palette window beside it, with the Grass tile selected.

items.text: Click the **Paint** tool in the Tile Palette toolbar (shortcut B).
In the **Scene** view, click or drag to paint the three Grass tiles of Platform 1.
Paint the three Grass tiles of Platform 2.
Paint the three Grass tiles of Platform 3.
Click the **Game** tab and compare with the picture below.

shot.alt: Game view: floor of dirt and grass, three grass platforms rising left to right, one empty row under each platform.
shot.caption: Your Game view should match this level.
shot.shows: The Game view at 16:9 Aspect with the whole level painted: floor along the bottom, Platform 1 left of center and low, Platform 2 starting at the middle and higher, Platform 3 to the right and highest. No Hero yet.

items.text: Choose **File > Save**.

page.title: Fixing a mistake
page.text: If a tile lands in the wrong place, press Ctrl+Z (Command+Z on a Mac), or choose Edit > Undo. To rub tiles out, use the **Erase** tool in the Tile Palette toolbar (shortcut D) and drag over them.

The Game view shows a floor of dirt and grass along the bottom and three grass platforms stepping up to the right, with one empty row under each platform. It went wrong if the floor stops short of the Game view edges, if platforms touch each other, or if any platform sits directly on another row with no gap.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

Nothing paints: **Active Tilemap** is not set to **Level**, or no tile is selected in the palette. Set it and click a tile.

The Tile Palette window shows no tiles: the palette dropdown is not set to **HopPalette**. Choose it.

The Scene view looks tilted: click the **2D** button in the Scene view toolbar to switch it to a flat view.
Make the ground solid

Right now the tiles are only pictures: Hero would fall straight through them. You add colliders to Level so the physics can feel the floor and platforms, and you give Level a layer so Hero’s script can find the ground later.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, click **Level**.
In the **Inspector**, open the **Layer** dropdown near the top and choose **Add Layer...**.
In the **Layers** list, click the box beside **User Layer 6**, type Ground and press Enter. If **Layers** is closed, click its triangle first.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Level** again.
Open the **Layer** dropdown and choose **Ground**.
With **Level** selected, choose **Component > Tilemap > Tilemap Collider 2D**.

shot.alt: Scene view: thin collider outlines around each tile on the floor and Platform 1, one box per tile.
shot.caption: Before Merge: an outline around every tile.
shot.shows: The Scene view with Level selected and Tilemap Collider 2D just added, before any Composite. Zoomed in on the floor and Platform 1, so the collider outline boxes can be seen around every single tile.

items.text: Choose **Component > Physics 2D > Composite Collider 2D**. A **Rigidbody 2D** is added to Level.
In the **Rigidbody 2D**, set **Body Type** to **Static**.
In the **Tilemap Collider 2D**, set **Composite Operation** to **Merge**.

shot.alt: Scene view: one collider outline around the floor and a separate outline around each platform; Inspector shows Composite Operation Merge and Body Type Static.
shot.caption: After Merge: no lines between touching tiles.
shot.shows: The same Scene view after Composite Operation is set to Merge. The Inspector beside it shows Tilemap Collider 2D with Composite Operation Merge, a Composite Collider 2D, and a Rigidbody 2D with Body Type Static.

items.text: Choose **File > Save**.

page.title: What merging does
page.text: Tilemap Collider 2D gives each tile its own box. Composite Collider 2D, with Merge, joins boxes that touch into one outline. Your floor is one connected shape, so it becomes one outline. Each platform floats apart from everything else, so each stays its own outline: four outlines in all. The Rigidbody 2D set to Static means the level never moves, whatever hits it.

With Level selected, the Scene view shows no lines between neighboring floor tiles, one outline around the whole floor, and a separate outline around each of the three platforms. Level’s layer reads Ground. It went wrong if you still see a box around every tile (Composite Operation is not Merge), or if you expect one outline joining the floor and platforms: they do not touch, so they stay separate.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

There is no **Composite Operation** field: the **Tilemap Collider 2D** is missing. Add it with **Component > Tilemap > Tilemap Collider 2D**, then add the Composite Collider 2D again.

Level falls in Play later: **Body Type** on its Rigidbody 2D is **Dynamic**. Set it to **Static**.

There is no **Ground** in the Layer dropdown: you did not type the name into **User Layer 6** and press Enter. Open **Add Layer...** again.
Add Hero with a Rigidbody 2D and a collider

A character is a sprite plus two components: a Rigidbody 2D, which lets physics move it, and a 2D collider, which gives it a shape that can touch the ground. You add both now, and let Hero fall onto the floor to prove they work.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the **Sprites** folder, then drag **Hero** into the empty space of the **Hierarchy**. An object named **Hero** appears.
Click **Hero** in the **Hierarchy**.
In the **Inspector**, set **Transform > Position** to -7, -2, 0.
In the **Sprite Renderer**, open **Additional Settings** and type 1 into **Order in Layer**.
Open the **Tag** dropdown and choose **Player**.
Click **Add Component**, type Rigidbody 2D and press Enter. Pick **Rigidbody 2D**, not **Rigidbody**.
In the **Rigidbody 2D**, type 3 into **Gravity Scale**.
Open **Constraints** and tick **Freeze Rotation Z**.

shot.alt: Rigidbody 2D on Hero: Mass 1, Gravity Scale 3, Freeze Rotation Z ticked.
shot.caption: Gravity Scale is 3 and Freeze Rotation Z is ticked.
shot.shows: The Inspector with Hero selected, the Rigidbody 2D component open: Mass 1, Gravity Scale 3, Constraints expanded with Freeze Rotation Z ticked. Outline Gravity Scale and Freeze Rotation Z.

items.text: Click **Add Component**, type Box Collider 2D and press Enter.
In the **Box Collider 2D**, type 0.8 into **Size** X and 1 into **Size** Y.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.title: What these settings do
page.text: Gravity Scale 3 multiplies the project’s 2D gravitational acceleration by 3. Hero gains downward speed more quickly, which makes jumps feel snappy instead of floaty. Order in Layer 1 draws Hero in front of the tiles. Freeze Rotation Z stops Hero from tipping over when it bumps something. The collider is 0.8 wide, a little narrower than the 1-unit picture, so Hero does not catch on edges.

items.text: Click **Play** at the top center of the Editor.
Watch the **Game** view: Hero drops about half a tile and lands on the grass.
Click **Play** again to stop.

page.alt: Game view in Play mode: Hero standing on the floor’s grass row, left of Platform 1.
page.caption: Compare Hero standing on the floor: its feet rest on the grass row.
page.shows: The Game view in Play mode, 16:9 Aspect: Hero standing on the grass row at the left of the level, a little left of Platform 1. Whole Game view.

page.text: Hero falls a short way, lands on the grass and stays there. It went wrong if Hero keeps falling out of the view, or if the whole level falls with Hero.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

Hero falls through the floor: Hero has no **Box Collider 2D**, or Level has no **Tilemap Collider 2D** and **Composite Collider 2D**. Add what is missing.

The whole level falls away: Level’s **Rigidbody 2D** has **Body Type** Dynamic. Set it to **Static**.

Hero is hidden behind the tiles: **Order in Layer** on Hero’s **Sprite Renderer** is not 1.
Make Hero run
Running is a script that reads the Move action every physics step and sets Hero’s horizontal speed. You do it now because the jump in the next part builds on the same file.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the **Scripts** folder under **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type HeroController and press Enter.
Double-click **HeroController**. In Visual Studio Code, select everything in the file and delete it.
Type or paste the code from the next block.
Save the file and return to Unity. Wait until the Console shows no red lines.
Drag **HeroController** from the **Project** window onto **Hero** in the **Hierarchy**.
Click **Hero** and check that the Inspector shows a **Hero Controller** component with **Move Speed** 6.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.caption: HeroController.cs

page.text: Line by line. `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` lets the script use the Input System, the only input system this project has. `[SerializeField] float moveSpeed = 6f;` shows a field in the Inspector you can change without editing code. In `Start`, `GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>()` finds Hero’s Rigidbody 2D, and `InputSystem.actions.FindAction("Move")` finds the Move action in the project’s own actions: it covers the A and D keys, the arrow keys and a gamepad stick. The text must match exactly, capital M included. The friction line gives Hero a physics material with no friction: without it, Hero holding against a wall in mid-air would cling to it. In `FixedUpdate`, which runs before each physics step, `ReadValue<Vector2>().x` gives -1 for left, 1 for right and 0 for no key. Setting `rb.linearVelocity` gives Hero that speed. The y part is copied from the current speed so falling is not disturbed. The old `Input.GetAxis` does not work in this project: it throws an error.

items.text: Click **Play** at the top center of the Editor.
Click inside the **Game** view.
Hold D or the right arrow key. Hero runs right along the floor.
Hold A or the left arrow key. Hero runs left.
Click **Play** again to stop.

page.alt: Hero runs right along the floor then back left, stopping at once when the keys are released.
page.caption: Compare with your own run: Hero moves smoothly and stops the moment you let go.
page.shows: The Game view in Play mode, 16:9 Aspect. Hero starts at the left on the floor, runs right to the middle of the view, then runs left again and stops. Frame only the Game view. About 10 seconds, no sound.

page.text: Hero runs left and right at a steady speed and stops when you release the key. It cannot jump yet. It went wrong if Hero does not move, or if the Console shows red lines.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

The Console shows InvalidOperationException about the Input class: the script uses old input such as `Input.GetAxis`. Replace the file with the code above. If a box titled **Script Updating Consent** opens, click **No** and fix the line by hand.

The Console shows NullReferenceException at HeroController: Hero has no **Rigidbody 2D**, or “Move” is mistyped. Check both.

Hero does not move and the Console is clear: you did not click inside the **Game** view first, or **HeroController** is not on Hero.
Make Hero jump

A jump is an upward push, but only if Hero is standing on something. You add a ground check now so Hero cannot jump in mid-air, and you test it where it could most easily fool you: against the side of a platform.

Think about what the check must tell apart. The side of a platform and the top of a platform are both on the Ground layer. If the check used Hero’s whole collider, a wall against Hero’s side would count as ground, and Hero could climb a wall by tapping Space. So the check is a thin box at Hero’s feet that is a little narrower than Hero: 0.7 wide, against Hero’s 0.8. A wall at Hero’s side is 0.4 from Hero’s middle, but the box only reaches 0.35, so it never touches the wall. Only ground directly under Hero’s feet overlaps it.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy**, click **Hero**.
Choose **GameObject > Create Empty Child**. Type FeetCheck and press Enter.
With **FeetCheck** selected, set **Transform > Position** to 0, -0.5, 0.
In the **Project** window, double-click **HeroController**. In Visual Studio Code, select everything and delete it.
Type or paste the whole new file from the next block.
Save the file and return to Unity. Wait until the Console shows no red lines.

page.caption: HeroController.cs

page.text: This file still does everything the last one did: it reads Move, sets `linearVelocity` and removes friction. The new parts are these. `jumpAction` is the Jump action, which the template binds to Space. `WasPressedThisFrame()` is true for one frame when the key goes down. It is checked in `Update` and stored in `jumpRequested`, because `FixedUpdate` does not run every frame and could miss a quick tap. In `FixedUpdate`, a jump happens only if a jump was requested and `IsGrounded()` is true. The jump first sets the up-down speed to 0, so a jump started while falling is not weakened, then `AddForce` with `ForceMode2D.Impulse` adds one upward push. `IsGrounded()` asks `Physics2D.OverlapBox` whether any collider on the Ground layer overlaps the feet box, and returns true if one does. The last method only draws the box so you can see it. Check the numbers on paper: Gravity Scale 3 gives a pull of 3 × 9.81 = 29.43 units per second squared. A jump at speed 12 rises 12 × 12 ÷ (2 × 29.43), about 2.45 units. Each platform is 2 units above the one before, so Hero clears it with room to spare.

items.text: Click **Hero** in the **Hierarchy**. In the **Inspector**, the **Hero Controller** now shows **Jump Force** 12 and **Feet Check** None.
Drag **FeetCheck** from the **Hierarchy** onto the **Feet Check** field.

shot.alt: Hero Controller: Move Speed 6, Jump Force 12, Feet Check set to FeetCheck.
shot.caption: Feet Check holds FeetCheck.
shot.shows: The Inspector with Hero selected, the Hero Controller component showing Move Speed 6, Jump Force 12 and Feet Check filled with FeetCheck. Outline the Feet Check field.

items.text: With **Hero** still selected, look in the **Scene** view for a thin wire rectangle at Hero’s feet.
Choose **File > Save**.
Click **Play** at the top center of the Editor, then click inside the **Game** view.
Press Space. Hero jumps and lands.
Run left of Platform 1, then jump toward it with D held and land on top of it.
From Platform 1, jump onto Platform 2, then onto Platform 3.

Drop back to the floor and run toward the side of Platform 1. Jump so Hero meets its side, hold D, and tap Space many times while Hero slides down the side. Hero must not climb: it does not jump again until it lands.
Click **Play** again to stop.

page.alt: Hero jumps up the three platforms, then slides down the side of Platform 1 without gaining height while jump is tapped.
page.caption: Compare with your own: one jump per landing, and nothing happens when you tap Space against a wall.
page.shows: The Game view in Play mode, 16:9 Aspect. Hero jumps onto Platform 1, then Platform 2, then Platform 3. Then Hero drops to the floor, jumps against the left side of Platform 1 holding right, and taps jump several times while sliding down. Frame the whole Game view. Under 40 seconds, no sound.

page.title: Why a thin box and not the whole body
page.text: The ground check is a box at Hero’s feet that only finds ground beneath them. A wall at Hero’s side cannot reach it, so tapping Space against a wall does nothing. A box that hit walls too would make wall-climbing possible.
Hero runs, jumps once per landing, and reaches all three platforms. A tap of Space in mid-air does nothing. It went wrong if Hero jumps twice in a row, jumps off a wall, or never jumps.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

Hero never jumps and the Console shows UnassignedReferenceException: The variable feetCheck of HeroController has not been assigned. Drag **FeetCheck** onto **Feet Check**.

Hero never jumps and the Console is clear: **Level** is not on the **Ground** layer. Select Level and set **Layer** to **Ground**.

The Console shows InvalidOperationException about the Input class: remove `Input.GetKey` or `Input.GetAxis` from the file. Use the code above.

page.label: HopCheckpoint.zip is the Hop project as it should stand now: level painted, Level on the Ground layer with merged colliders, and Hero running and jumping. Download it from this page, unzip it into your Documents folder in a new folder named HopCheckpoint, never over your own Hop folder. Then open Unity Hub, click Projects, open the Add dropdown, choose Add project from disk, select the HopCheckpoint folder and click Open. The first open takes a few minutes.

page.text: Record and capture a practice run of Hop

You made a recording and a screenshot last week. Here are the steps again for each system, so a practice run now means no surprises later. These are practice files only. They show you the tools and where files land, and you make nothing of them yet.

On Windows you record the Unity window with Xbox Game Bar. Game Bar records one application window, so it films the Unity Editor and nothing else, which is enough to show Hop. It saves the recording on its own. On a Mac you record with the built-in screen tools.

items.text: Open **Settings**, choose **Gaming**, then **Xbox Game Bar** (it may read **Game Bar**), and switch it on.
Click the title bar of the Unity window so Unity is the active window.
Press the Windows key + Alt + R. A small recording timer appears. If a message asks whether this is a game, tick **Yes, this is a game**, then press Windows key + Alt + R again.
In Unity, click **Play**, then click inside the **Game** view.
Run along the floor and jump onto Platform 1 and Platform 2.
Click **Play** to stop.
Press the Windows key + Alt + R to stop recording. A message says the clip was recorded.
Open File Explorer, go to Videos > Captures and double-click the new .mp4 file to check it plays.

Press the Windows key + PrtScn to save a screenshot of the whole screen. It lands in Pictures > Screenshots. On some laptops, press Windows key + Fn + PrtScn. As another way, press the Windows key + Shift + S, drag a rectangle, click the preview that appears and press Ctrl+S. In the save window, choose Pictures > Screenshots, name the file HopPractice.png and save it. If the Screenshots folder does not exist, create it inside Pictures first.
Open File Explorer, go to Pictures > Screenshots and check the new image.
Press Shift+Command+5. A toolbar appears at the bottom of the screen.
Click **Options** and, under **Save to**, choose **Desktop**.
Click **Record Entire Screen**, then click **Record**.
In Unity, click **Play**, then click inside the **Game** view.
Run along the floor and jump onto Platform 1 and Platform 2.
Click **Play** to stop.
Click the **Stop** button in the menu bar at the top of the screen, or press Command+Control+Esc.
On the Desktop, double-click the new file named Screen Recording followed by the date and time, and check it plays.
Press Shift+Command+3 to take a screenshot of the whole screen. It lands on the Desktop as a PNG named Screenshot followed by the date and time.
Double-click the screenshot on the Desktop to check it.

page.text: You have a recording of Hero running and jumping that plays back, and a screenshot of the Unity window with Hop in it. On Windows they are in Videos > Captures and Pictures > Screenshots; on a Mac both are on the Desktop. It went wrong if the recording is black, or shows another window, or if you cannot find the files.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Check these causes in order.

On Windows, Windows key + Alt + R does nothing or the clip is empty: Unity is not the active window, or Game Bar is off. Click the Unity title bar, check **Xbox Game Bar** is on, press Windows key + G, and click the **Capture** panel’s record button instead.

The Windows clip is black or short: stop **Play** first, then stop recording. Try again with Unity filling the screen.

On a Mac, the recording is missing: Options > Save to was not set to Desktop. Look in the folder named there.
Challenges

These challenges have no steps, because working out the change is how scripting sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks. If you get lost, the HopCheckpoint project from last part has the working file to compare with.

Challenge: Hero faces the way it runs. Hero’s picture faces right. Pressing A should turn Hero to face left, pressing D should turn it back to face right, and letting go of both should leave Hero facing the way it last ran. Try it on paper first. Hero is facing right and you hold A: x is -1, so Hero flips to face left. You release: x is 0 and nothing changes, so Hero still faces left. You hold D: x is 1, so Hero faces right.

page.title: Hint for the challenge
page.text: Store Hero’s Sprite Renderer in a field in `Start`, the way the Rigidbody 2D is stored. Read it with `GetComponent<SpriteRenderer>()`. After you read x, change its `flipX` only when x is not 0, and make `flipX` true when x is below 0.

Optional challenge: a shorter hop when you let go. Hold Space and Hero rises about 2.45 units. Release Space early while Hero is rising, and Hero should reach a lower peak. Try it on paper. If the upward speed were cut from 12 to 6 immediately at takeoff, the rise would be 6² ÷ (2 × 29.43), about 0.61 units. In play, Hero has already risen before you release Space. The total height depends on when you release it. Compare an early release with a held jump; the held jump should still reach the platforms.

page.title: Hint for the optional challenge
page.text: `jumpAction.WasReleasedThisFrame()` is true for one frame when the key comes up. Remember it in `Update` in a second `bool`, as you did for the press. In `FixedUpdate`, after the jump code, if that flag is set and `rb.linearVelocity.y` is above 0, set the y speed to half of itself, then clear the flag.

Reading for next week. Read Chapter 7, The Game Begins with an Idea, in Schell, J. (2019). The art of game design: A book of lenses (3rd ed.). CRC Press. Read it for how a designer finds an idea and decides whether it is worth building, and jot down one idea you could make as a small game. To get the book, search your university library’s catalogue for its title: open the e-book from there, or borrow a print copy. If your library has neither, post in the forum and your instructor will tell you what to do. The reading is in your checklist and is due Sunday night.

Hop now has a painted level, a Hero that runs, a jump that works once per landing and reaches all three platforms, and a practice recording and screenshot. If you did the challenge, Hero also turns to face the way it runs. It went wrong if Hero faces right while running left, or if the Console shows red lines.
Wrap-up

You can now start a 2D project, paint a tilemap level, give a character 2D physics, and script running and jumping with the Input System. Test yourself. How do Pixels Per Unit and the tile size decide how big a tile is in the world? What do a Rigidbody 2D and a Box Collider 2D each do for Hero, and why does Level need a Composite Collider 2D? Why does the jump check use a thin box at Hero’s feet, not Hero’s whole body? Next week you animate Hop, add collectibles and a following camera, and write the proposal for your own game. Read Schell, Chapter 7, before then.

facilitation.announcement: Welcome to the week we start Hop, our 2D platformer. You start a brand-new project named Hop from the Universal 2D template (not Universal 3D), paint a level from tiles, and make Hero run and jump. Everything you need is on this week’s page, including a sprite pack and a checkpoint project in case anything fails. The one thing to get right: Level must be on the Ground layer with Merge turned on, or Hero will not jump. Deadlines: your first forum post by Thursday; replies, the self-check quiz, the Schell reading (Chapter 7, for next week’s proposal) and the Weekly builds submission by Sunday night. If you cannot find the Schell book, tell me in the forum and I will help.
watchFor: Students who made Hop from Universal 3D: they will report that GameObject > 2D Object has no Tilemap. Ask them to make a new project from Universal 2D named Hop and re-import the sprites.

Hero falls through the floor, or the whole level falls: usually no collider on Hero or Level, or Level’s Rigidbody 2D Body Type left on Dynamic. Point them to Part 3 and Part 4 and ask for a Hierarchy screenshot.
Hero never jumps: check that Level is on the Ground layer and FeetCheck is dragged into Feet Check. Ask for the Console text. UnassignedReferenceException means the slot is empty.
Old input code or rb.velocity pasted from the web: they get InvalidOperationException or the Script Updating Consent box. Tell them to choose No, then replace the file with the page’s code.

Windows students who cannot record with Game Bar: check that Game Bar is on and Unity is the active window. A recording of the Unity window is accepted. Mac students who record the wrong screen or save elsewhere: remind them of Options > Save to.
Students who cannot get the Schell chapter: tell them to search their library catalogue for the e-book first, and answer them in the forum if the library has no copy.
feedback: Your level reads clearly: the floor, the steps up and the empty rows under each platform are all where the page put them. Nice work keeping the gaps even.
Your jump check works as intended: tapping Space against the side of a platform does nothing. Say in your forum post why a thin box at the feet does that.
Your recording shows Hero running and jumping together. Next time, keep Play going a few seconds longer so the whole jump is visible.
Your Hero reaches every platform. If a jump feels too floaty or too sharp, try changing Jump Force or Gravity Scale by small steps and watch what happens.
Your Console is clear and your scripts match the names on the page, which makes your work easy to check. Keep that habit.
If the sprites look soft, select them in the Project window and check Filter Mode and Compression, then click Apply.
facilitation.atRisk: By Wednesday, contact anyone who has not posted in the forum or has not created the Hop project, and anyone who has reported a Hub or template problem. Send a short message: say what you can see from their work or the forum, point them to the HopCheckpoint project and the Stuck? list, and ask which part they are on. For students with a hardware problem (Unity will not install or run), suggest the Unity Hub Installs tab and ask what the Editor shows, then offer a short extension if they are blocked.

l_39fad0da5d1b.summary: Animate Hop, add collectibles and a following camera, and write your own game's proposal; submit the proposal, graded as part of the final project.
suggestedReadings: Schell, J. (2019). The art of game design: A book of lenses (3rd ed.). CRC Press
keyIdeas: An Animation Clip stores which picture a sprite shows at which moment. An Animator Controller decides which clip plays, using parameters that a script sets.
A collectible is a trigger that reacts when Hero touches it. It adds to the score and then removes itself.
A camera that follows the player moves in LateUpdate, after the player has moved, so it never lags a frame behind.
Scope is how much game you try to make, measured against the time you have. A small game you finish beats a big one you cannot.

vocabulary.definition: A short recording of what an object changes over time, such as which picture a sprite shows.
One saved moment in an Animation Clip, such as show this picture at 0:06.
A diagram of states and transitions that decides which Animation Clip is playing.
One clip in an Animator Controller that can be playing, such as Hero_Run.
A value in an Animator Controller, such as true or false, that a script sets and transitions read.
An arrow between two states that fires when its condition is met.
An object the player gathers by touching it, which then changes the score and disappears.
A Unity method that runs after every Update has finished, used for a camera that follows.
How much game you try to make, measured against the time you have to make it.
The action a player repeats again and again, with a reason to keep going.
One thing the player can do or meet in a game, such as jumping or collecting a coin.

study.overview: This week you made Hop feel like a game and began planning your own. You can now make Hero change picture depending on what Hero is doing, add coins that count themselves, and keep the camera on Hero as the level scrolls. You can also judge how big a game idea is and cut it down to something you can finish. Reread this page before next week, when you cut your idea to a playable core and build a prototype. The proposal you submit this week counts toward your Final game project.

points.heading: Animate a sprite with a clip and a controller
points.explanation: An Animation Clip stores which picture a sprite shows at which moment. Hero_Run, for example, has four keyframes at 0:00, 0:06, 0:12 and 0:18, showing Hero_Run1 to Hero_Run4, with Loop Time ticked so the run repeats. An Animator Controller decides which clip plays. It reads parameters, here the true or false values `isRunning` and `isGrounded`, and follows a transition when its condition is met. Idle goes to Run when `isRunning` is true, and Any State goes to Jump when `isGrounded` is false. With Has Exit Time off and a duration of 0, Hero changes pose the moment a parameter changes. A short script, HeroAnimation, sets the parameters every frame with `animator.SetBool`. The names in quotes must match the Animator exactly, including capital letters. If Hero stays in the jump pose on the floor, check that FeetCheck is named exactly that and that Level is on the Ground layer.

points.heading: Build collectibles and a camera that follows
points.explanation: A collectible is a trigger that reacts when Hero touches it, adds to the score and then removes itself. Your Coin has a Circle Collider 2D with Is Trigger ticked, so Hero passes through it and the coin is told about the touch. In `OnTriggerEnter2D`, `other.CompareTag("Player")` checks that it was Hero. Then `counter.AddCoin()` adds one, the label redraws as “Coins: 1", and `Destroy(gameObject)` removes that coin. Because Coin is a prefab, one edit to the prefab, such as adding the Coin Pickup script, changes all five copies. The camera follows in `LateUpdate`, which runs after the frame’s `Update` calls. It moves toward Hero’s current position, so it never lags a frame behind. `Vector3.SmoothDamp` gives a soft slide, and the camera keeps its own z of -10. If the picture does not move in Play, the Target slot on Camera Follow is probably empty.

points.heading: Scope a game you can finish
points.explanation: Scope is how much game you try to make, measured against the time you have. A small game you finish beats a big one you cannot. Start with a core loop in one sentence: In (name) you (do this) to (get that), while (this gets in the way). Then sort every feature you imagine into Must, Should and Could. A Must is a feature the game stops working without. To test one, ask what happens if you remove it: if the game still works, it is not a Must. Next to each Must, write which of Orb Collector, Dodge or Hop you built something like it in, or write new. Keep five or fewer Musts, and move any new Must that is too big for an evening of tutorial work down to Should. If you have ten Musts, or most say new, keep cutting. Use this method when you write your proposal for the Final game project.

page.text: Last week Hero learned to run and jump. This week Hop starts to feel like a game. You give Hero idle, run and jump animations, add spinning coins that Hero can collect, and make the camera follow Hero along the level. Then you turn from Hop to your own idea. You learn how to judge how much game you can really finish, and you write the proposal for the game you will build next. By Sunday night you have an animated Hop and a proposal submitted toward your Final game project.

page.text: Hop is your project from last week, so you carry on in it and add to it. You start by checking that it still runs, then you bring in the pictures that make Hero look alive.

This page is written for Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6.4f1), with your Hop project made from the Universal 2D template and Visual Studio Code for C#. When Hop is open, the Editor window title ends with Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1). If yours shows a different version, open Unity Hub, click Installs, install Editor 6000.6.4f1, then open Hop with that Editor. Do not upgrade the project to a newer Editor.

Click **Hop** in the list and wait for the Editor to open.

In the **Hierarchy**, check that you see **Main Camera**, **Global Light 2D**, **Grid** and **Hero**. If **SampleScene** is not open, double-click **SampleScene** in the **Scenes** folder in the **Project** window.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Art and press Enter.
Click the **Art** folder to open it.

page.text: A project made from Universal 2D imports a picture as Sprite Mode Multiple, which cuts it into trimmed pieces with names like Hero_Idle_0. Single keeps each picture whole. Pixels Per Unit 32 makes a 32-pixel picture one unit tall, the same scale as your tiles.

Hop still runs and jumps as it did last week. The Art folder holds ten pictures, each with Sprite Mode Single and Pixels Per Unit 32. If a picture still shows a small arrow on its thumbnail, it is still Multiple: select it and set Single again.

page.alt: Art folder holding Coin_1 to Coin_4, Hero_Idle, Hero_Jump and Hero_Run1 to Hero_Run4
page.caption: Compare with your Art folder: ten pictures.
page.shows: The Project window with Assets > Art open in grid view, showing Coin_1 to Coin_4, Hero_Idle, Hero_Jump and Hero_Run1 to Hero_Run4. Outline the window.

page.text: Pictures look blurry: Filter Mode is not Point (no filter), or you did not click Apply. Fix the setting and click Apply. Pictures show a small arrow or have names ending in _0: Sprite Mode is still Multiple. Set it to Single and click Apply. Hop will not open in Unity Hub: the Editor is not 6000.6.4f1. Install it from Installs, or open the HopStart project instead.
Make the Idle, Run and Jump clips
A sprite animation is one object showing a series of pictures, one after another. You build three clips so Hero can stand, run and jump.

An Animation Clip is a short recording of what an object changes over time. A keyframe is one saved moment in a clip. For a sprite the change is which picture shows, so a keyframe says: at this time, show this picture. Time in the Animation window reads as seconds and frames, so 0:06 is frame 6 of the first second.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click **Assets**, choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Animations and press Enter.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Hero**.
Choose **Window > Animation > Animation** (Ctrl+6 on Windows, Command+6 on a Mac).
If the window opens floating, drag its tab onto the area beside the **Console** tab.
Click **Create** in the middle of the **Animation** window.
In the save window, open the **Animations** folder, type Hero_Idle as the name and click **Save**. Unity also makes an Animator Controller named Hero and adds an **Animator** component to Hero.
In the **Project** window, open **Assets > Art** and drag **Hero_Idle** into the timeline area of the **Animation** window, at 0:00.
Click the clip dropdown at the top left of the **Animation** window (it reads Hero_Idle) and choose **Create New Clip...**.
Type Hero_Run, keep the **Animations** folder, and click **Save**.
In **Art**, click **Hero_Run1**, then hold Shift and click **Hero_Run4** so four pictures are selected.
Drag the four pictures together into the timeline area of the **Animation** window, starting at 0:00.
Check that four keyframes sit evenly apart. If they are bunched together, drag them so they sit at 0:00, 0:06, 0:12 and 0:18.
Click the clip dropdown again and choose **Create New Clip...**.
Type Hero_Jump and click **Save**.
Drag **Hero_Jump** from **Art** into the timeline area at 0:00.
In the **Project** window, open **Assets > Animations** and click **Hero_Run**.
In the **Inspector**, make sure **Loop Time** is ticked.

page.text: The Animations folder holds Hero_Idle, Hero_Run, Hero_Jump and a controller named Hero. The clip dropdown in the Animation window lists the three clips. Hero_Run shows four keyframes and has Loop Time ticked. If the Animation window says it needs an Animator and a clip, Hero is not selected, or you skipped Create.

The pictures drop in with odd names like Hero_Run1_0: they are still Sprite Mode Multiple. Fix the import settings from the first part, then drop them in again. The Animation window says To begin animating Hero, create an Animator and an Animation Clip: click Hero in the Hierarchy, then click Create. Hero’s pose changes in the Scene view when you click in the timeline: that is only a preview and is fine. Press Ctrl+Z (Command+Z on a Mac) if you moved Hero by mistake.
Connect the clips and make Hero play them
Three clips do nothing until something chooses between them. The Animator Controller is that chooser, and a short script tells it what Hero is doing.

An Animator Controller is a diagram of states. A state is one clip that can be playing, such as Hero_Run. A parameter is a value, here true or false, that the controller reads. A transition is an arrow between states that fires when its condition is met: for example, go from Hero_Idle to Hero_Run when `isRunning` is true.
Build the controller

items.text: Choose **Window > Animation > Animator**.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Hero**.
In the **Animator** window, find the boxes **Hero_Idle**, **Hero_Run** and **Hero_Jump**. If one is missing, drag its clip from **Assets > Animations** into the **Animator** window.
Click the **Parameters** tab at the top left of the **Animator** window.
Click **+** and choose **Bool**, type isRunning and press Enter.
Click **+** again and choose **Bool**, type isGrounded and press Enter.
Click the **Layers** tab to go back to the diagram.
Right-click **Hero_Idle**, choose **Make Transition**, then click **Hero_Run**.
Click the new arrow.
In the **Inspector**, under **Conditions**, click **+**. Check it reads isRunning and true.
Untick **Has Exit Time**.
Open the **Settings** foldout and type 0 into **Transition Duration (s)**.
Right-click **Hero_Run**, choose **Make Transition**, then click **Hero_Idle**.
Click the new arrow and click **+** under **Conditions**.
Set the value in the condition to false, so it reads isRunning and false.
Untick **Has Exit Time** and type 0 into **Transition Duration (s)**.
Right-click **Any State**, choose **Make Transition**, then click **Hero_Jump**.
Click the new arrow and click **+** under **Conditions**. Change the name to isGrounded and the value to false.
Untick **Has Exit Time**, type 0 into **Transition Duration (s)**, and untick **Can Transition To Self** in **Settings**.
Right-click **Hero_Jump**, choose **Make Transition**, then click **Hero_Idle**.
Click the new arrow and click **+** under **Conditions**. Change the name to isGrounded and the value to true.
Untick **Has Exit Time** and type 0 into **Transition Duration (s)**.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.text: Has Exit Time makes a state finish its clip before the arrow can fire. With it off and a duration of 0, Hero changes pose the moment the parameter changes, which feels right in a game.

The Animator window shows four arrows: Hero_Idle to Hero_Run, Hero_Run to Hero_Idle, Any State to Hero_Jump, and Hero_Jump to Hero_Idle. The Parameters tab lists isRunning and isGrounded. If you press Play now, Hero stays in the jump pose, because nothing sets isGrounded yet. That is expected, and you fix it next.

page.alt: Finished Animator graph with four transition arrows between Hero_Idle, Hero_Run, Hero_Jump and Any State
page.caption: Compare your Animator window with this finished diagram.
page.shows: The Animator window on the Layers tab showing the finished diagram: Entry to Hero_Idle, and arrows Idle to Run, Run to Idle, Any State to Jump, Jump to Idle. Outline the four arrows.

page.text: Write the script that sets the parameters

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the **Scripts** folder under **Assets**.
Choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type HeroAnimation and press Enter.
Double-click **HeroAnimation**. In Visual Studio Code, select everything in the file and delete it.
Type or paste the code from the next block.

page.caption: HeroAnimation.cs

page.text: Read it top to bottom. `private Animator animator;` makes a box that will hold Hero’s Animator. `rb` holds the Rigidbody 2D and `feetCheck` holds the FeetCheck child you made last week. In `Start`, `GetComponent<Animator>()` fetches the Animator that Create added to Hero, and `transform.Find("FeetCheck")` finds the child by its exact name. In `Update`, `Mathf.Abs` drops the minus sign, so running left and right both count. `bool` is a true or false value. `Physics2D.OverlapBox` asks whether a thin box at FeetCheck touches the Ground layer. Use the same width and height in HeroController and HeroAnimation so jumping and animation agree. `SetBool` writes the two answers into the parameters you made, so the names in quotes must match the Animator exactly.

items.text: Save the file and return to Unity. Wait until the **Console** shows no red lines.
Drag **HeroAnimation** from the **Project** window onto **Hero** in the **Hierarchy**.
Click **Hero** and check that the **Inspector** shows a **Hero Animation** component and an **Animator** component with **Controller** set to Hero.
Choose **File > Save**.
Click **Play**. Stand still, then hold D, then press Space.
Click **Play** again to stop.

page.text: Standing still shows the idle picture, holding D plays the run, and Space shows the jump picture until Hero lands. If Hero stays in the jump pose on the floor, check that FeetCheck is at Hero’s feet, Level is on the Ground layer, and HeroAnimation uses the same ground-check box dimensions as HeroController.

Hero stays in the jump pose: Level is not on the Ground layer, or the child is not named exactly FeetCheck. A Console error reads NullReferenceException on the line with feetCheck.position: the same cause, a missing or misspelled FeetCheck. A yellow warning reads Parameter ‘isRunning’ does not exist.: the parameter name in the Animator and the name in the script differ, so compare capital letters. If the file will not attach, the class name inside must be HeroAnimation, matching the file name.
Make a spinning Coin and place five copies
A collectible needs a picture, a shape Hero can touch, and a reason to look alive. You build one coin, turn it into a prefab, and place five copies, so one change later fixes all of them.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click **Assets**, choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Prefabs and press Enter.
Open **Assets > Art** and drag **Coin_1** into the empty space of the **Hierarchy**.

In the **Sprite Renderer**, open **Additional Settings** and type 1 into **Order in Layer**.
Choose **Component > Physics 2D > Circle Collider 2D**.

Count coins with TextMeshPro
A game that does not say what happened feels broken. You add a label that counts coins and a script that adds one each time Hero touches a coin.
Add the label

items.text: Choose **GameObject > UI (Canvas) > Text - TextMeshPro**.
When the **TMP Importer** window opens, click **Import TMP Essentials**. If a box titled **Unofficial Unity source** follows, click **Import Anyway**, wait, then close the window.

shot.alt: TMP Importer window with Import TMP Essentials button
shot.caption: This opens once per project.
shot.shows: The TMP Importer window with the Import TMP Essentials button. Outline the button.

In the **Hierarchy**, click **Text (TMP)** under **Canvas**, choose **Edit > Rename**, type CoinsText and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, in **TextMeshPro - Text (UI)**, click the **Text Input** box and type Coins: 0.
Type 36 into **Font Size**.
In **Rect Transform**, click the anchor preset square at the top left and choose the top-left preset.
Type 150 into **Pos X**, -40 into **Pos Y**, 250 into **Width** and 60 into **Height**.

page.text: Write the counter

items.text: In the **Project** window, click **Scripts**, then choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type CoinCounter and press Enter.
Double-click **CoinCounter**. In Visual Studio Code, select everything and delete it.
Type or paste the code from the next block.

page.caption: CoinCounter.cs

page.text: `using TMPro;` lets the script use TextMeshPro. `[SerializeField] private TMP_Text coinsText;` makes a slot in the Inspector where you drop the label. `private int coins = 0;` is a whole number that starts at zero. `public void AddCoin()` is a method other scripts can call: it adds one and redraws the label. `"Coins: " + coins` joins the words and the number into one piece of text.

items.text: Save the file and return to Unity.
Choose **GameObject > Create Empty**, then **Edit > Rename**, type GameManager and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, set **Transform > Position** to 0, 0, 0.
Drag **CoinCounter** from the **Project** window onto **GameManager** in the **Hierarchy**.
Click **GameManager**. Drag **CoinsText** from the **Hierarchy** into the **Coins Text** slot of **Coin Counter** in the **Inspector**.

shot.alt: Coin Counter component with Coins Text set to CoinsText
shot.caption: The slot should read CoinsText, not None.
shot.shows: The Inspector for GameManager showing the Coin Counter component with the Coins Text slot filled with CoinsText. Outline the slot.

page.text: Make coins count themselves

items.text: In the **Project** window, click **Scripts**, then choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type CoinPickup and press Enter.
Double-click **CoinPickup**. In Visual Studio Code, select everything and delete it.
Type or paste the code from the next block.

page.caption: CoinPickup.cs

page.text: `FindAnyObjectByType<CoinCounter>()` finds the counter on GameManager, so no slot is needed. `OnTriggerEnter2D` runs when something enters the coin’s trigger circle. `other.CompareTag("Player")` checks it was Hero, not a platform. `counter.AddCoin()` adds one, and `Destroy(gameObject)` removes this coin.

items.text: Save the file and return to Unity.
Drag **CoinPickup** from the **Project** window onto the **Coin** prefab in the **Prefabs** folder.
In the **Hierarchy**, click **Coin (2)** and check the **Inspector** shows a **Coin Pickup** component.
Choose **File > Save**.
Click **Play**, run to a coin and touch it.
Click **Play** again to stop.

page.text: Touching a coin removes it and the label goes up by one each time. If a coin is touched and nothing happens, check the prefab has Coin Pickup and Is Trigger is ticked.

page.alt: Game view with the label Coins: 2 at the top left
page.caption: After three coins: the label reads Coins: 3.
page.shows: The Game view in Play at 16:9 Aspect showing Hero beside the remaining coins and the label Coins: 2 at the top left. Outline the label.

page.text: A red error reads UnassignedReferenceException: the Coins Text slot on Coin Counter is empty. Fill it from the Hierarchy. A red error reads NullReferenceException in CoinPickup: there is no CoinCounter in the scene, so check GameManager has it. A coin is touched but stays: Is Trigger is off, or the Hero tag is not Player. A red error with a TMP or font name: repeat the TMP Importer step.
Make the camera follow Hero
Right now the camera stays still, so Hero can leave the screen. A following camera lets a level be wider than one screen, which is why you do it before designing your own game.

items.text: In the **Project** window, click **Scripts**, then choose **Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script**. Type CameraFollow and press Enter.
Double-click **CameraFollow**. In Visual Studio Code, select everything and delete it.
Type or paste the code from the next block.

page.caption: CameraFollow.cs

page.text: `LateUpdate` runs after the frame’s `Update` calls. Hero moves through physics steps in `FixedUpdate`; the camera then follows Hero’s current displayed position. Smoothing adds a small following delay. `target` is the object to follow. `Vector3 goal` is where the camera wants to be: Hero’s x and y, with the camera’s own z, because a 2D camera must stay back from the scene. `Vector3.SmoothDamp` moves the camera toward the goal over about `smoothTime` seconds, which gives a soft slide instead of a hard jump. The word `ref` lets the method update `velocity` for you each frame.

items.text: Save the file and return to Unity.
Drag **CameraFollow** from the **Project** window onto **Main Camera** in the **Hierarchy**.
Click **Main Camera**. In the **Inspector**, set **Transform > Position** to -7, -2, -10 so it starts on Hero.
Drag **Hero** from the **Hierarchy** into the **Target** slot of **Camera Follow**.

shot.alt: Camera Follow component with Target Hero and Smooth Time 0.15
shot.caption: Target should read Hero.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Main Camera showing Camera Follow with Target set to Hero and Smooth Time 0.15. Outline Target and Smooth Time.

items.text: Choose **File > Save**.
Click **Play** and run right along the level.
Click **Play** again to stop.

page.alt: Camera slides to keep Hero near the middle of the Game view as Hero runs and jumps
page.caption: Compare: the view slides along with Hero.
page.shows: The Game view only, 16:9 Aspect, Play on. Hero runs right along the floor and jumps; the level scrolls past while Hero stays near the middle. Silent, about 15 seconds.

page.text: Hero stays near the middle of the Game view while the level slides past. If the picture does not move, Target is empty. If everything disappears, the camera Z was changed: set it back to -10.

A red error reads UnassignedReferenceException in CameraFollow: drag Hero into Target. The camera shakes while Hero runs: first check that CameraFollow uses `LateUpdate`. Physics updates can also make Hero appear to move in small steps. With Play off, add `rb.interpolation = RigidbodyInterpolation2D.Interpolate;` immediately after `rb = GetComponent<Rigidbody2D>();` in HeroAnimation’s `Start`. Save the script, return to Unity and test again. You see empty space left of the level: that is fine for now.

page.shows: The Hop project as it should stand now: Assets with Art, Animations, Prefabs and Scripts (HeroController, HeroAnimation, CoinCounter, CoinPickup, CameraFollow), and SampleScene with Hero animated, five Coins, GameManager, CoinsText and a following Main Camera.

To open it, go to Unity Hub, click Projects, open the Add dropdown, choose Add project from disk, select the unzipped HopAnimated folder, then click HopAnimated in the list with Editor 6000.6.4f1 chosen.
Scope a game you can finish
A first game can become too big to finish when its feature list outgrows the time available. This part gives you a way to measure size, so your own game starts small enough to complete.

page.alt: Instructor explaining scope with a Must, Should, Could table for an example game
page.caption: Watch once, then use the steps below with your own idea.
page.shows: The instructor on camera beside a simple table on screen with three columns headed Must, Should and Could. The table fills in as the instructor talks: Lantern Run, a game that is only an example, with its features sorted into the columns.
page.transcript:
A first game can become too big to finish. Each feature adds work to build, connect and test. This video gives you a way to measure size, so your proposal describes a game you can complete.

Start with a word: scope. Scope is how much game you try to make, set against the time you have. You cannot see scope on a screen, so you measure it by counting features. A feature is one thing the player can do or meet: run, jump, collect a coin, dodge a hazard, win.

Look at Hop. Its whole game is four features: Hero runs, Hero jumps, coins can be collected, and the camera follows. That is a complete, playable game. Orb Collector and Dodge were small in the same way. Notice how little is in them.

Next, find your core loop. The core loop is the action the player repeats again and again, with a reason to keep going. In Hop it is: move, jump, reach a coin, repeat. In Dodge it is: move, avoid, survive longer. Say yours in one sentence: in my game you do this to get that, while this gets in the way. If you cannot say it in one sentence, the idea is still too big, or too vague.

Now sort every feature you imagine into three piles. Must is what the core loop cannot work without. Should makes the game better, but it still works without it. Could is everything else. Sound effects, a second level, a boss, a shop, a save system: nearly all of these are Should or Could. Be harsh.

Here is a made-up example. Suppose you imagine a game called Lantern Run, where you carry a lantern through a dark cave and collect gems. Move and jump are Musts. Collecting gems is a Must. A dark cave that only the lantern lights is the whole idea of the game, so that is a Must too. A second cave, bats and a high-score table are Could.

Then test your Musts against what you can already do. For each one, ask: have I built something like this in Orb Collector, Dodge or Hop? If yes, it is safe. If an essential feature is new and too large to learn and test in an evening, simplify it or change your core loop so the game works without it. Then sort the revised features again. New features cost far more than they look, because each one brings new errors to find.

Finally, plan to cut. Everything takes longer than you expect, and testing always shows a problem to fix. Keep a short Must list, no more than five, and decide now what you will drop first if time runs out.

A small game you finish teaches you more, and shows better, than a big one that is half built. Your proposal should describe the small one. Now make your own notes with the steps on the page.

items.text: Open any notes app or word processor and make a new document named GameScope.
Type your core loop as one sentence: In (name) you (do this) to (get that), while (this gets in the way).
Draw a table with three columns headed Must, Should and Could, then write every feature you imagine under one of them.
Beside each Must, write the name of the game among Orb Collector, Dodge and Hop where you built something like it, or write new.
Move every Must that is new and too big for an evening of tutorial work down to Should, until five or fewer Musts remain.

page.text: You hold a one-sentence core loop and a table with five or fewer Musts. Most Musts name a game you have already built. If you have ten Musts, or most say new, the game is still too big: keep cutting.

You cannot say the loop in one sentence: pick the one action the player repeats and cut the rest. Everything feels like a Must: ask what happens if you remove it, and if the game still works, it is not a Must. Your idea is a copy of a game you love: that is fine, but shrink it to one screen and one verb.

Optional, outside this week’s hours: Schell, J. (2019), The art of game design: A book of lenses (3rd ed., CRC Press), the chapter on ideas that last week asked you to read (Chapter 7). Read it for how a designer turns a first idea into something that can be built. Nothing this week depends on it.
Challenges: collect them all and recover from a fall

These challenges have no steps, because working out the change is how scripting sticks. Save your work first, keep Play off while you edit, and read the Console if something breaks. If you get lost, compare with HopAnimated from the earlier part.
Challenge: all the coins

Make the label read You got them all! as soon as Hero has collected all five coins. Try it on paper first. Hero has collected four, so the label reads Coins: 4. Hero touches the last coin: the count becomes 5, which equals the number of coins in the level, so the label changes. Until then it keeps showing Coins and the number.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Add a second whole-number field to CoinCounter, such as `[SerializeField] private int totalCoins = 5;`. In `UpdateLabel`, use an `if` that asks whether `coins` equals `totalCoins`. If it does, set `coinsText.text` to the message. Otherwise keep the old line. Then check totalCoins matches the number of coins you placed.
Optional challenge: back to the start

Optional, outside the week’s hours. Make Hero return to the start when it falls off the level. Try it on paper: Hero walks off the left edge and falls, and its y keeps dropping. When y goes below -8, Hero is moved back to -7, -2, 0 and stops falling. While y is above -8, nothing changes.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Work in HeroAnimation, or a script of your own on Hero. In `Update`, ask whether `transform.position.y` is below -8. If it is, set `transform.position = new Vector3(-7, -2, 0);` and `rb.linearVelocity = Vector2.zero;`. Without the second line, Hero would keep its falling speed after the move.
Wrap-up

You can now animate a sprite with an Animation Clip and an Animator Controller, add collectible coins that count themselves, make the camera follow the player, and scope a game small enough to finish. Test yourself. How do a parameter and a transition decide which clip Hero plays? Why must a coin have Is Trigger ticked, and why does the camera follow in LateUpdate? What makes a feature a Must in your own game, and how do you check you can build it? Next time you cut your idea to a playable core, build a prototype and learn to debug, then submit the prototype toward your final project.

facilitation.announcement: This week Hop comes alive: Hero gets idle, run and jump animations, you add spinning coins that count, and the camera follows Hero. You also scope your own game and write its proposal. The one thing to get right: the parameter names isRunning and isGrounded must be spelled exactly the same in the Animator and in the script, capital letters included. Post your first forum post by Thursday. Replies and the proposal are due Sunday night, and the proposal counts toward your Final game project. If you get stuck, start with the Stuck? list, then ask in the forum.
watchFor: Hero stuck in the jump pose: usually Level is not on the Ground layer or the child is not named exactly FeetCheck. Ask the student to check both and reply in the forum with the Console text.

feedback: Your Animator shows all four arrows and Hero plays the right clip each time. That is a clear way to link what Hero does to what you see.
Your coins spin and count correctly. Next, try placing them so each one asks something different of the player, such as a longer jump.

t_77f2885b3038.prompt: You want to find a warning Unity showed while opening your project. Which window should you check?

choices.text: Project, where Unity messages appear.
Inspector, where Unity messages appear.
Hierarchy, where Unity messages appear.

t_0cb83ea709b9.prompt: A Cube has Scale Y set to 4. What Position Y places it on a flat ground at Y = 0, with its bottom resting on the ground?

choices.text: 0, because Position marks the bottom of the Cube.
1, because Position is one quarter of its height.
2, because Position is half of its height.
4, because Position matches its scaled height.

t_0cb83ea709b9.explanation: A Cube is 1 unit tall at Scale 1, so Scale Y of 4 makes it 4 units tall. Position gives the center, so the center must be half the height above the ground: 4 ÷ 2 = 2. Position is not the bottom or the full height. Review “Build the courtyard from primitive shapes.”

t_0f7ca91a0fb3.prompt: Every GameObject has a Transform with Position, Rotation, and Scale settings.

choices.text: True
False

t_0f7ca91a0fb3.explanation: The Transform stores where an object is, how it is turned, and how big it is. Review “Build the courtyard from primitive shapes.”

t_e40eed3aafac.prompt: Name the three things that work together to determine what appears in the Game view.
t_e40eed3aafac.answer: The camera’s position and rotation, its field of view, and the shape or aspect ratio of the Game view.
t_e40eed3aafac.explanation: The camera’s position and rotation set where it looks. Its field of view sets how wide an angle it sees, and the Game view’s shape affects how much fits across the picture. Review “Frame the camera, press Play and save.”

t_b67eb6e40eb8.title: Weekly builds: components, materials and physics
t_b67eb6e40eb8.prompt:
This build gives you practice using components to change how a GameObject looks and moves. It contributes to Weekly builds, which counts for 40% of your course grade.

In your OrbCollector project, add a sphere named Color_Drop at Position -6, 7, 4. Create a material with a Hexadecimal color you choose and assign it to the sphere. Add a Rigidbody, keep its Sphere Collider enabled and Use Gravity ticked, then press Play to check that it falls and stops on the floor. With Play off, change the Directional Light’s Light Appearance to Color and choose a Hexadecimal color that changes the scene’s look. After you have captured your work you may set it back to FFF4E0, the page’s warm white. Save Arena. Click Color_Drop in the Hierarchy so the Inspector shows its components, then take a screenshot of the whole Unity Editor with the Game view visible. Make a short screen recording showing the sphere fall as you press Play and stop it. Upload both to the LMS by Sunday night this week. In your submission, explain your color choices and note any help you used, including AI tools.

steps: In the OrbCollector project, add a Sphere named Color_Drop. Set Position to -6, 7, 4 and Scale to 1, 1, 1.
Create a new material with a Hexadecimal color of your choice and assign it to Color_Drop. Add a Rigidbody; make sure Use Gravity and the Sphere Collider are enabled.
Set Directional Light’s Light Appearance to Color and choose a Hexadecimal color. Press Play to check that Color_Drop falls and stops on the floor, then stop Play. Save Arena.

Click Color_Drop in the Hierarchy so the Inspector shows its Transform, Sphere Collider and Rigidbody. Take a screenshot of the whole Unity Editor with the Game view visible. Make a short screen recording showing you press Play, the sphere fall, and Play stop.
Upload the screenshot and recording to the LMS by Sunday night this week. Include an explanation of your color choices and a note of any help you used, including AI tools.
t_b67eb6e40eb8.answerKey:
1. In Assets > Create > Material, create M_Color_Drop; assign a chosen color, for example Hexadecimal 3287D3, to the Base Map color box. Create Color_Drop with Position (-6, 7, 4) and Scale (1, 1, 1).
2. Add Rigidbody (not Rigidbody 2D) to Color_Drop. Its Sphere Collider is enabled; Rigidbody Use Gravity is ticked.
3. Set Directional Light’s Light Appearance to Color and choose a color, for example Hexadecimal FFF4E0. In Play, Color_Drop falls and comes to rest on the floor. Stop Play and save Arena.
4. The screenshot shows the Unity Editor with the Game view and the added sphere visible. The recording shows Play start, the sphere fall, and Play stop.
5. The LMS submission contains the screenshot, short screen recording, an explanation of the chosen colors, and a note of any help used, including AI tools.

t_50fb228f7c9d.prompt: A Sphere has its Mesh Renderer switched off while its Sphere Collider and Rigidbody remain enabled. What should happen during Play?

choices.text: It stays visible but falls through other objects.
It becomes invisible and passes through other objects.
It stays visible and no longer falls.
It becomes invisible but still falls and collides.

t_50fb228f7c9d.explanation: The Mesh Renderer draws the Sphere. The Sphere Collider provides its solid shape, and the Rigidbody lets physics move it. Turning off the renderer does not turn off the other components. Go back to Build the arena and read its components.

t_faa59eb08394.prompt: Which control sets the surface color of a material in this project?

choices.text: An Albedo field in the material Inspector
The color box in the Directional Light’s Emission section
The color box beside Base Map in the material Inspector
The checkbox beside Mesh Renderer in the object Inspector

t_faa59eb08394.explanation: The material’s color is set with the color box beside Base Map. This version has no Albedo field. The Directional Light’s color changes the light, and the Mesh Renderer checkbox turns drawing on or off. Go back to Color the arena with materials and Light the arena.

t_ec050264e550.prompt: A ball with an enabled Rigidbody falls and bounces off a ramp even when its Sphere Collider is switched off.

choices.text: True
False

t_ec050264e550.explanation: The Rigidbody can make the ball fall, but without its Sphere Collider the ball has no solid shape for the ramp to hit. It falls through. Go back to Test what a Rigidbody and a collider each do.

t_488cf0d6097d.prompt: A Cube platform has a Box Collider but no Rigidbody. Why does it stay in place when you press Play?

choices.text: The Box Collider enables gravity-driven motion; a Rigidbody supplies a shape.
The Box Collider supplies a shape; a Rigidbody enables gravity-driven motion.
The Mesh Renderer enables gravity-driven motion; a Box Collider supplies a shape.
The Transform enables gravity-driven motion; a Rigidbody supplies a shape.

t_488cf0d6097d.explanation: A collider defines the solid shape used in physics. A Rigidbody lets physics apply gravity and move the object. A Mesh Renderer draws the object, and a Transform stores its position, rotation, and scale. Go back to Make the ball and the ramp, and add a Rigidbody.

t_de50e8bada38.prompt: Changing a material’s Base Map color can change how its surface looks even when the scene’s light color stays the same.

choices.text: True
False

t_de50e8bada38.explanation: The material sets the surface color, while the light has its own color. What you see depends on both, so changing the material can change its appearance while the light stays the same. Go back to Color the arena with materials and Light the arena.
